chapters.title: On the Outskirts of Manoharpuri
paragraphs: On the Outskirts of Manoharpuri Manoharpuri is about ten miles from Suvarnapur. In ancient times it was a great city and the capital of learned, independent and able kings. Over time, these kings were vanquished by the mleccha. All that remained of this once glorious and flourishing city was a village, and with that its name also came to be corrupted—people called it Manohariyu or Manoriyu. In the present time, it formed part of the territories of the kingdom of Ratnanagari. The Karbhari of Ratnanagari, Vidya Chatura was born in this same village. Vidya Chatura’s maternal family and his wife Gunasundari’s parents belonged to this village. The couple had spent their childhood and adolescence here. For this and other reasons, they were both very attached to Manoharpuri. The village had revived through their efforts and was well looked after by the Karbhari, who was learned and endowed with a historical sensibility. Albeit its manmade glory had been destroyed, the village was still widely known for its natural beauty. Manoharpuri was situated on the borders of Suvarnapur, Ratnanagari and the territories of British India. On its west was the sea, forming a natural boundary. The westerly winds brought cool breezes which eased the impossible heat of summer. On its eastern side, there was a large mango grove, huge banyan trees and sugarcane fields. To its north were the hills of Sundargiri. It was flanked by dense forests on the other two sides. Tall taad trees on the southern side enhanced the beauty of the village. A tributary of river Subhadra meandered through the region from the east to the south. The river nurtured a diversity of flora and fauna in the forest. Leaves and fruits of the teak trees were carried by its sluggish flow until it met with the sea. It was Shukla Paksha, the fortnight of the waxing moon in the month of Chaitra which signalled the passage of spring and the onset of summer. The mango grove was fragrant with mango blossoms. The road from Suvarnapur, which separated the grove from the taad forest, skirted around the forest to reach Manoharpuri. Dusk, hitherto hidden in the forest, now emerged fearlessly to roll the sun down behind the taad trees. The rays of the setting sun lingered over the tree tops as their long yellowish green leaves fluttered like so many flags. At this hour, a slow-moving cart could be seen on the dusty but now cool road. Dear reader, this was the selfsame cart in which Sarasvatichandra had set out from Rajeshwar Mahadev. The cart driver was also the same; but neither Sarasvatichandra nor the other passengers were to be seen in the cart. The lone ascetic who was last seen walking alongside the cart now sat inside it. The bullocks who knew nothing of the events that had taken place in the interim were glad to carry a lighter load and pulled with renewed vigour as they neared their resting place. The cart driver and the ascetic joked and laughed with each other as the cart moved along lurching noisily. The ascetic’s staff which he had carried in his hand while walking now rested on one side of the cart; one end of it was smeared with blood. The driver appeared calm and composed but the ascetic seemed anxious, his alert eyes constantly darting in all directions. The three riders who had been following the cart from Suvarnapur were nowhere to be seen. They were part of the contingent that had gone to Suvarnapur to accompany Kumud Sundari on her proposed journey to Bhadreshwar. Concerned by Sarasvatichandra’s sudden departure, Kumud Sundari had sent Abdullah, Fatehsinh and Harbhamji to follow him. The beating of drums and the shouting had also ceased. The mango grove was in British territory. The teak forest was in the territory of Suvarnapur. The road led to Manoharpuri. Roads from three directions met at that spot. A lane oriented east to west met the road that came from the south. As darkness descended to embrace the earth, the cart now lurched to a halt under a banyan tree at this three‑way junction as instructed by the ascetic. The cart driver unyoked the bullocks and he and the ascetic conversed softly in the falling dark. The moon peeped out briefly from the clouds and withdrew. Cart driver:  ‘Thakore, let me go now. The danger is three-fold here. You are a free man, but I will lose my house and all else besides!’ Ascetic:  ‘Be quiet! My right leg pains to the bone. That Harbham’s blow was hard. I cannot walk. I need to cross the mango grove and reach Virpur. I need you to take me there in your cart.’ Cart driver:  ‘And which father of yours is going to give you shelter in Virpur? Rana Khachar will arrest us both and hand us over.’ Ascetic:  ‘Never! You do not know the reach of this Sursinh. These hands have rocked Bhupsinh’s throne and given sleepless nights to Buddhidhan. Wait for two days and watch the havoc I wreck.’ Cart driver:  ‘What will you do in Virpur?’ Sursinh:  ‘Rana Khachar is our supporter. You have no cause for worry. He might say whatever he likes to the British and write all the reports they want, but he won’t allow even a hair on my body to be harmed.’ Cart driver:  ‘And what do you intend to do with those brahmin and bania passengers?’ Sursinh evaded the query. Just then a bugle was heard in the distance. Sursinh responded with a fox-like call. In a short while, footfalls could be heard. Sursinh went and stood near the hanging roots of the banyan and lit his clay pipe. Soon, some men approached the tree and sat down under it. One of them sat near the hanging roots to keep watch along with the cart driver. There were no strangers among them. They opened their heart and spoke freely. There was a soft rustle of leaves from above as if someone were hiding in the tree. Sursinh looked up sharply, straining his ears to catch the slightest sound as he lit his pipe again. Just the wind. Reassured, he joined in the conversation. Something shone like a fire fly in the light of his pipe but no one noticed. As the darkness enveloped them, the outlaws became engrossed in their talk. The wind carried their softly spoken words upwards.
chapters.summary: An injured Sursinh, traveling by cart, anxiously meets shadowy figures under a banyan tree on Manoharpuri's outskirts, hinting at a dangerous plot.

chapters.title: The Outlaws
paragraphs: The Outlaws In a short time, about fifty to seventy-five persons gathered under the banyan tree. No one spoke at first. Only footfalls and the clink of weapons broke the silence. One man lit a torch and went around to each man present, peering closely at their faces to ascertain their identity. He then sat down close to Sursinh. Four or five men with lit torches stood encircling the group. Four others with loaded guns stood guard around the banyan. All of them had stout bodies. Some were short, some were tall and some broad, but all of them looked brave. They carried an assortment of weapons; some were of olden times while others were of more recent make. Four elderly and two young garasias sat in a circle around Sursinh along with a brahmin. The elder of the two young men spoke first. ‘Bapa, Buddhidhan is caught in our net. His son’s wife has set out for Bhadreshwar. If Goddess Amba is with us, she will be in our clutches by early morning. We will capture her right here at this banyan tree. He has snatched away our Dhirpur, but he will not be able to stomach it. It will be like a fly he has swallowed.’ The brahmin came closer and said, ‘Thakore, Pratapsinh Bapu is right, but you must listen to what a brahmin has to say. If you take that woman captive, you will make another enemy. You will gain nothing by making an enemy of Ratnanagari. The decision is yours, but mine is the counsel of a cautious brahmin’. Pratapsinh’s younger and more intelligent brother Vaghji said, ‘Bapa, Shankar Maharaj is right. It is our norm that we do not harass women and children. People support us because of our adherence to these norms. If we do what Pratapjibhai suggests, we will lose their support’. Pratapsinh spoke up angrily, ‘Vaghji, you are still incapable of thinking right! Rana Khachar harbours greater enmity towards Vidya Chatura than towards Bhupsinh. Therefore, he extends greater support to Samant Mulu than he does to us. If we were to join hands with Samant Mulu, Khachar would support us even more’. Vaghji looked at his brother, perplexed. Maniraj was the king of Ratnanagari. Samant Mulu was waging a baharvatu against him. Kumud Sundari was Vidya Chatura’s daughter; taking her captive would have strengthened the friendship between Sursinh and Samant Mulu. This was obvious, but it was not the real motive behind Pratapsinh’s suggestion. He was a lascivious man; he wanted to satisfy his desire for Kumud by capturing her. His father’s interest was secondary to his passion. Sursinh understood what Vaghji alluded to. He felt differently. Sursinh was a bhayat, a cousin of Jadsinh. Shathrai had snatched away Dhirpur from him. Denied justice, Sursinh had taken to baharvatu and become an outlaw. Bhupsinh and Sursinh had once shared an affectionate relationship. Sursinh expected that his garas would be reinstated to him once Bhupsinh became the ruler. But Shathrai was careful not to allow the two cousins to meet. Last year, Sursinh had sent a secret message to Bhupsinh, to which Bhupsinh had replied: ‘Be patient. It will be done in due course of time’. Sursinh had refrained from causing any harm to Bhupsinh. Bhupsinh wanted to get rid of Shathrai before taking any action. Sursinh was unaware of this; his patience ran its course and goaded and encouraged by Shathrai, he started robbing people so as to intimidate Bhupsinh and force his hand. Sursinh’s plan was to get his men to hold Kumud Sundari captive but conceal his own participation in the plot. His intention was to ensure Kumud Sundari’s safe return and thereby regain his garas from a grateful and frightened Buddhidhan in exchange for her. Pratap cared little for his father’s wishes. If his desires were to be thwarted, Pratap was capable of spoiling the entire plan. Sursinh wanted to keep both his sons quiet. He ignored their advice and asked an elderly band member, ‘Bhimji, so what news have you brought for us? Chandandas, do also update us’. Bhimji was an elderly garasia. His Rajput blood had cooled with age and wisdom. He had joined ranks with Sursinh out of pure and selfless affection. He was a leader of a special group of outlaws and trusted by all members of the group. He was in charge of the bordering regions of Ratnanagari and Suvarnapur. It was Bhimji who had attacked the carriage by which Chandrakant was travelling. Chandandas, though a bania, was a stout warrior. Through his close contact with Rajputs, he had also acquired some of their qualities. The only difference was that he did not like to use force until he had exhausted all possibilities of conciliation, bribery and dissension to win over an adversary. It was contrary to his nature to pick up a quarrel, unless his interest was violated. When the cart carrying Sarasvatichandra left the fields behind and reached the part where the mango grove and taad forests began, it was about three in the afternoon. Chandandas was hiding in the forest with his group of outlaws and waiting for Sursinh, who had gone to ascertain the situation in Suvarnapur disguised as an ascetic. Sursinh had met Shathrai in the prison. He had established direct contact with Garbaddas and arranged for an exchange of letters. He knew that Sarasvatichandra was among the select group that had met at the Suvarnapur palace on the evening of the fateful day. He had assumed that capturing Sarasvatichandra would be advantageous for them, and had followed the cart. When the cart reached the forest area, Sursinh walked faster and overtook the cart. On a signal from him, Chandandas came out of hiding and attacked the cart with eight outlaws. One man cut loose the bullocks. The cart driver stood aside shaking with fear and said, ‘Bapa! The bania, brahmin passengers are no match for you. Do not kill or hurt unnecessarily. They will give you whatever they have and will do as told. I am just a poor cart driver’. One outlaw picked up the bania and flung him to the ground. The bania started to weep loudly. The young woman was frightened. In her hurry to climb out of the cart as told, she fell down. A few ornaments on her body fell to the ground and two outlaws promptly gathered them. Stunned by her fall and fear, the young woman could neither move nor speak. Her tongue got caught between her teeth and she sobbed helplessly. One man caught the poor woman by her neck and pinned her down; she all but lost consciousness. The old woman proved to be the most astute. She had some money tied in a small cloth; it was easy to conceal it in her clothes. She left all her belongings in the cart and climbed out. She stood to one side and said, ‘Bha, I have come out with nothing but the clothes on my body. All my belongings are inside. Take whatever you want. I am a brahmin, I should be seeking alms from you. But take whatever you like if you ought to do so’. ‘Shut up, old wretch!’ One outlaw came forward to slap her. But she moved away and meekly said, ‘Bha, kill me if you want to. I will die in a year or two anyway. Death can come today if you so wish. You too shall be old one day. Like me, may you live to be a hundred years old, son’. The outlaw was taken aback by this speech. He glared at the old woman sternly, but he let her be. The old woman thought, If I try to flee now, I will be in danger. But if I just stand quietly, what can they do to me? She sat down on a stone by the roadside and watched the spectacle in silence. Sarasvatichandra, as you will recall dear reader, was fast asleep in the cart. A dhoti covered him from head to toe. His body was still feverish from the heat and dust of the journey, and his mind, with thoughts of Kumud Sundari. The dream-filled sleep had quietened him somewhat when the sudden commotion jolted him awake. He saw the bania couple in trouble and jumped to the young woman’s aid. He knew he was powerless against the outlaws, yet he somehow managed to free the woman from the outlaw’s grasp. But he was promptly encircled by the men. How could an unarmed, delicate young man confront a gang of outlaws? Sursinh watched all this from a distance, amused. He laughed and said, ‘Chandandas, now stop this drama. Let the women go. Take the men captive. Chandarbhai, I know you well. Go with them’. Sarasvatichandra was angry but did not know what to make of it all. He stood there, clenching his fists.

‘Chandarbhai, we don’t want to rob you. I know who you are. I have some work with you. Please go with them.’ Sarasvatichandra stood there unmoving. Sursinh saw three riders approaching and shouted an alert, ‘Chandan, get going now. Drag this young man away and keep an eye on him. If he doesn’t listen, use force. He is a wretched brahmin, won’t budge without a beating’. As Sarasvatichandra was being dragged away by Chandandas and his men, the three riders reached the spot. Sursinh challenged them to a fight. Sarasvatichandra struggled to free himself from his captors. Sursinh hit him hard with his staff and knocked him unconscious and bleeding. The outlaws swiftly carried away his inert body with the three riders in hot pursuit. We know that Sursinh was also hurt by a blow on his calf and that he travelled by the cart. But what happened to Sarasvatichandra? Chandandas had not brought him to the meeting under the banyan tree. Kumud Sundari had sent three riders to follow Sarasvatichandra. They were only three, but they were brave, carried superior weapons and were riding sturdy horses. They pursued the outlaws energetically. The outlaws were certainly more in number; but they were all foot soldiers, they had gone hungry for three days, their weapons were no match for the riders and they were weary of ten long years of futile baharvatu. They had joined Sursinh’s band out of false pride. They found carrying two men burdensome, pointless and dangerous while being pursued by powerful riders. Chandandas thought like a bania. He could not imagine that Sursinh could have any other motive but robbery for capturing these travellers. These men are beggars, he thought, let them be. He dumped them on a grassy patch of land and fled. The riders did not realise that Chandandas had abandoned Sarasvatichandra. They followed Chandandas who made good his escape. Dejected, the riders gave up the chase and headed towards Manoharpuri. A hesitant and frightened Chandandas now related all these events to Sursinh under the banyan tree. Having heard his account, Sursinh said, ‘Chandandas, you are brave, but you are a bania after all. You may understand something of political matters, but you think like a trader. You acted within the limits of your capabilities. It is for the king to judge if the person he assigns to a task is capable of fulfilling it. You did what you were capable of. It is not your shortcoming. The mistake was mine that I gave you the task. Truly, for ten long years I have ceased to be a ruler and become an outlaw. How can I think like a ruler? If I had any intelligence and foresight left, what could I have not achieved in company of brave and proud associates like all of you?’ Sursinh was dejected. The big chance had slipped out of his hands. He turned to Bhimji. ‘Bhimji Bha, do you have anything better to report? Fate helps those who are ascendant and turns against those who are falling. Tell us, no matter how unpleasant the news might be.’ Old Bhimji came forward. He looked straight at Sursinh and spoke: ‘Sursinh, your father faced much greater hardships. But he was not weak-hearted like you. He was strong. If you are defeated by so little, what will you achieve? It is your duty to give courage to others. Bapa, aren’t you, the son of a Rajput, ashamed of such weak words? Those who ride a horse will fall. Those who never do so will not. Be patient. You may have to endure fifty years in such a state. At least the forest gives us food. What if you had to go into hiding in the barren mountain caves for a few years? Will a bania or a brahmin ever face such hardship? A Rajput is not a Rajput just by wielding a sword. A Rajput can laugh in the face of hardship, the greater the hardship, the greater his resolve. He gains his strength from suffering. A Rajput may worry about himself alone, but a Rajput king worries about the welfare of his subjects, too. Haven’t you seen a lion cub growl at dark rain clouds? Sursinh, you are a lion cub. Remember who you are. Remember your father. Your mother. The family you belong to. So long as you do not give up this soft-heartedness of a bania-brahmin and be true to yourself and to your ancestors, I will say nothing. If you are such a weakling, the sun may well rise in the west. Who would see you as a Rajput? If I be with you, I would defile myself. I may be old, but I am a Rajput. I served your father, and I served you as long as you remained a Rajput. Let out a roar and prove that you are still the brave fearless Sursinh I once knew. I have nothing more to say till then’. Bhimji turned his back towards Sursinh and sat down.

Sursinh caught the old man’s shoulder and pleaded with him, ‘Bhimji Bha!’ ‘Bapa, I don’t wish to be either a father or a mother figure to you. I recognise only Rajputs as kin and no one else. Tell me that Sursinh has not lost his courage.’ Sursinh got up and faced Bhimji. He held Bhimji’s hands and said, ‘Bhimji Bha, rise! I acted like a bania with a bania. Don’t think that I too have become one. Chandandas, if you do not have raging hot blood in you, open your veins and take some of mine. It is true that when the chief of an army loses heart, his army is certain to be destroyed. An army is a fighting body; its chief is the soul. The chief ’s valour is the hot blood that flows through his army. That blood runs in my veins. I am not going to accept Bhupsinh’s promises. The Karbhari can be anyone—Shathrai or Buddhidhan. How does that concern me? My only objective is to reclaim Dhirpur. My group has been wandering in the wilderness for ten long years. My soul tells me that this is about to end. Bhimji Bha, forget everything else and tell us what we should do and where we should use our force. My young blood can fight, but it needs the guidance of the old’. Bhimji stood up, embraced Sursinh and asked, ‘What is to be done?’ The hot Rajput blood cooled somewhat. ‘Bha, war is not about jumping into fire. Some people were on their way from Ratnanagari to Suvarnapur. We robbed them. But at times, the fate of the outlaws also forsakes them. They had nothing apart from these bags. The bags contained clothes in the style of sahibs and some papers. We kept the goods and let the people go. We had hoped to be able to buy at least food to last us fifteen days. But these clothes and papers are so useless even a bania won’t buy them from us. I feel that we should stop striking in the air. We are not so strong that we can bring the ruler to his knees just by robbing people. We have men, but hungry legs and unarmed hands have no power. We must change our tactics. We should take Shathrai’s help. Earlier we robbed his money; now we should accept what he gives. We should be careful about the information he gives us. Bhupsinh may make promises, but once he has the throne, he and us cannot be equal. We should enter the palace with Shathrai’s help one night and take what we want. But the time is not ripe for such an adventure. ‘I like Pratap Bapu’s proposal. There is some merit in Vaghji’s caution, but once Buddhidhan is in our grip, we can get him to do what we want, can’t we? Even Vidya Chatura will not hesitate in satisfying our demands. We must look after his daughter well once we capture her. If we do that, she may have a good word to say about us once she is released. If that happens, the enmity would come to an end. Vaghji Bha, do you have any objection? If anyone else has different views, voice them now.’ Vaghji did not reply. The others sat in quiet anticipation. Sursinh turned to Bhimji and softly said, ‘Shathrai is useless for the present. I found that out yesterday’. Bhimji responded aloud, ‘We must do as decided. We should not waste this opportunity’. The whole group got up. Sursinh announced, ‘We shall meet early in the morning on this side of the Subhadra river. Bhimji, you take position in the ravines. Chandandas, you keep watch over this road; you must signal when you see the party approach. One man should hide in a large leafy tree near the bridge on the river with a drum. All must act on the signal of the drum. Pratap, you hide in the mango grove and come out at the right time. Vaghji, you guard this side of the banyan tree. I will move around in all directions. All men must stay dispersed and come together only when the time is right. It is beyond doubt that Lord Shankar is with us. Our years of hardship are about to end. ‘Chandandas, I spent the day in Suvarnapur. Our plan will bear fruit. Kumud Sundari is accompanied by only about ten riders from Ratnanagari. There is a difference though; we are like paupers while they are well-armed. Some of Buddhidhan’s men may be with the group as well. We must be cautious. If we do not succeed in our plan tomorrow, we shall never succeed. Then we must give up all hopes of Dhirpur. My brave companions, my brothers, you have stood beside me for years in sorrow and hardship. You have wandered through woods and forests with me. You have for my sake walked on thorns.

You have waged battles in the sinking mud of the river. You have stayed without shade in the blazing heat of summer and without warmth in the bitter cold of winter. You have waded through quicksand and braved torrential rains. You have not been frightened by the roars of lions. You have gone hungry for days and faced starvation even in absence of a famine. You have been shelterless at home and away from home. You have not met your wives nor served your parents. You have spent so many years in such harsh conditions. How can I ever repay you? You have done so much for me. I ask you for this one last thing: capture the enemy so I can give to you your due happiness! Our trials and woes are about to end! Jai Ambe! Jogini Maiya, we cannot do without your blessings. Jogini! Amba! Bhavani! Jai, Jai!’ All shouted in unison, ‘Ambe Mata ki jai!’ Their voices pierced the night and the darkness trembled. Talking excitedly among themselves, the outlaws dispersed. Only two men stayed back. The villagers of Manoharpuri had for long seen torch flames come together under the old banyan on some nights and had heard voices. They believed it was the ghosts of soldiers long dead. Hence, no one was suspicious of these gatherings. Soon, silence reigned under the banyan tree once more. Vaghji and Shankar Maharaj sat in the dark, speaking in low voices. ‘Vaghji Bapu, it seems your brother’s ploy has worked. Sursinh Bapa has not realised that Pratap lusts after Kumud Sundari.’ ‘Shankar, I know that. I will not be able to go where the confrontation is to take place, or else I would have taken control of the situation. I must do the task I am assigned. You go. I will go and meet father.’ Saying so, Vaghji left. Alone, Shankar Maharaj talked aloud to himself: Buddhidhanbhai, these people have failed to recognise you. I must go and warn the group accompanying Kumud Sundari. These people do not know your generosity, Buddhidhanbhai. They will now know your wrath. So be it. I know what I must do. Saying so, the athletic brahmin warrior moved like a gazelle through the dark and disappeared. Someone quietly slid down the tree.
chapters.summary: Under a banyan tree, Sursinh's outlaws plot to capture Kumud Sundari, while Sarasvatichandra faces a brutal attack.

chapters.title: The Injured Man
paragraphs: The Injured Man The endeavour to transform the pining lover into a renouncer has begun. You can see it all, and yet you cry foolishly! Having forsaken riches as illusion, what is it you now seek to grasp? You can see it all, and yet you cry foolishly! Chandandas and his men abandoned Sarasvatichandra and the bania on the grassy knoll. Sarasvatichandra was bleeding from his hand and still unconscious. But not a hair on the cunning bania’s body was harmed. The bania was a resident of Ratnanagari. His name was Aarthdas. He belonged to a family of petty grocers but he had made some money from speculation. He was hooked to it and had amassed about forty, fifty thousand rupees. His fortune turned; he lost his all and incurred debts. He tried his luck in Bombay, but failed. He chanced his hand at different things in different places, but to no avail. During his few days of prosperity, he married a dark-complexioned woman called Dhankaur. His family had a low social standing and hence had to pay about eight thousand rupees to Dhankaur’s father as the bride price for the marriage. Dhankaur had amassed about eight thousand rupees by sheer duplicity. She had lied, stolen and demanded money from her husband, and did not let him lay a finger on the money. And today, Dhankaur was lost along with all the ornaments on her body. As Sarasvatichandra lay unconscious and bleeding, Aarthdas mourned his misfortune. When he married Dhankaur she was seven or eight years of age, and eleven when she came to live with him. She was sly, lied easily and was greedy. Aarthdas was a good match for her. The man wouldn’t part with a pie, while she would want to steal two pies from him. He would scold her, but secretly he felt pleased. The rand is clever, he thought. She is cunning enough even to fool me! Let her steal and hide all she wants. When the creditors come and take it all, what she has amassed will stay. But Dhankaur proved to be so covetous that she wouldn’t part with a pie even if her husband were about to die. Aarthdas tried all his tricks, but in vain. He accepted defeat but felt satisfied. The rand is a tough nut to crack, he thought; she is the perfect match for me. Dhankaur was a consummate miser. She was a terror in the house. She could even make her mother-in-law weep; she would not allow the husband’s sister to cross the threshold of her house; she would mock the elder sister-in-law and get the younger one to do all the household chores. She would bark like a rabid bitch at her brother-in-law and then go and weep copious tears before her husband. Thus she ruled over the house. Dhankaur had one quality, however—she was not debauched. Her tendency to lie had created a genuine possibility that she would become debauched. But Aarthdas had given her a free rein in the house. She became so immersed in the household that her other tendencies had no scope of flourishing. Her greed for money overpowered her lust. So, though an annoying nag, Dhankaur was respected and tolerated by everyone in the household because she never budged an inch when she was right. Aarthdas was anxious about her. Who knows where she is now, how she is, but that rand has all the ornaments. Manoharpuri is nearby; there is nothing to worry about. But she is a woman after all; her body and her ornaments are both endangered. The rand will get a good and proper thrashing today. The outlaws must have given her a hard time. But she is a good match for them. Let her face some hardship; the bitch has tied up all her money and won’t give me any even to buy poison with. But then all her gold ornaments will be robbed. And however bad she might be, she is still childlike, isn’t she? What will they do to her? Alas, I won’t ever get another like her! Aarthdas’ mind was buzzing with such varied and contrary thoughts. He glanced at Sarasvatichandra lying unconscious on the ground and felt sorry. He decided to revive him. Then he thought, Is he alive or dead? Shouldn’t I better go home? What if other outlaws arrive? Why should I invite trouble for myself? Then he remembered that it was while trying to rescue Dhankaur that Sarasvatichandra got wounded. His sense of gratitude proved more powerful than his selfishness. The bania approached the unconscious brahmin, his heart brimming with compassion. Sarasvatichandra had lost a lot of blood, but for some reason he had stopped bleeding. Aarthdas brought some water from a pond nearby, sprinkled it on Sarasvatichandra’s face and revived him. Sarasvatichandra opened his eyes and looked around the unfamiliar place. He seemed timid, frail and sorry. The weakness of injury, fever, fatigue, hunger and being in strange surroundings had given rise to this disoriented state. His father’s hurtful words still echoed in his ears; he had found the ill-will towards Kumud Sundari intolerable; he had wept like a child before Chandrakant; he had abandoned immense wealth and luxuries; he was heartbroken when he had to abandon Kumud Sundari. And yet in his moment of renunciation, he had not once regretted his decision or hesitated. His faith in God was so deep that he never asked the question: What will become of Kumud Sundari? His innate sense of renunciation was strengthened by his Indian learning while his Western education had given him the autonomy and the will to take the final step. Sarasvatichandra, as we know, was born into wealth. This wealth had made his desire for renunciation so acute that to many, he appeared haughty. To his mind, wealthy merchants or gentlemen with a vast following were like subalterns who had earned some familiarity with the British. Even prostitutes possessed both wealth and admirers, he knew; he therefore did not consider his wealth and admirers of great value. He believed that high British officials, governors and even princes were mere playthings in the hands of time. He described newspapers and writers as ‘bards of reform’ and considered them useful only to that extent. But he refused to consider their views any more important than views expressed by a friend or even by a rank commoner during conversation. He knew very well how the world would judge his adventure; he knew the opinions that the advocates of both the old and new ways of thinking would advance. His dearest friend Chandrakant had also put forth his views; yet Sarasvatichandra had remained steadfast in his decision. We know this. Sarasvatichandra believed that Time was like a great potter who created difficult situations which produced in men a sense of their own insignificance and smallness. This sense of insignificance also corresponds to one’s external context. Under different circumstances, individuals fail to realise that they are embodied beings and to recognise their own insignificance as also the salience of others. Sarasvatichandra knew that this was true for him as well. A person who was important in one context was not so in another. There was hierarchy and a sense of high and low everywhere. Born into wealth, he imagined that all the wealthy were suffused with nobility. These ideas had matured with education and age. His learning, his poetic imagination told him that a sense of inadequacy and a sense of nobility could not exist together at one place. ‘To possess a sense of relative importance and unimportance of persons, things and events was a sign of inadequacy, and to be conscious of the world and its joys was the only true wealth, the only sign of nobility.’ Sarasvatichandra was possessed by this definition. Its power had startled his mind and dragged him into deep dark difficulties. We must still wait for the divine being who shall tell us how our schools and universities show stars to our youth and lead them astray. In such a situation, those who are mere spectators of this drama may find the movement of the actors magical. How is the world, in deep slumber of night, to imagine what the next day will be like? They might even consider the unfolding events and actors as merely imaginary. Until the curtain rises and the drama begins to unfold, for a spectator it is all imaginary. In countries where the curtain has been lifted and the drama has begun, it has seemed strange to onlookers. The same strangeness will be felt in this country as well. Only God can tell what the offspring of this inter‑racial marriage of Sanskrit knowledge and Western learning will be like. Sarasvatichandra imagined himself to be a child of just such a marriage. He could do the unexpected, tread paths untrodden because of his nobility. He now described his renunciation as an act of nobility. To be an aesthete but also a renouncer, to put his sacrifice on trial, to visit Suvarnapur to test his hypothesis that Kumud would adjust to the new situation, forget her past and be happy—all these acts were a test of his own character and nobility. It was not his intention to be a cause of Kumud’s sorrow; that was accidental. He realised that: I have been the cause of so much sorrow, and that bodily passions are difficult to curb. With this realisation came the understanding that: I am foolish, my nobility lacks something, and human beings are inherently weak. He had experienced strongly conflicting emotions at the time of leaving home, attachment and dislike, anger and sorrow; and yet his act of renunciation was also the result of a deeply felt need. Therefore despite deep sorrow, he had hitherto not felt a sense of inadequacy. He felt inadequate and meek now as he regained consciousness. He was utterly alone; he had no one to turn to except the vast sky above and the expanse of earth below. There were trees all around if they could provide him any succour. Sarasvatichandra remembered Kumud Sundari, and for the first time in his life he truly pined for her. It was his first realisation of the hardships he must confront. His body cried out in pain. Richness of mind seemed to him at that moment like smoke—forever beyond grasp. Oh sage, I do not want your knowledge The hungry child craves food, bring that and I will touch your feet Thirsty, feverish, frail and fatigued, the unhappy man looked at the wounds on his body and felt even more wretched. He stared at Aarthdas who seemed to be saying: You reap what you sow. His vacant mind went into a spin when he realised that there was no one who would take pity on him, for they had no reason to. He realised there was no one who would come to his rescue. He felt abandoned even by God. He remembered the lines of an English poet.

And thorns of life; forgetting the great end Of poesy, that it should be a friend To soothe the cares, and lift the thoughts of man.⟨fn:41⟩ Once he had wealth to match Kuber, luxuries to match Indra, respect among men of learning, prestige in a city like Bombay, the companionship of a true friend like Chandrakant, and the divine fragrance of Kumud that combined with the power of renunciation and a sublime song of love. But all that was in the past. What was he now? There was no one in the world from whom he could even beg; he was a beggar among beggars. He did not even possess the ash that a mendicant smears on his body to protect himself from heat and cold. Even fools did not respect him and his social standing was so low that he was abandoned in the forest like a dead fox. In place of a friend he had the bania for a companion, and in place of Kumud, a heartless, dark forest. In place of the serenity of renunciation, he had an orphaned mind and a body in pain. Love had given way to heart- wrenching repentance. Sarasvatichandra felt such emotions surge like waves in his unsteady mind. ‘Keats! Keats! How true you were! Even you had such experiences?’ He spoke these words out aloud and startled the bania. Aarthdas went up to Sarasvatichandra and helped him to sit up. He examined Sarasvatichandra’s wounds and pressed something like cotton to the wounds. Then he asked, ‘Do these outlaws know you? That man disguised as an ascetic had spoken your name’. Aarthdas recalled that the outlaws had called the injured man Chandarbhai. ‘Chandabhai!’ he addressed him, ‘Such is the grace of Thakorji that your wounds are as good as healed. Here, take this’. Sarasvatichandra felt revived at the mere mention of healed wounds. He sat up straight, pondering this further corruption of his name. He asked the bania, ‘Bhai, what is this?’ ‘It is called gha bajariyu, a grass that heals wounds. It grows in this grass and it got stuck to your wounds and stopped the bleeding.’ ‘Oh, is that its quality?’

‘Yes, it heals wounds; your wounds are as good as healed. Are you in pain now?’ ‘No, in fact there is none.’ Sarasvatichandra was overcome with gratitude. He looked up to the sky with misty eyes and murmured to himself, Lord, you ease our trials and tribulations, Never taking to heart our foolish ways As I lay unconscious in the forest, You took on the form of this healing grass. This prayer came to him by itself. He felt a new energy and excitement surge through him, as if God Himself had come to reside in his sad eyes, subdued heart and excited mind. Hitherto he had found all the prayers contained in books, in societies and temples dry and empty of meaning. His suffering had given him his first glimpses of divinity. Sarasvatichandra looked at the bania with grateful eyes, his heart filled with reverence, and the awareness that the bania had acquainted him with his own worthlessness. In a state like that of Dattatreya, he came to believe that the bania had guided him to the path of God; he was the guru who had helped him see God face to face. ‘Bhai, what is your name?’ he asked. The bania was the kind who would give away nothing for free. This proved to be a tough question for him. He thought, That ascetic in disguise knew his name. What if this man is also one of those outlaws? Aarthdas is not so stupid as to reveal his name. He laughed to himself, evaded the question and asked a string of counter-questions, ‘Chandabhai, you will now feel better; it will just take a little longer. But how did you fall in with these people? What is your business? Which native village do you come from? Where are you going?’ ‘You know well where I have come from and you have seen how I came to be in this state.’ ‘But what is your business?’ ‘Business? Eat, drink and travel.’ ‘Oh, is that so?’ The bania became even more suspicious, even fearful. ‘And where do you intend to go from here?’

‘Wherever my fate takes me, bhai. I will gladly come with you if you allow me to; both of us are hungry.’ Aarthdas said to himself: This man is certainly an outlaw. He wants to come to my house. But then why did he jump to her rescue and invite injury? Who knows! He could be an informer of the outlaws and that could explain his behaviour. A fish of selfish waters, the bania could neither imagine nor comprehend selflessness in any form. Sarasvatichandra enquired once again, ‘Bhai, will you take me home with you? I will prove useful to you. I am a stranger in these parts, but you must be well acquainted with all roads’. Aarthdas muttered to himself, Hah! Take you home and invite death? I am Aarthdas. You can’t fool me. I am more than a match for you. But he said, ‘Of course, why not? But on the condition that my wife must be returned to me’. Perplexed, Sarasvatichandra replied, ‘But bhai, how can I do that! Let us go to your house and I will certainly help you look for her’. So crafty! Aarthdas thought and said aloud, ‘All right, Chandabhai. How long can we stay here anyway? Let us go towards the village,’ telling himself, I will take you straight to the Ratnanagari police. After that they can deal with you. They got up and began to walk towards Ratnanagari. On the way, Aarthdas started his drama. He suddenly sat down on the road and started wailing, ‘Oh mother! What will happen to you now?’ Sarasvatichandra was utterly baffled, but tried to comfort the man nevertheless. ‘What is it, bhai? What happened to your mother?’ ‘Oh, they have taken away my wife. The poor woman must be in a wretched state ... Oh mother! Oh my poor wife!’ ‘Be patient, bhai. Let us go to the village. I am sure we will find a way out.’ ‘But she has the ornaments! That is all the wealth I have! I don’t even have a pie to buy poison with. How will I pay the rent? What will I eat? I will have to sell the utensils and everything else. With what will I pay the grocer? How will I pay the state to mount a search for my wife? Oh Chandabhai, I must give up my life right here!’

Sarasvatichandra tried everything he could, but Aarthdas refused to budge. He went on moaning and wailing, ‘I will hang myself right here. If God had made me a brahmin, I could have lived on alms. My stomach churns. I can’t get up. I can’t speak. Oh Chandabhai, a ... bab ... ab ...’ The bania pretended as if his tongue had got stuck. He lay down in the dust, rolling his eyes and dribbling from his mouth. Sarasvatichandra thought: What can I do to relieve this man’s misery? Even my hunger has vanished in his wretchedness. He is not sorry for the loss of his wife. He is bemoaning the loss of his wealth. I had enough riches to end all his miseries, but that I have given up. Little did I realise that wealth could be so useful in ways. God has not given him learning; he was also not born into wealth. My nobility has turned to dust. His only remedy is money. From where shall I get money? If I had not given up my wealth, such a day would never have come. He looked at Aarthdas again and thought, But if I had not given up my wealth, how would I have known that people have miseries such as those of Aarthdas? Sarasvatichandra’s mind cleared and he could think with a calmer head. He remembered the ring tied to his janoi, and his face lit up. Ah, the remedy is at hand! He took out the jewel-studded ring and looked at it. O ring, you were meant to grace Kumud Sundari’s finger. I had you made for the delight of her heart. You would have dazzled on her finger like a little sun. But all that is futile now. You and I are banished from Kumud’s life. The sun is about to set; its light will be sullied. Now you will bring joy to another’s house. That is your destiny. Is there any comparison between Kumud and this bania? No. But I, too, do not deserve you. You were the last gift of my father’s wealth, the last reminder of my beloved Kumud. But the wretched hand that caused her heart to break does not deserve you. My sacred janoi is impure, my body defiled. O ring, the charred ash of my cremated love, I give you away having soiled you with my tears. Go and light up a poor man’s home! Sarasvatichandra sat down beside Aarthdas and slipped the ring onto his finger. And at that instant, the hungry, exhausted, miserable youth pining for his lost beloved suddenly fainted.

Aarthdas had taken Sarasvatichandra for an outlaw. He had staged this drama of poverty and wretchedness to get rid of him. Instead, the drama took an unexpected turn. He peered closely at the jewel encrusted ring. The bania understood nothing. The ring fitted him well. Sarasvatichandra had fainted. His thief-like cunning saw an opportunity. He got up and ran without once looking back.
chapters.summary: Injured Sarasvatichandra, revived by Aarthdas, gifts him a precious ring, only to faint again, leaving the cunning bania to consider his unexpected fortune.

chapters.title: Gunasundari
paragraphs: Gunasundari The outlaws’ selection of the junction where the three roads met was not without reason. It was difficult to capture them as they moved between the boundaries of three states. If they were pursued by the police of one state, they could easily enter another. The road itself had many turns and forks which allowed them to disperse quickly. Moreover, the sea, the hills, the mango grove, the taad forest, the grasslands and the river facilitated quick movement and offered easy and diverse hiding places. Manoharpuri was a small village and its inhabitants were simple-minded. The outlaws did not harass them. The day the outlaws created trouble on the outskirts of Manoharpuri, the village was also bustling with activity. The arrival of newcomers gave some business to the village folks. The same evening on which the outlaws captured and injured Sarasvatichandra, who gave his ring to Aarthdas, who slipped away like a thief, we know that Chandrakant who had set out from Ratnanagari for Suvarnapur was also robbed by the outlaws. On the way Chandrakant had received a message from Vidya Chatura, warning him that the outlaws of Suvarnapur were expected to strike and asking him not to proceed further until the additional soldiers he had dispatched for Chandrakant’s protection reached him. The soldiers from Ratnanagari had also warned him. But impatient to meet Sarasvatichandra, Chandrakant decided to brave the danger. He was robbed, but his life was saved by the soldiers. Forced to halt at Manoharpuri that evening, Chandrakant became a guest of Gunasundari’s once again.

Gunasundari, as we know, was on her way to the temple at Bhadreshwar. There was no danger from outlaws on that side. She had decided to halt at Manoharpuri with her family and retinue. They were all waiting for Kumud Sundari’s arrival. That evening, there were about forty armed riders in Manoharpuri. They included the soldiers accompanying Gunasundari, Chandrakant, and the soldiers stationed at the local post. The three riders sent by Kumud Sundari for Sarasvatichandra’s protection had failed in their mission; dejected, they had turned towards Manoharpuri. On the way they heard rumours that the outlaws were to meet that night under the banyan tree. Harbhamji decided to spy on them and concealed himself in the tree, while his two associates went on to Manoharpuri. Vidya Chatura and his family shared bonds of deep affection with the villagers, who in turn responded with equal warmth. Women of the village would freely approach Gunasundari and share with her their joys and sorrows, their dreams and aspirations and claim her time for many such matters. Occasionally, she, too, would share small details of her family life with them, much to their surprise. Hearing of Gunasundari’s arrival in Manoharpuri, the women rushed towards her rest house like a monsoon river in spate. Religious brahmin women, generous garasia women, bania women adept at running the household with severe economy, industrious Kanbi women, and even the poorest of the poor outcaste women gathered at the back door of the house, talking excitedly among themselves, all eager to meet her. Enthused by the presence of their minister’s wife in their midst, the villagers did all they could to accord due hospitality to her. The peasants were engrossed in conversation with the forty- odd soldiers. They accepted payment from them, as was customary, but provided superior fodder for the horses in return. Some patted the horses, asked after their history and pedigree; some engaged the soldiers in talk about their families; others enquired about news of Vidya Chatura’s staff. As the evening sky turned crimson with the dust raised by cows returning from pasture, the peasants broke into song. Gunasundari witnessed these tranquil and joyous scenes from the raised platform of her rest house and welcomed the women who had gathered in large numbers to meet her.⟨fn:42⟩ The village had a population of about three or four thousand. Most of them were peasants, hardworking and brave. The thanedars and other local administrators dealt with them honestly and justly. The landlords and peasants of Manoharpuri were seen as worthy of emulation by the neighbouring villages. Manoharpuri had a small but well-run school; a few of its students had even gone up to Bombay for further studies. Vidya Chatura followed a strict code: no one in his family should accept anything from the villagers for free. His family’s conduct served as an example for his subordinate officials. The villagers, through their long association with state officials, had cultivated a sense of pride and a superior morality. The agricultural produce of the village was traded by land as well as by sea. This had attracted a few bania merchants to the village. In earlier times, bania money lenders from the surrounding villages had made it their business to lend money to the residents of Manoharpuri and they would visit the village occasionally to collect their repayments. Over time, encouraged by Vidya Chatura and advised and educated by his officials, the peasants learnt from the example of the higher castes how to reduce wasteful expenditure. They also became more industrious and learnt how to economise in both production-related as well as social expenditure like marriage, birth and death rituals. The only tax levied was on the land and this, too, was insignificant. Vidya Chatura encouraged the peasants to lend money to each other. By doing so, they learnt the value of money. As they managed their own money and expenses better and learnt how to accumulate wealth, from debtors the peasants gradually became creditors. This change had several important consequences. Agriculture became an independent and energetic activity. The whole village was motivated to try new experiments and apply intelligence to farming. With the improved living conditions and all-round contentment, the children of the farmers found new pride in the traditional occupation handed down to them by their forefathers. They used their education to make improvements in existing age-old agricultural practices. They were grateful to their prime minister for the low taxes they had to pay and considered themselves more fortunate than villages under British administration. In times of famine and other hardships, the people of Manoharpuri were self-sufficient and hence not a burden on the state exchequer or on the British administered areas. Vidya Chatura was satisfied with all these developments. In India, inspired by a sense of religious obligation, people have dug wells, step wells and ponds, built village squares or chotras and diverse other such structures. The prime minister in his wisdom considered it his duty to encourage this sense of religious obligation. It was not surprising therefore that the people of Manoharpuri felt such deep affection for him. Vidya Chatura wanted nothing for himself. He urged people to pay their taxes honestly and gladly. He also impressed upon them that in times of need the state may be forced to impose higher taxes as taxes were not subject to the people’s will. Vidya Chatura strongly believed that discontentment, bitterness and resentment of the people was far worse than the annexation of the state itself; their goodwill and prosperity was for him far superior to the British Agent’s pleasure or any titles awarded by the British government. He thus endeavoured to cultivate a similar philosophy of governance in the ruler of Ratnanagari, Maniraj. If the state treasury amasses more revenue than the state expends, it amounts to depriving people of their wealth. Rulers tend to misuse this excess revenue while state officials waste it on satisfying their lusts and whimsies, childish aspirations or vain attempts to secure personal glory; they spend it on women, luxuries, sports, expensive crafts, foreign travel, and on foreigners. Such surplus revenue inebriates the ruler’s mind and becomes the envy of neighbouring rulers. Instead, if this surplus wealth is with the people, the state can levy higher taxes in times of crisis and need. And, if the taxes are lowered once the crisis is past, why should the people not have faith in their rulers? Surplus wealth is far safer with the people and hence they should be treated as a ‘bank’. Such was the counsel given by Vidya Chatura to Maniraj, and the king in his wisdom would generously heed his prime minister.

Being under Vidya Chatura’s direct care and supervision, the village of Manoharpuri was an example to be emulated. Other state officials closely followed developments in Manoharpuri as an indication of the desires of the king and his prime minister. Consequently, many villages had prospered. Vidya Chatura had closely studied the governance of British administered provinces and native states. Based on his observations he had formulated a principle that if the administrators of native states have the wisdom, intelligence, conscience and will, they can work for the welfare of the people and uplift the state to a level which subjects under English rulers cannot even dream of; for the British, however well-meaning, are ultimately guided by self-interest alone. Those who have carefully observed and compared the conditions of villages under native states and under British India cannot but conclude that even where the rulers are immoral, selfish and tyrannical, villages under native states still tend to be more prosperous. Vidya Chatura wanted to set an example and demonstrate the heights that people could attain if the rulers were not tyrannical. Gunasundari often heard such talk from her husband. These ideas left a deep impact on her mind. She sought to fulfil his wishes by working for the people of Manoharpuri. This gave him greater joy than even the birth of a son would—he could rest content that the education he had given his wife had borne fruit. And his joy enthused Gunasundari even more. Where two hearts experience the same emotions, the same pleasures and provide mutually nurturing joy, a marriage is said to be consummated in its true sense. Gunasundari was delighted by their marriage. Just as friends who share personal details feel their friendship grow and strengthen, just as a clerk who knows his employer’s trade and business secrets considers himself his confidant, just as a prime minister acts autonomously when he knows his king reposes total confidence in him, just as subjects feel devoted to a righteous and wise king, just as a pure conscience coupled with virtue generates supreme bliss, in the same way Gunasundari knew and understood the thoughts and aspirations of Vidya Chatura. She considered herself his confidante. Secure in his love she acted autonomously; she was devoted to her husband and her love, as distinct from bodily desire, grew and illumined their relationship. Unlettered but intelligent women tend to be expert at household work and social relationships. Gunasundari saw Manoharpuri much as an extension of her household and visited it often to work for the welfare of its poor and illiterate. Children, in imitation of elders, play with their toys as if they are real people and derive great joy from such play. Gunasundari was akin to a child in matters of statecraft. Vidya Chatura observed her experiments in Manoharpuri with great delight; he would express his joy by a squeeze of her hand, a furtive kiss of her fingers and in moments of solitude, an embrace. These moments of togetherness came back to Gunasundari in Manoharpuri. Like a peacock’s feathers ruffled gently by the wind, her heart beat faster at these warm and pleasant memories. Gunasundari was about thirty-five years of age. She had given birth to two daughters who were now grown up. Only careful observers could tell her real age from her face. She had a well-proportioned body, neither slender nor fat. Her complexion was neither golden nor silver. Her features were well formed. Her hair was smooth, black and shiny, and when not tied up in a bun, it reached down to her knees. She had a broad forehead. Though not very large, her eyes were bright, playful and sharp. Her voice was not as refined as Kumud’s but it had the delicacy of a woman’s voice. She could sing as well as Kumud. Both of them were of similar height. Gunasundari was always smiling. There were many who wished to see her face first thing in the morning and believed that their day would pass well if they did so. Like her husband, Gunasundari was hardworking and conscientious. She preferred to do her own work without meddling in the affairs of others. The forbearance and virtues possessed by Kumud Sundari were her inheritance from her mother. So were her childlike eagerness and enthusiasm. Gunasundari loved her family, was always forgiving and bore no malice towards anyone. She had cultivated these qualities through her association with older women from her paternal as well as her in-laws’ family. All those who came in contact with Gunasundari and Vidya Chatura were familiar with these qualities of hers. The people of Manoharpuri believed that Gunasundari had a special place in her heart for them, but no one would ever abuse her kindness as no one could bear to see her unhappy or hurt. This was not a quality that her husband possessed; his position required him to judge the conduct of others and also wield punitive power when necessary. Gunasundari’s natal home was in this village. Vidya Chatura, who was five or seven years older to her, had spent his early years at his maternal household. The house of his maternal grandparents was adjacent to that of Gunasundari’s parents. Even before Gunasundari was born, her mother had a great fondness for little Vidya Chatura. She would play with him, tell him stories, comb his hair, give him food and pamper him. The young boy was playful, sharp and talkative. When a daughter was born to her, she fixed her child’s marriage with the boy without waiting to consult an astrologer. When Gunasundari was old enough to talk, her mother would play with both the children, make them speak lines and enact roles for her own amusement; too young to understand or know any shame, they would happily oblige. But soon afterwards Vidya Chatura’s maternal uncle, who had no children of his own, called him to Ratnanagari for further studies. Vidya Chatura went on to Bombay to complete his education. When he returned to Ratnanagari after his studies, he was twenty-three years old. Gunasundari was about sixteen or seventeen and had been visiting her in-laws’ house for the past three years or so. She would regularly write to her husband while he was in Bombay. In her letters she often composed verses or duha, sakha and garba, much to their mutual pleasure, and she joyfully shared his responses with her friends. Vidya Chatura, who read and studied English and Sanskrit poetry of love and desire, was delighted with these letters of his young betrothed. Their long separation only served to strengthen their love. Marriage in infancy proved for him to be a matter of great joy. So much that Vidya Chatura often wondered later in life if his staunch opposition to child marriage had any basis at all. Our universities have placed books filled with love and longing in the hands of our young men. One result of this is the cultivation of an artificial sense of chivalry towards women. Often, the child bride becomes the recipient of such chivalry. Many women, themselves unlettered, but married to educated men have felt too. Those who have read the first part of the book know how she learnt to read and understand poetry in company of her husband. The couple lived apart during the years that Vidya Chatura spent studying. Gunasundari thus began her conjugal life at an age when both her body and mind had matured and developed, and she was well poised to enter a new phase of life. Soon after he completed his education, Vidya Chatura obtained a teacher’s position in a school in Ratnanagari. His job was undemanding. They did not have a child for another two-three years. This was the best and most blissful period for the young couple. They experienced the heights of passion and love, an intimacy which was at once intellectual, aesthetic and sensual. During these years, the young wife and husband would often sit together after dinner with books. They would read books together, discuss burning political and social issues of the day. The wife would ask pithy and pointed questions, the husband would respond in detail as if engaged in solemn debate. Sometimes the adolescent wife would raise doubts based on her newfound education which would force him to rethink, even change principles he had firmly established for himself. And their intellectual camaraderie would find its fulfilment when he would close the doors of their room and take her to the window overlooking a garden, kiss her lips over and over again and sing, Sleep’s embrace is as delicate as yours: The world rests, enticed by its touch The moon smiles upon this peaceful scene Open your eyes slowly: Look, my beloved! The bright moon moves, clinging to the sky Wait a while: Listen— Hear what the moon whispers to the stars The pleasures of these moments, and many like these, were repeated over many days. Gunasundari heard this poem many times and she not only understood it but her heart and being felt suffused by its meaning. Initially, she was unable to appreciate simple romantic verses like, ‘Touching foreheads we remained/Conversing in soft whispers’, but she soon acquired the sensibility. The experience of understanding a poem, its meaning, the arrangement of words and the ability to take pleasure in it is one kind of aesthetic experience. Some poetic rhythms capture the mind which sways to their cadence just as a serpent sways to a flute. One is immersed in an experience at once intensely erotic and sublime, like the gopis who were captivated by the melody of Krishna’s flute. One who is bound by love experiences a sense of unity and oneness; the poem of Jaydev and Padmavati is a fine example of this. One who is immersed in devotion forgets the world around him. The lives of many saints bear testimony to this. A soul who experiences the supreme bliss of Brahman knows the world to be a dark place and craves only for the one permanent and pure light—such is also the experience of immersing oneself in beautiful poetry. Vidya Chatura held forth in such a manner to Gunasundari that her thirst for aesthetic experience grew stronger with each passing day. That day, the song oft repeated by her husband assumed a life of its own. Perhaps this was due to the familiarity gained by repetition; or because her eyes had been opened by education; or because of the aesthetic lamp lit in her mind and heart by the great poets; or because she was at an age when erotic experiences are deeply felt; or in anticipation of being in bed with her husband; perhaps because of one or all of these reasons, by divine grace as her eyes turned inwards, they saw what they had never seen before—Gunasundari gazed unblinking upon her husband, lovelorn. As he beheld his own perfect tiny image in her shining eyes, Vidya Chatura felt: Today, in the form of a poem, I have entered your heart. Like your eyes, your unwavering heart and your entire being captures my image. He looked at his wife with temperate joy. For both of them this was the first experience of intellectual love. Like a woman experiencing the joys of first pregnancy, Gunasundari spent that day in bliss. She who wrote songs to her husband composed a poem for him, as if she too, like Valmiki, were blessed by God. Once again that night, Vidya Chatura thirsting for that experience recited the same verse. They felt their hearts unite once again, but the experience of oneness was much deeper than before. She responded unabashedly to her husband. Her eyes intent upon his face, she placed her fair and delicate hands on his shoulders like the rays of the new moon that reach out to rain-filled clouds, and was flooded by desire at his touch. She softly began to sing the poem she had composed for him. Bright stars of the night sky My heart sings the song of my love As the moon spreads its light in the sky So your heart spreads its joy within me In the blessed silence of the night Look how Solitude delights in the moon’s company As they are one, my love, be one with me In the moon’s embrace, Silence itself shines forth Look how well they are suited As they are one, my love, be one with me Vidya Chatura was immersed in her song as long as it lasted. As she finished, he felt as if he had a revelation and he saw Gunasundari anew—like the first flowering of erotic desire in an untouched girl. As the young woman abandoned her shyness and opened her heart, he saw her latent poetic abilities emerge. Vidya Chatura was astonished, enthused and delighted at this discovery. He felt that Gunasundari’s poem was more delicate than his and had a natural energy that his own verse lacked. His heart filled with joy and pride as he took both her hands in his and kissed them. Experiences of pure joy are rare and fleeting. As the enchanting night passed, this priceless moment proved to be the first and the last such experience for Vidya Chatura. Vidya Chatura’s maternal uncle Jarashankar called him the very next day. Jarashankar was the private secretary to the then ruler of Ratnanagari, Mallaraj, who was the father of the present ruler Maniraj. The British Agent Buskin Sahib, whom you may recall we have met in the first part of this story, insisted that young prince Maniraj should be taught English. A trustworthy teacher was required. Jarashankar recommended Vidya Chatura, who was made the prince’s tutor. Vidya Chatura was under the impression that he was simply required to be a conventional teacher who taught from a book. But he was wrong, for this proved to be only a secondary task.

Mallaraj was a staunch kshatriya in disposition and physique. He was considered to be the finest example of pure royal lineage among all the native rulers. He had witnessed the early wars with the British at a young age and treacherous diplomacy and enemies both within and outside the state. He liked to first ascertain his final goal and then searched for the means appropriate to accomplish that goal. Statecraft for him was a game of chess, and he played his games accordingly. For him, that was the beginning and end of statecraft. Mallaraj was not acquainted with English learning and hence did not value it. For him, English education was a means to an end. He had no objection if Maniraj were to acquire this means. Mallaraj gave elaborate instructions to Vidya Chatura that he might teach Maniraj English, but that he should under no circumstance forget his principal duty. ‘I give you my prince, but not so that you turn his mind and make him English. He is at an impressionable age— nurture and guide him carefully. I do not want to turn him into a brahmin like you or even a vaishya. Teach him to understand the ways of the brahmin, the vaishya, the mleccha, the English and all others; teach him to fathom their tricks, teach him his duties towards all. But take this as a warning: if I see him acquiring any traits of the English or the brahmin or anyone else, even you, I will take it as a sign of your negligence. Your duty is to imbue him with the qualities of a pure Rajput, a kshatriya. That young prince will be my support in old age. He is the hope of this state, the future of my lineage, the glory of my family; and you, although his teacher, are my servant. He is destined to be a king and not a subject; hence you must make him fit for all his duties. My kshatriya warriors will work with you to develop his body and to enhance his valour. Do not hesitate to ask for any facilities you might need to teach him statecraft. Make Maniraj a king. It is our ancient custom that a Rajput learns his own dharma from a brahmin teacher. I give Maniraj to your care. Jarashankar will tell you what else you need to do in your free time. Remember, Vidya Chatura, you are not to be a school teacher here. Let me list for you the duties of a woman. She raises children, serves elders, takes work from servants, looks after the household and household goods, protects and enhances the family’s prestige and is virtuous. At night a woman must rule over the husband in amorous games. Even an ordinary woman does all this. She must also gracefully bear the brunt of people’s words, silently bear insults and torture in the house, disregard her own suffering and always be generous and forgiving. All women are required to do so. If she fails in her duties, she is neither a woman nor a man. In the art of sex she is called shankhini; such a woman is required to be equally adept in social intercourse. Now tell me, if a woman is required to perform so many duties, how many duties would a man, her master, need to perform! A man who cannot do what a woman does is incompetent and unfit to serve my state. Only one who can perform the duties of a woman as also those of a man is fit to serve my state, and you must acquire that fitness. Secondly, I do not say that you should not be greedy, but your greed should not damage another’s house. My priest often quotes a Sanskrit verse which says that a cow should be milked only after the calf has drunk his due; likewise, a king’s treasury should be filled only after his subjects are content. I say to you that think of your interest only after the interest of the king and his subjects are secure, or else be clear that we shall have nothing to do with each other. Vidya Chatura, I know that you are honest, but honesty is not only about not being corrupt. Experience will teach you that honesty has many other aspects. Such honesty will appear easy to practice; but once you acquire authority you will understand the saying that wealth tempts even the sages. Do not let your pride lead you astray because I have put young Maniraj in your charge. Remember that he is a jewel, but that jewel is placed on the head of a serpent, and you have to deal with the serpent. If the serpent is pleased, it will open the treasure chest for you; but if displeased, death lurks in his bite. Always remember that Mallaraj is like that serpent.’ These words became etched on the heart and mind of the man appointed to be the prince’s tutor. To Vidya Chatura, each word seemed to encompass the wisdom of books. He realised that a man unsheathing his sword from the scabbard must also protect his own fingers. This took possession of his rational mind in such a way that from that day onwards his love of poetry, music, his amorous play on observing and teaching statecraft to Maniraj that he only caught fleeting glimpses of the goings on in his own household, much as one glimpses a falling star. Around the same time, Gunasundari came to be embroiled in the complex web of family relationships and responsibilities. The training she had received from her husband proved useful in untangling this web. Vidya Chatura considered Mallaraj’s advice priceless; he had it written down in a notebook. Gunasundari read these notes and learnt from them how to deal with the situation she suddenly found herself in. Even the erudite learn from the experiences of the intelligent; in fact, one who is learned gains much more than an average person. A library is a key to the thoughts of many scholars. Vidya Chatura believed that learned is one who understands the key to knowledge; others merely possess bookish knowledge. He considered the experiences of the intelligent as valuable as the wisdom contained in books. The excessive kshatriya wisdom of Mallaraj’s first instructions to him as a tutor left a lasting impression on Vidya Chatura. He considered the king’s pride in his rule and his kingdom worthy of devotion. And just as a bee collects honey from a flower considered beautiful by all, Vidya Chatura took vital lessons from Mallaraj, which came to form the seed of his morality. While he found them most instructive in statecraft, Gunasundari used these same lessons in the domain of the household. As we know, Vidya Chatura was raised in his maternal household as his maternal uncle Jarashankar had no children of his own. At the time of Vidya Chatura’s birth, his father Manchatura was about thirty- five years old and a clerk in the office of a mamlatdar or revenue officer in a British administered area. Though not highly educated, Manchatura was considered intelligent. Those who believed that the intelligent are more prone to youthful excesses would give Manchatura’s example— he could not restrain his debauchery even in old age, contracted a grave and incurable disease, had to resign his post and was forced to go and live with Vidya Chatura. Vidya Chatura had four elder siblings: two brothers and two sisters. Manchatura’s eldest son had died young; his widow Sundargauri lived with her parents. When Sundargauri’s parents died, her brother and sister-in-law had no use for her. One day they beat her and drove her out of the house. Hungry, thirsty, Sundargauri spent the entire night on the doorstep, shedding copious tears. Gunasundari came to know of this, and she went and brought home her elder sister-in-law who had nowhere else to go. Ganchatura, Gunasundari’s other brother-in-law, was ten to twelve years older than Vidya Chatura. Spoilt by the father, Ganchatura had adopted all his bad habits and taken to a life of pleasure from a young age; repeated attempts to educate him had failed. After much pleading with the mamlatdar, his father had obtained the position of a talati, a village revenue official, for him. Ganchatura had several addictions and expensive habits. He saved nothing. There were also rumours about his relations with the wife of the village headman, who thus had cause to harbour animosity towards him. One day, Ganchatura took four- five annas from a farmer as bribe. The headman made a ‘report’ of this to the mamlatdar and got him suspended. Ganchatura was forced to return to Ratnanagari with his wife Chandika and four children, and became Gunasundari’s guest. Vidya Chatura’s elder sister Dukhba was married to Sahasrai who had incurred several debts in business. Sahasrai began to speculate in the hope of paying off his debts; instead he incurred even heavier debts which were beyond his capacity to repay. Harassed and ashamed, he left town and went into hiding, sending his wife Dukhba to her brother’s house. They had a daughter of marriageable age, Kumari. Dukhba was unhappy and anxious about the bleak prospects of Kumari’s marriage. Unable to share her concerns with her brother and sister-in-law, Dukhba withered with a sorrow that gnawed at her every day. Vidya Chatura’s other sister Chanchalba was widowed around the same time. She had the qualities of her name; she was quick with household work but proud and had a habit of lying. Therefore, she found no place at her in-laws’ and was tolerated only as there were no other women to look after household chores. Once her young sister-in- law grew up and learnt to manage the house, her brother-in-law had no need for Chanchalba. She faced daily insults. Finally, when she could no longer bear the insults, at Gunasundari’s urging she went to live at her brother’s house. Chanchalba had a fifteen-year old son, Yashprasad; his wife Salasba had begun menstruating; but once Chanchalba moved in with her brother, Salasba went to stay with her parents. The year in which Vidya Chatura was appointed tutor to Maniraj, Manchatura, Sundargauri, Ganchatura, Chandika, Dukhba and Chanchalba along with their respective children came to live with Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari. All of a sudden, Gunasundari was expected to bear their burden. She had to nurse their individual sorrows, adjust to their diverse dispositions and also endure their bad habits and idiosyncracies. Her youthful passions which had just begun to flower were crushed under the weight of this burden, and Gunasundari was required to search deep within herself for the forbearance and wisdom of old age. Their house was small and Vidya Chatura’s income was far less compared to the expenditure involved. But the expectations and demands from his relatives were high as he was seen to be occupying a high position. Hence their desires and aspirations remained forever unfulfilled, they were forever discontented and disgruntled, and they blamed Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari for it. When this immense change was thrust upon her, Gunasundari was barely twenty. She was not yet worldly wise. She could not even begin to imagine how this burden would crush her being or what infinite restraint and patience would be demanded of her. She had spent her childhood and youth with her husband. She hungered for family ties. She truly believed that her life would be fulfilled if she could extend her love for her husband to his entire family. She imagined everyone to be as pure-hearted and generous as she was. Raised by kindly older women, Gunasundari had imbibed their affectionate nature, kindness and virtues, and with these qualities she hoped to carry the yoke of family responsibilities. She had experienced only the pleasant and positive aspects of social life and hoped that the web of family would help her further her own goodness. She was thus filled with many hopes and aspirations, but experience taught her the unbearable drudgery and pain that family responsibilities could be. As their house overflowed, Gunasundari was initially pleased and felt at ease. There were some difficulties; the house was small and felt cramped, but the joy of having everyone around her, the hustle and bustle of a large family compensated for it. At least for a time. The women and children were accommodated in the verandah or parsal, which led into rooms; they also slept there. Above the parsal there was a room accessed by a staircase; this was given to Ganchatura and his wife as their bedroom. The room adjacent to theirs was used to store valuables. It now had a human lock; grains were stored in this room which had to be accessed from the room occupied by Ganchatura and his wife. They were disturbed only when grains had to be taken out from there. There was an inner courtyard or khadki facing the parsal. On one side of it were the kitchen and water storage.
