On the other side were two rooms; Manchatura was given the exclusive use of one while the other was given Vidya Chatura’s mother, Dharmalaxmi. There was a room above the courtyard and a terrace. Before his family moved in, Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari used a room above the parsal as their bedroom while the room above the courtyard, accessed by another staircase, was used by Vidya Chatura as his office. They now moved their bedroom to the office and shifted his office downstairs. A curtain was hung between the chowk and the rooms of the khadki; this made a separate enclosure for the women. There was a smaller quad which could be approached from the parsal; a kitchen door opened into this quad and meals were served in this area. There was a small storeroom adjacent to the quad, a narrow passageway, and also a water storage room. Vidya Chatura often spoke of the wisdom of the ancestors and marvelled at their ability to create innovative spaces in homes with judicious use of money and space. He was extremely pleased that his wife could provide a space for each one of his large family in his small house. Gunasundari had done justice to the vision of those who had built the house. He called her to their new room and embraced her. As she received this gift of love, she said, ‘Pitaji keeps indifferent health. He needs solitude and would find the young ones bothersome. If he were given a room on the first floor, he would have to shout for someone every time he needed something. Therefore, I made a ground floor room available. I had to give up what used to be my sitting area, but this is most convenient for him. Motabhai would have found all the noise bothersome; he likes to be by himself and sing. The new arrangement would be agreeable to him. There are so many people around now that I will not be able to visit you as often as I used to in your office, but we have the whole night to ourselves, don’t we?’ Vidya Chatura was happy and proud of Gunasundari’s willingness to sacrifice her own convenience and pleasure to accommodate and provide for his family. He smilingly embraced her once again and said, ‘You did well, my Gunial’. She would remember these words for years to come. She did not forget the embrace either. For many days thereafter, in her rare moments of solitude, she brought his embrace alive in her memory and enveloped herself in its warmth. Vidya Chatura usually called her Gunial, but that day his utterance had a very different import for her. Running a large household is akin to administering a state. The responsibilities of a woman are as complex as that of a minister in a state. Foresight, abnegation of self-interest, forbearance, conscientiousness, generosity, managerial abilities, capacity for service to others and many other such qualities are required of a woman in charge of her household. A woman’s responsibilities cannot be fulfilled by hired servants. For this and other reasons Vidya Chatura did not like the Western practice of degrading household work and pushing women into the outside world under that pretext. Gunasundari expressed similar views to him one day. A Parsi newspaper had published an essay about bringing women out of their homes. She read the essay and while returning the newspaper to her husband, she commented, ‘My beloved Chatura, do you think what they write has any merit? Do we not do enough? Our bodies raise and nurture the race. To push such a body into the world of men is to desire that the tongue should behave like the teeth. You men are like teeth; we women are like the tongue. You do what is given to you to do, and we shall do what we ought to do. You go out and earn; we shall manage the household. Who but women could render your work meaningful? If you live to earn a livelihood and we also do likewise, who shall care for your children, your family, your household, your mind, your pleasures and your religion? Has God made the world such that even women should strive after money? You should assist us to learn better the task that is before us. If you have more money, accord us a higher status in what we do. Poor, unmarried men are their own servants and cooks; so are women married to poor men. People who say that women have been degraded because they are required to cook speak without thought because under certain conditions both women and men are required to do it. Which God has made cooking inferior to hard labour that earns ten miserly rupees, or to the duties of a doctor who must boil medicines and wash people’s oozing wounds for a few hundred rupees? We will use our intelligence in cooking. If you have greater means and can keep someone to cook your meals, we shall convert your houses into palaces, raise your sons to befit you. We shall cultivate learning for which you may not have the time. We shall nurture your aesthetic desires, your poetic inclinations, your learning, your valour, your patriotism according to our fate and ability. The tongue shall perform delicate tasks, while the teeth shall bite into hard things. You cannot do what is required of us. Only when we do what is required of us well can you manage your worldly affairs. If you cannot deal with your affairs well, we too are at a loss for it. This is what I think.’ Vidya Chatura smiled and said, ‘You argue well, Gunial. Among us, women call themselves servants of their husbands. A servant accords to the master the higher status. But I have received English education; hence you and I have equal rights’. Gunasundari said, ‘Who says we do not enjoy equal rights? Food and drink we need as much as you do. But by claiming equal rights you will not be able to bear a child, and we cannot give up what is given to us. No one becomes higher or lower just because one is called master and the other a servant. The master cares for the servant just as the servant toils for the master. On the surface it appears that the master is higher and the servant lower, but both need each other. The hands are in the upper part of the body while the feet are lower, but for that reason God does not consider hands more valuable than feet. Can we do without either? The same is true for men and women. You and I have equal rights, but God made me a few inches shorter than you. Can I be taller than you or become a man instead of a woman? Yes, you would certainly be at fault if you place unnecessary impediments in our way, treat us callously or consider us bovine instead of human! But what is all this talk? Some say men should do what they have been doing but women should not look after the house; they should dress up and chat all day, be idle and tell the husband that I need delicious food, good clothes and a cook. Some say, so what if your parents are old, shall I give up my youth for them? It is like saying that what belongs to you belongs to both of us, but what is mine is exclusively mine. If we adopt such ways, we would spoil our households and our daughters who would then bring grief to our sons-in-laws—that would be nice, isn’t it? If you become a dewan, I would keep your house as befitting a dewan’s status, give joy to your family, and when you return home tired from the problems of the state and world, I would bring delight to your heart. The joy of your home would be as high as the position you occupy in the world outside. This is my work and also the source of my pride and glory.’ Vidya Chatura said, ‘All right, do that when I become a dewan. For the present, demonstrate your cleverness in this cramped household of ours. How are you doing with your reading?’ He had expected a weak response. But Gunasundari retorted, ‘Reading? Isn’t all this education? A book printed on paper, and a book of the world—one can learn much from either. I will go back to reading gradually once the household settles down. Right now the household is a source of great delight for me. Do you know that I get up at four a.m. when the cock crows for the first time? Then I go down and light the lamps which bring light to your still dark house. The servants go to sleep at around midnight. The second thing that I do is to commit the sin of waking them up. What else can I do? I wake them up quietly so as not to disturb the sleep of others. Sometimes they wake up, but there are times when they just can’t get up. I take pity on them and allow them to sleep. Once they wake up, they heat up the water. Meanwhile I clean my teeth, perform other daily functions, bathe, comb my hair, apply the bindi and get ready. After this I put together everything that mother-in-law needs for her daily worship. I can assign this work to someone else, but she is finicky about these things and can also be harsh, which can cause friction between her and the one who does her work; therefore I prefer to do it myself. Meanwhile, everyone wakes up and performs their daily ablutions. During this time I organise the meals. Dukhba is preoccupied with her own woes and tends to neglect the task at hand. She cannot rush around or do things in a hurry, so she prefers to cook. Kumari assists her in cooking as she needs to be trained in it. If I try and teach her, Kumari does not always approve, but she does not mind it much even if Dukhba scolds her. There are many children in the house these days. Sundarbhabhi likes to bathe and dress them, which she does without being asked to. Chanchalbehn spends the morning preparing tea and medicines for Pitaji. I run all the other errands in the house, organise provisions and keep an eye on the servants. I am compassionate towards them but do not make a show of it because then they tend to get spoilt. The whole day passes in such activities. There is great joy in the house.’ Vidya Chatura asked, ‘But Gunial, how does this prove your cleverness?’ Gunasundari’s face betrayed concern and she replied, ‘About that, God only knows. But I am seven months pregnant and I cannot do as much as I need to. Once I am delivered of the baby, I will be able to do nothing and I am worried about that. Let us see what happens’. Just then someone called for her from downstairs and she was required to attend to that. Gunasundari’s concerns were not misplaced. Each member of the family had a different character and peculiarities. She ensured there was no cause of conflict and intelligently accommodated herself to all of them. She was agile and did most of the work herself. But Gunasundari was convinced that at the time of her confinement after childbirth, she would no longer be the link that held the household together; people would go their separate ways like beads unattached to a string. She anticipated differences about work, expected wastage of provisions and disputes in the household. Even after her confinement was over, she would have to look after the newborn child and would neither have the energy or the scope to resolve these conflicts. This, too, was a cause of worry for her. She now had a good measure of each one’s disposition, their qualities and faults. She had taken precautions to ensure that no conflict broke out in the family. She knew that precaution was easier than resolution of conflict. In her sweet and kind voice, she would give instructions in guise of requests, make gentle suggestions and assign responsibilities for which the person was best suited. Her conduct never suggested superiority or condescension. She set an example by working tirelessly and with enthusiasm all day long. She possessed the art of patient counselling. She loved the family greatly. She was generous, self-sacrificing and clever. Thus, young Gunasundari navigated the family’s ship through stormy waters with ease. The joy and sense of oneness in the family was at its height. We recognise goodness only in absence of it just as we value happiness greatly in times of sorrow. Similarly, Gunasundari’s absence was felt by all when she gave birth and was in confinement. Gunasundari possessed untiring industriousness, youthful enthusiasm and an affectionate, generous temperament usually associated with elders. Vidya Chatura was indeed fortunate to have her as his wife. The time to test her true worth was approaching. He desisted from praising her, but felt happy and satisfied as her hitherto unknown qualities came to light and flowered in service of his large family. He thanked God for his fortune and kept in mind the instructions of Mallaraj in his service of the state. As time passed he found these instructions to be even more valid. His own experience had taught him patience while dealing with all sorts of people; he had learnt to turn them useful. He had become both forgiving and generous. Vidya Chatura saw many similarities between his experiences and Gunasundari’s. The presence of the extended family proved quite useful at the time of Gunasundari’s simant. But even on that day, she had to ensure everyone’s happiness and oversee all the other arrangements as well. Ganchatura proved quite useful in organising the feast for the caste and in purchase of provisions for the feast. Jarashankar and other relatives also did their bit, but it was Gunasundari’s care that prevented total anarchy and mismanagement. Everyone was eager to do their bit, but Gunasundari had to assign them the tasks and ensure that they were done on time. The reason was obvious: no one had the sense to think that this is my house, too, and it is I who must ensure that the ceremony passes without a glitch. The women were glad to who needed what and also point out where exactly they were kept in the house. Moreover, there was also a lot of wastage, some of which could have been prevented while one had to overlook the rest. No one else had this fine judgement. There were many instances of friction and conflict, but Gunasundari managed to prevent a flare-up and also ensure minimum wastage. The caste norms were stringent and so were the rituals. Gunasundari’s mother-in-law Dharmalaxmi was an expert in social exchanges within the caste. She was also old and infirm. She rarely came out of the house and consequently could not keep a watch over the transactions. She operated from within the house with the help of intermediaries. Gunasundari accorded her mother-in-law all respect due to her and always sought her opinion. Despite that, Dharmalaxmi made enquiries as to whether her advice was followed or not, whether the daughter-in-law acted independently; she wanted to know if people spoke ill of her or praised her. She used Chanchal to obtain such information. Chanchal added her bit to make the tales juicier. Dharmalaxmi was wise and understood her daughter- in-law’s worth, but in her mind she still held Gunasundari at fault. Sometimes her face betrayed her displeasure in ways apparent to Chanchal. At times she counselled Gunasundari and at other times she singed her with her words. Gunasundari felt hurt but kept a large mind. She would constantly remind herself that the mother-in-law was after all an elder and made an effort to put the unpleasantness behind her. The simant should have been the responsibility of the elders in the family, but in this case it became the responsibility of the woman whose simant was to be celebrated. At a time when her body needed rest and her mind sought joy, Gunasundari worked from early morning to midnight without pause. And instead of praise she received only criticism. Dukhba was given the responsibility of welcoming the guests and dressing the children in new clothes and ornaments. She behaved as if it was Gunasundari who had brought ruination to Sahasrai and grudged her for holding this auspicious ritual when her husband was away. She moaned unhappily every time she saw Gunasundari and wept and spoke ill of her to anyone willing true to her patient and calm disposition, she responded to each with temperance and did not take these stories to heart. Chanchalba was to look after Manchatura and Dharmalaxmi; any other work had to be secondary to this responsibility. She was a help to Gunasundari and lightened her burden. But she blamed Gunasundari for any neglect on part of Dukhba in caring for her children. Chanchal carried her complaints to Dharmalaxmi. Sooner or later Gunasundari received reprimand for these lapses. Gunasundari never talked back. She did not transfer the blame on to Dukhba; instead she arranged the affairs even better. Chandika was given the task of inviting the guests. She liked to dress up and go out visiting but she lacked courtesy; she also gossiped with other women and brought their quarrels home. These tales were inevitably carried to Gunasundari, who was blamed for Chandika’s lack of courtesy. Chandika routinely taunted Gunasundari. Gunasundari would allow her elder sister-in-law to have her say, reasoning with herself: Chandikabhabhi is angry and incapable of appreciating my side of the story; she will understand once she cools down. Gunasundari would praise Chandika for her good work, send her off on an errand and go back to her own work. Sundargauri was given the responsibility of keeping a watch over the ornaments and was also made responsible for the provisions. Gunasundari trusted her completely. A destitute widow, Sundargauri was overwhelmed by this trust and hence immensely grateful to Gunasundari. The other women in the family were jealous of this relationship and felt pleased every time Sundargauri made a mistake. Gunasundari knew this and was prompt to protect this widow who had no other support. But she was discreet, for she also knew that if her support for Sundar were made apparent, Sundar would be subjected to even greater hardships. Sundargauri’s brother and sister-in-law were also invited to the celebration. Aware that Sundar enjoyed Gunasundari’s support, they felt slighted and openly showed their displeasure. During the feast, Sundargauri was required to come out of the house for some work. Her brother saw his opportunity. He caught her by the hand, dragged her and abused her. ‘Rand, you have brought discredit to our family! Have we ever denied you food that you had to seek shelter in your brother-in-law’s house?’ Poor Sundargauri wept helplessly. On hearing the commotion, Gunasundari came out with servants and freed Sundargauri from her brother’s clutches. She issued strict instructions that under no circumstances was Sundargauri to be sent on any errand outside the house. In return, Sundargauri’s brother and sister-in-law showered abuses on Gunasundari. Gunasundari went inside the house and the weary abusers gave up. But people kept whispering, ‘Why should Sundargauri be given so much prestige? The rand brings bad luck. Why do we need to keep her in the house? Would we lack for anything if she were not here?’ Chanchal made faces, Chandika made odd noises. Gunasundari saw and heard all this and more. Her heart was filled with pain. She had so much to do, but she sat with Sundargauri right in the middle of the chowk, holding her hands. Sundargauri was fair and extremely beautiful. Her golden hued cheeks grew flushed as she wept, her bosom heaving with her sobs. Just as ambers covered by ash flare up at the slightest touch of fire, attired in a widow’s simple clothes her whole body trembled with pain and anger. As Sundargauri cupped her face in her palms and wept, Gunasundari sat beside her and held her close; Gunasundari’s eyes also filled with tears as she tried to console the distraught woman. Other family members came and stood around them, joining Gunasundari in consoling Sundargauri, even those who had berated her. Sundargauri did not want to appear weak and feeble. She composed herself, wiped her tears, got up and went back to work. There were many such dramas during the simant celebrations. This was also the time that the English Sahib was visiting the state. Vidya Chatura thus had no time for domestic matters. The tasks that he could have shouldered also became Gunasundari’s responsibility. The simant celebration received praise from all quarters; among men Ganchatura and among women Dharmalaxmi received all the credit. No mention was made of Gunasundari’s contribution. Still, Gunasundari was content that the event was a success and that the praise due to her had gone to her brother-in-law and mother-in-law. the day she was delivered of her child. The house was hers. No one found it strange that she should work in her own house. Gradually, it became difficult for her to work. She could no longer assuage hurt feelings or avoid conflict. Others began to shirk responsibility; mismanagement increased. People devoted their free time to family squabbles. Even Dukhba changed colour. Gunasundari, out of consideration for her, had assigned the task of cooking to her. Dukhba complained, ‘I am the family’s cook. I eat a handful of grain and cook all day long’. Dharmalaxmi supported Dukhba. The matter eventually reached Gunasundari’s ears. She did not feel offended. Instead, she entered the kitchen. She was in the ninth month of her pregnancy. Therefore, at least for the sake of form, the others initially tried to stop her, but only half-heartedly. Gunasundari was eventually cooking for the entire household of seventeen-eighteen individuals when she was about nine and half months pregnant. There was no help, no relief. She had to get up many times. One day just after she had filled a heavy pitcher with water and carried it to the kitchen, her labour pains started. Gunasundari rushed to the room of confinement and lay down on the cot that was kept ready. For once she felt sorry for herself and cried. Sundargauri followed her. Chandika saw the two of them go towards the room of confinement but made no enquiries. Chanchal was busy chatting with Chandika. Dharmalaxmi was engrossed in her rituals. Dukhba was in the khadki feeling sorry for herself as usual. The only other person who felt for Gunasundari was Manchatura. Old and ailing, he saw the family drama play itself out. He often scolded his daughters and showed his displeasure to his wife. Manchatura was lying in bed when he saw Gunasundari rushing to the room prepared for her confinement. Forgetting his illness, he immediately got up from bed and came out of his room leaning on a stick, screaming, ‘Dukhba! Chanchal! Are all of you dead? Let your mother and her worship go to dust! Is there anyone who cares for this poor woman about to deliver a child?’ On his call everyone turned towards the delivery room like a tide. Dharmalaxmi’s weary body moved with a youngster’s agility as she snapped out of her rituals. Chanchal rushed down. Dukhba walked slowly. Manchatura berated her, ‘Oh! As if you are the only one to carry the burden of sorrows. Are your legs broken? Run, or else I will give you such a shove that you will move faster!’ Dukhba moved as if crushed by some great tyrannical force. Chandika was the last to come down, making faces of contempt. Manchatura saw her and muttered to himself: God knows from where we got her! Her husband earns nothing, and she behaves as if the slightest movement will erode her body! Everyone converged in the room. Gunasundari was almost unconscious. Sundargauri sat next to her, holding her. The women encircled them. Chanchal called out to her elder brother and sent him to fetch the midwife. He woke up inebriated with opium and song and walked off in a daze. Manchatura heaved a deep sigh of disappointment. Dharmalaxmi was old, ritualistic and superstitious; she was stern of speech but affectionate and capable of rising above her prejudices at such moments. She was experienced in matters of birth. She sat down beside the writhing Gunasundari, issued instructions to Chanchal and had the necessary things fetched. Gunasundari’s labour pains became intense. She went cold. With great effort she took out a key and handed it to Sundargauri saying, ‘Give it to him’ and she lost consciousness. Sundargauri burst into tears. Chandika was incredulous that even in such critical moments Gunasundari should repose such trust in Sundargauri. Everyone else was anxious. Even the otherwise useless Dukhba turned useful for once. She got up, went to her father’s room and said, ‘Who will call Bhai? I fear that Bhabhi may not survive’. Sundargauri, who had never before encountered such a situation, helplessly looked at her mother-in-law and sisters-in-law. Chanchal, who was more experienced, quickly lit a fire, brought healing herbs and warmed Gunasundari’s cold body with hot poultices. Sundargauri assisted her. Manchatura had trouble walking; despite this he raised himself with the support of a stick. He contemplated if he should go and fetch Vidya Chatura. If he were to go there would be no other male member in the house. But he made up his mind and stepped out. He asked Dukhba to watch the door. As he stepped out he saw the midwife approach. In the distance he could see Vidya Chatura approaching accompanied by Ganchatura. He was satisfied that Ganchatura had used his intelligence. Dukhba took the midwife to Gunasundari. As soon as the two brothers had walked in, Sundargauri came out of the labour room, handed the key to Vidya Chatura and, giving him the frightening news, hurried back. Vidya Chatura immediately sent his brother to call a doctor. This was his first experience of deep shock. He went cold and felt as if he were breathing hot air, his tongue became dry, his mind was in a whirl and tears welled up in his eyes. Hindu social custom forbade him from going to his beloved to comfort her, to be by her side. It would be a transgression. He looked at the key in his hand and wondered why she had sent it to him. He could only guess her intentions. He went up to their room and opened Gunasundari’s trunk with the key. There was a letter kept on top. He picked it up and read it through. My beloved Chatura, I will bathe again to go into the kitchen, but my body is giving up on me. I feel that by this evening I may no longer be alive. For the last two months there has been so much work in the house that I have not spent even fifteen minutes with you. At night you come to bed tired and wanting to sleep. I could not make myself disturb you with my idle chatter and I would let you rest. As a result, much has remained unsaid. How much can I write in a letter? And today, I don’t have the strength to write. Oh beloved, what will befall you once I am gone? Why did you love me so that now you must suffer my absence? I am so unfortunate that even in death I will become the cause of your sorrow. I believe that the child will die with me. But if it were to live, I am not worried about it. I have full faith in your love. Once I am gone, our child will remind you of me. Is it possible that you will not care for your child? It is possible that the love I received will be directed towards someone else. Even so, my beloved, you are wise, impartial and thoughtful. You have so many precious qualities apart from your love. May God keep you virtuous. I have full faith that you will care for your child, and with that knowledge I will accept the snares of the God of Death. If I have a worry, it is about Sundar. Her brother has snatched away her ornaments. She has no place where she can even go and weep. Take care of her. Our family has good people, but you must take special care of her because she has no one else. Give all my ornaments to her, only then will my soul find peace. And my last memory, my child, if it survives, should be given to Sundar to raise. Please do this much for me, dearest beloved! And what will become of you? Why did you love me so that now you must suffer? Won’t you do something for me? I have already spoken to Yashoda. Her daughter is ten years old; she will prove to be even better than me as a wife. Will you not accept her once I am gone? I am worried for you, dearest. You must do what I ask of you. Those who are unmarried suffer less, but a fish that has lived in the waters of love cannot live without it. Forget me. All the pleasures and joys that we have shared flash before my eyes as I write. My marriage to you filled my life, my being. God, pray grant me my beloved as a husband in the next life as well. But for now, you must forget all that. Take it that none of this ever happened. My beloved, are we then to part? God’s will be done. My dearest, you must forget our love and drown your sorrows. Forget that we once wandered this illusory world together. Your virtue-less Gunial. Vidya Chatura ran his hand over his forehead and looked up from the letter. These words written by his wife in the face of death left a deep impact on his heart. If he could, he would have cried. His mind grappled with the past, the present and the future as depicted in the letter. He felt somewhat calmer then. There cannot be a man harsher than me, he thought. Two months have passed. We live in the same house; yet we could not talk to each other. It is natural for her to feel this way. I was caught in my work and she in hers. I had no time. She, too, had no time. I allowed her to be caught up in work and other worries—all this is a result of that. I also pushed her to the limit. I should never have allowed things to come to such a pass. What a brave woman! She is still so young, and yet she freed me from all responsibility towards the family. But her mind seems to have weakened. There is no danger to her life as she fears. No, no! If she were to die, that would be my misfortune. If she were my brother, she could have been the Karbhari, she is such an able woman. She is my fortune. God, whatever You do will be for the good. I must be firm. I must not waver. Today is the day of my trial. What a noble and generous heart! How much she cares for my family and me! Gunial! My dearest Gunial! What can I possibly do for you? I cannot do even a fraction of what you do for me. I am grateful. Oh God! Just then Doctor Asharansharan Babu’s carriage drew up outside. Vidya Chatura snapped out of his reverie at the sound of the approaching carriage. He got up and said aloud: ‘The first thing I will do is not care for customs. I will accompany the doctor to my Gunial. I will stand beside her and assist the doctor. It is my duty to break custom and give up shame. I will do so. Customs are not dearer to me than my Gunial’. Vidya Chatura accompanied the doctor into the room where Gunasundari lay unconscious. The women stared at him as he walked past them. Vidya Chatura said without hesitation or shame, ‘Sundarbhabhi, please tell Doctor Sahib everything in detail’. Vidya Chatura was the breadwinner of the family. Who could chastise him? Who could have said: This is a woman’s domain and such transgressions are not permissible? If Ganchatura had so transgressed, the skies would have fallen on him. But everyone adjusted themselves to Vidya Chatura and made a show of concern for Gunasundari. Sundargauri, who was sitting with Gunasundari’s head in her lap, had just begun her narration to the doctor when Gunasundari stirred and seemed to regain consciousness. Her heavy-lidded eyes slowly opened and she saw her husband standing next to her bed. As she gazed at him unblinking, these words uttered softly seemed torn from the very depths of her being. Bereft of compassion, O Yama Your fearful eyes blind me Today, you must wait: let me look Upon my love to my heart’s content Even at the hour of death, you

Are implacable, O Yama, fixed like inlaid gold Let me gaze upon him a while yet— I see him, and still the heart yearns Though the light in my eyes dims He remains engraved upon my iris Wait, O Yama, wait! I cannot leave with you just yet! Demon, how can I abandon my beloved for you? He is the jewel of my heart—not worthless like you Let me cry, let me cry just once in his embrace My beloved, you must forget our love Yama pays my entreaties no heed Dying, I chant your name and weep Yet I smile and pray that in another birth I will find my Chatura again Gunasundari caught Sundargauri’s hand and said, ‘Sundarbhabhi, do not consider me shameless. Do I not have the right to say even a few words of affection to my beloved from the deathbed?’ And exhausted, she slumped back in bed. Vidya Chatura could no longer curb his emotions. He told the doctor, ‘I will be back,’ and almost ran up the stairs to his room. He kneeled down on the bed and wept without restraint. He got up, washed his face but the tears still flowed unabated. He composed himself and washed his face again. But he could not bring himself to go down. His pride in his equanimity had vanished. Finally, he looked down from the window and told Kumari, ‘Please tell Doctor Sahib that I am upstairs and that he should come up when his work is over’. The doctor was long in coming. As he waited anxiously, Vidya Chatura’s mind was full of strange thoughts. Once Mallaraj’s dearest friend was killed in battle. In order to attack the enemy, Mallaraj had to walk over his friend’s dead body. That is true equanimity. How can I even compare my feebleness with his forbearance? A kshatriya is a kshatriya, and a brahmin just a brahmin! Even Jarashankar Mama says that social responsibility and the feebleness of love do not go together. That should be the motto of doing one’s duty. The dharma of performing one’s duty lies in overcoming all personal sorrow to face one’s obligations. Gunial, you have proved far superior to me! You have done penance by performing your duty to perfection—till the very last. What supreme sense of duty! You kept things from me so as not to cause me pain. Such industry and so much love! Will I be true to your love if I show forbearance in the face of this adversity? Let the kshatriya do his duty; but even if I am considered effeminate, my Gunial, I will weep for you. You remembered me even in the face of death! ‘Yet I smile and pray that in another birth, I will find my Chatura again.’ God is compassionate. You shall live, Gunial. God is merciful, both on you and your Chatura. Fortitude, which had eluded Vidya Chatura even on consideration of his duty, came to him at last on the realisation that God was merciful. He rose. His eyes lit up, his heart filled with new life and hope. He thought: How can I, a man, cry? As he slowly began to climb down the steps, he was suffused with joy and pride. A smile played on his lips. My Gunial, it is you who have made me aware of God’s mercy. Even if I were to put aside your love, your virtues alone would enable me to conduct myself in this and the next world. Unknown to yourself, you have taught me how to administer the state. You have also shown me the path to God. Mallaraj had said that the administrator requires the qualities of a woman. If that be true, Gunial, I shall be made the Karbhari someday. There can be no love without partiality. Moved by a profound gratitude and love, the husband regained his composure and came down to meet the doctor. Some respect vaidyas and hakims and disparage doctors. Others do the reverse; they praise only the doctors. Jarashankar and Mallaraj were of the same age. Jarashankar also had the right to jest with the king. He would say, ‘People are not at fault. It is the doctors and vaidyas who decry each other; so people learn to do the same. When healers fight amongst themselves, people get their services cheaply, so it is in their interest to fuel these quarrels’. Mallaraj was partial to neither doctors nor vaidyas. For him, whoever could heal effectively was good. He gave the example of Emperor Akbar who had collected men from all faiths in his court. Similarly, Mallaraj had made place for the doctor, vaidya, hakim and barber. He encouraged all of them and would say that if they competed among themselves, it would benefit the people of his state. However, in two or three native states, doctors had taken advantage of their English education to gain proximity to the British

Agency, and used this proximity to further their influence in the state and meddled in the Karbhar. This had greatly angered Mallaraj and prompted an outburst. ‘Merely because he knows English, a doctor becomes a Karbhari. If tomorrow a barber learns English, should he also lay claim on the Karbhar? With such doctors and barbers, the state will turn upside down! I have no use for people who neglect their own work and meddle in other people’s work. These dakshini doctors are given to doing such things. And all doctors are dakshinis! We shall do without a doctor.’ Vidya Chatura, quite naturally, was partial to doctors. He was in fact instrumental in the appointment of a Bengali doctor in the state, and he did this so skilfully that Mallaraj had no objection. There were several reasons for this. The Bengali doctor was learned and able; he had come on a relatively low salary; he had travelled far in search of livelihood and hence his only interest was in doing his job well. Moreover his relatives were less likely to visit him often here; he also had little chance of gaining favour of the government in Bombay; and though he appeared tough as a tiger, he was in fact meek as a cow. For all these and similar reasons, Mallaraj had agreed to his appointment, and the credit for it went to Vidya Chatura. The doctor knew he had obtained the job on Vidya Chatura’s recommendation. He also considered Vidya Chatura a man of refinement and kept cordial relations with him. The wise doctor now gauged the reason behind Vidya Chatura’s sudden departure from the labour room and allowed the husband to take control of his emotions alone. The men sat around the doctor. In a while Dukhba walked up to them and gave them the news that Gunasundari had given birth to a girl. While it was not considered to be a matter for great celebration, it was also not devoid of the contentment typical of Indians at a child’s birth. The new child was duly welcomed. ‘Good, Goddess Laxmi has come to our house.’ Manchatura enquired about the new mother. Her good health and wellbeing was something to cheer about. The doctor gave necessary instructions for care of the new mother and child and got up to leave. Vidya Chatura walked with him to the door where the two conversed softly for a while. He went up to his room after that. others did their assigned work. Things worked well for three or four days, after which the wheels of the household began to move sluggishly and erratically. The absence of the one person who looked after the household was now felt. Her true worth was recognised. Initially, everyone felt that their own needs were not met well. Manchatura felt a slackening in his care as the person responsible for his care was now also required to do other tasks in the house. Not just that, the woman who assigned everyone their tasks and ensured their perfect execution was confined to her bed. Her intelligence, patience, gentleness and affection were sorely missed. The old man was now neglected. There were daily disputes in the house. Gunasundari was also neglected. Dharmalaxmi could not move about easily. She tried to do her bit for Gunasundari, but for her, worship was most important and came first. A task that has to be jointly performed tends to be neglected as no one claims responsibility for it. As a result no one cared to make special food for the new mother; even the infant girl was neglected. One day, no one had prepared Manchatura’s medicines until noon. It was almost lunchtime and there was no sign of food either. The irate old man got up and silently walked around the house, observing everyone. He first went up to Vidya Chatura’s room. Vidya Chatura had come home tired and hungry from work and fallen asleep. Bed bugs walked in a line on his bed; the bed sheet was dirty and litter was heaped in a corner of the room. Manchatura cursed everyone and went down. He walked into the kitchen. Dukhba was freshly bathed and ready to cook, but the vegetables were still uncut. Manchatura found her staring undecidedly at the vegetables. His anger shot up. He walked towards the parsal. He could hear Ganchatura singing in his room. Chandika lolled on the swing while Chanchal stood talking to her with a broom in her hand. They were so engrossed in their chatter that neither noticed Manchatura. He walked towards Gunasundari’s room of confinement. Sundargauri was trying to prepare medicines for Gunasundari and also care for the infant in her cradle. Gunasundari was pressing her stomach to relieve her hunger pangs and issuing instructions to Sundar as to what should be done.

Manchatura felt sorry for her. He came out and saw the children rushing around and pushing each other on the terrace. The door of the house was left wide open. A street dog had walked in. A servant had gone out to the well to draw water, but Manchatura saw him chatting with someone. He drove away the dog, closed the door and went towards Dharmalaxmi’s room. She was absorbed in her worship. The wick and the ghee in her lamp were burnt out and the light had died. She was searching for a wick, ghee and a matchbox to light the lamp. Her back was towards Manchatura who was at the door. Unbathed, he stealthily went up to the shrine, picked up all the idols and walked out unnoticed, unheard. He was so angry he thought of throwing the idols into the water tank. On second thoughts, he kept all of them in the water pitcher, quietly walked back to his room and lay down to watch the drama unfold. Manchatura and Dharmalaxmi were quite unlike each other. But their conjugal life was not without substance. Manchatura was intelligent. He not only had the ability to become adept at any task he faced, he also wished to complete the task as soon as possible; he was ill at ease with incomplete tasks. He did not hesitate to remove any obstacle from his path—be it in his own character, the disposition of others, divine or manmade, of religion or morality, of his own self- interest or the good of others. The only thing he understood was that obstacles should be overcome and the goal attained. From his young days, Manchatura had become skilled at dealing with peculiarities of human nature. He could cajole, entice and, if necessary, tyrannise others and make them useful and valuable to him and adjust to his needs. If that person happened to be someone from his own family, he dealt with them in a high-handed way. If he found that his own disposition was coming in the way of his goal and that he was required to do something that was repugnant to him, he did not hesitate. Just as the elephant trainer uses a prod to guide the elephant, Manchatura prodded his conscience to do what was repugnant to him. He would convince himself that it was obligatory for him to do so and took pride in its fulfilment. He was not a non-believer, nor was he on the immoral path. He followed both religion and morality so long as they did not hinder the pursuit of his goals. He remained steadfast in his pursuit. The strength of his character enabled him to overcome all obstacles. Dharmalaxmi was born and raised in an atmosphere of deep religiosity and had an abiding faith in religion. She had imbibed all the traditional norms of social and religious conduct. She spent her entire day in observing these norms. She was required to exercise the same level of expertise and effort in resolving issues of social conduct as required by theologians to resolve questions of religious conduct. Women from her caste and the entire village brought to her problems and disputes of social conduct. Dharmalaxmi would cite precedents from olden times, authorities of texts and norms, and she would provide an acceptable resolution. This pleased Manchatura no end. He liked to pose new and difficult problems to test her intelligence. She was considered an expert in ‘women’s science’ and her prestige was a matter of pride for him. It was natural that a woman like Dharmalaxmi was superstitious beyond reasonable limits, that she would create hindrances even in the smallest of matters and stand like a stone wall when faced with larger issues. Manchatura was amused by her preoccupations so long as they did not hinder his activities. But he was prompt to remove any obstacles that she put in his way. He would mock her, at times order her out of his way, try to reason with her, and at other times create such situations that she would not want to displease her husband. Manchatura was also given to losing his temper in a way that could turn a wedding celebration into a funeral. He would thus try all possible means to shake off any obstacles that she might place in his path. He saw the household in utter disarray during Gunasundari’s confinement and realised that the wheels would not move smoothly so long as Dharmalaxmi did not take charge. Engrossed in her rituals she was oblivious to this. He felt that she needed to be jolted by some drastic measure. And so he took all her idols and kept them in the water pitcher. He appeared unconcerned but he was in fact quite anxious to see if his shot would find its mark. He bit his lower lip and twirled his moustaches and waited to see what would happen.

Dharmalaxmi found the matchbox and lit the lamp. As she placed the lamp in the shrine she realised that her gods had disappeared. Her devout heart fluttered—she was stunned. She looked for her gods all over. Dharmalaxmi could not understand this miracle. She came out of the room which housed her shrine and looked around. There was no one out there. She thought: Did someone come in and steal my gods when my attention was elsewhere? She opened the main door and found the dog that Manchatura had driven away patiently waiting outside. The servant was still chatting away. Dharmalaxmi asked the servant, ‘Did you see anyone come inside?’ He shook his head and said, ‘No, Mataji’. She scolded him and called him back to his chores. She shouted in irritation, ‘Chanchal! Chanchal! Where have my gods disappeared?’ Chanchal rushed in with a broom in her hand. Chandika, Sundargauri, Dukhba and the children followed her and they all crowded into the courtyard. There was much confusion and they all made a lot of noise. Ganchatura stopped singing and came down. Vidya Chatura woke up with a start and also came down. Everyone was simultaneously asking questions and suggesting possible explanations for the sudden disappearance of Dharmalaxmi’s gods. Instructions were shouted and a search was mounted. Dukhba suggested that the children could have taken them for their play. Chanchal and Ganchatura opined that mice might have dragged them away. Vidya Chatura suggested, ‘They might have fallen off the platform, just look around the shrine’. Finally, Manchatura came out rubbing his eyes and asked in anger, ‘What is all this ruckus about? No one is concerned about food. It is almost one o’clock and no one says come, the lunch is served. It is as if there are no women in this house!’ Vidya Chatura replied, ‘Pitaji, Matashri cannot find her gods. That is the problem. They have suddenly disappeared from the shrine and cannot be found’. Manchatura retorted, ‘The gods will be found if they wish to be found. But is anyone bothered about feeding all of us, the living gods? Gods will be displeased with those who don’t care for the living. When displeased, the gods can disappear even from locked temples, let alone home shrines. Dukhba, go and give us the food. She will have to fast until her gods are found.’ Dharmalaxmi’s distress only deepened with these bitter barbs. His words were not only harsh and sharp, he also insulted her gods. Her eyes filled with tears. She clamped her hands over her ears and said, ‘Oh why do you utter such things fit for a non-believer? The merit of organising the worship of gods in Kaliyug is greater than performing rituals in Satyug. You and I have suffered so much in this birth. Do you want suffering to be our lot even in the next birth? We share each other’s merits and sins. You do not worship nor do you allow me to do mine in peace. Woe be to your hunger and your grey hair! Your hunger has made you abuse the gods. You do not remember the gods even in your old age. If I earn some merit by worshipping, our children will see better days. Have some consideration. Dukhba! Chanchal! Chandika! It is because of you three wretches that I had to listen to such terrible words today! If the younger daughter-in-law were managing the house, I would never have seen such a day. Couldn’t all of you look after the house even for a month or two? Chanchal, I now know where my gods are. You know your father’s temper. Go, feed him and the others. I do not want to eat until my gods are restored’. Dharmalaxmi sat before the empty shrine and wept copiously. She pleaded and supplicated before the shrine, ‘Maharaja, You are all merciful. Please forgive us. Please disregard his words and deeds. Let my merit be his and let his sins be mine, but please forgive us’. Manchatura raged and shouted at everyone. He glared at Dukhba, pursed his lips at Chanchal, gnashed his teeth at Chandika and made faces at Ganchatura. He raised his hand at the servant as if to slap him. Manchatura did not wish to appear partial to Vidya Chatura and so he stood with his back to him. But he ignored Sundargauri. He pointed out to everyone their irresponsible and callous behaviour and showered abuses on them. Finally he sent Sundargauri to look after Gunasundari. Raising his stick at them, he drove Chandika and his two daughters out of the house and latched the door. Then he ordered Ganchatura, ‘Go and cook food for all of us. These wretches deserve what they get!’

Vidya Chatura had stayed away from the family since childhood. Witnessing his father’s wrath for the first time, he stood petrified not knowing what to do. Neighbours gathered outside the house and some of them banged on the door. Dharmalaxmi saw that the scene had gone out of control and that Manchatura would not relent. She wiped her tears and came out of her room. Just as a priest knows the character of her divine, Dharmalaxmi knew Manchatura. She knew that he was more concerned about everyday life and living than questions of dharma and right conduct. She saw that he was like a stormy sea at present. It would be easier to submit to him rather than try to go against the current. With this realisation, her mind cleared. She also recognised that Manchatura’s anger was not without basis. She could see that the house was in total disarray. She realised that to remedy it was well within her grasp. Dharmalaxmi felt it was also her duty to care for the family. With this thought, she felt at peace in her heart. Her visage grew grave. If she were to look after the family’s welfare, it would give a lot of people joy. If the good of so many was within her reach, why should that duty not be considered superior to her rituals? She felt that the Creator who loves all beings and who imbues creation with bliss must also hold duty towards the household as a supreme obligation. These thoughts acquired the conviction of faith for her. With her faith renewed, Dharmalaxmi forgot about her idols and decided to take the reins of the household in her hands. She resolved to put behind her the chaos of the house, Manchatura’s bitter words, the ignominy of the family drama being played out in full public view, and the distress that it had caused to everyone. She emerged from this quagmire feeling purified for having immersed herself deeper in her love for the family. Just like a river broadens its course as it approaches the sea, Dharmalaxmi became more expansive as she approached Manchatura. He recognised the change in her and knew that his ploy had worked. Dharmalaxmi’s basic constitution was religious. Women tend to develop some qualities more than men; their bodies and intellect also mature sooner than men. Dharmalaxmi was a good example of this. Her father was blindly religious. She had absorbed religious instructions from a very tender age; so her religious belief had formed and hardened quite early. Even at the age of ten Dharmalaxmi was considered to be the most religious among all the girls in her neighbourhood. She was also intelligent, but given the overtly religious atmosphere of her house, she could have grown into a blindly superstitious person. She was married to Manchatura who was frequently transferred and changed jobs. It was difficult for her to strictly adhere to all religious observances. Moreover, Manchatura was temperamental and she was required to constantly adjust and accommodate herself to his moods. This balancing act was like walking on a sword’s edge. If she had not possessed a sharp intellect, Dharmalaxmi could never have lived in harmony with her husband. Even outsiders knew this. ‘Only Dharmalaxmi can deal with Manchatura’s temper. Anyone else would not have lasted even a minute with him’, they would say. She was religious but not blindly superstitious. She lived with a Rishi Durvasa- like husband till old age, loved and received the love of a man of fiery temperament, and still remained steadfast to her religiosity. This was made possible by her pure affection, earth-like forbearance, Vishnu- like peace, her sharp intellect and superior virtues. Vidya Chatura had hitherto remained ignorant of these qualities. As they became manifest, he felt proud that he was born to such a mother. Manchatura had turned red with rage. His eyes were blood-shot, his brows furrowed. As he stood there still trembling, in this fearful aspect he looked like Lord Narasimha himself. Greatly anguished by the insult of her gods, Dharmalaxmi could not bring herself to smile. But she concealed her pain from her husband. As she approached him with a grave mien, her heart beat faster. Her cheeks appeared more sunken in her toothless mouth, a film of tears appeared in her bright intelligent eyes; her fair forehead was crinkled as her pristine white hair glistened with sweat, the kumkum in the parting of her hair was damp. She quietly said, ‘I have realised your intent. But you know me well, when I get absorbed in worship I forget household chores. I admit it is my fault. But so much anger is not good. You have driven those three out of the house. People have gathered to watch the scene. It brings us nothing but ill repute’.

Dharmalaxmi walked up to the door and asked the three women to come inside. Manchatura drove out the onlookers and closed the door. Then he turned to his wife and said, ‘Go and pick up your idols from the water pitcher. Today I threw them into the pitcher. But if I have to ever go hungry again, you will find them at the bottom of the well!’ It took better part of an hour for his anger to subside completely. Dharmalaxmi removed the idols from the pitcher; no one thought of doing this for her. Clutching her gods to her bosom, she tearfully put them back in the shrine. Then she turned her attention to the house. But until the day she died, Dharmalaxmi could never forget that her gods had been consigned to an impure place. This remained her lifelong regret. It seemed that the household would get back on track under Dharmalaxmi’s watchful eyes, but her concern by itself was not sufficient to set the house right. She assigned work to everyone but she did not have the energy to go around checking to ensure that each task was done. The situation was reminiscent of the saying: good counsel stays with one only till the house gate. Soon, the younger women began to see her as crotchety and nagging and their affection for her diminished. They also began to flout her instructions. Initially they abused her in private, but over time they also insulted the old woman openly and spoke ill of her. Dharmalaxmi was also fed up. She took her complaints to Manchatura and often went to Gunasundari and cried. Gunasundari seized his opportunity to obtain her mother-in- law’s affection. She also realised that she would have to achieve what her mother-in-law had failed to. She eagerly awaited the day when she would be allowed to take up household chores again. But little did Gunasundari know that she would be asked to perform tasks that she had neither previous knowledge nor experience of. In Hindu society, joys and sorrows come in myriad different forms. For those who have not experienced or observed them closely, it is difficult to imagine them or explain. Gunasundari had come to believe that she had experienced all that one possibly could within the realm of the household. But knowledge and experience are limitless, and a young mind cannot fathom that apparent experience conceals deeper import and meanings. As one gains in education and age, new forms of experience and knowledge reveal themselves, just as having climbed to the top of a mountain, one glimpses higher peaks beyond. Experiences come like sea weaves. As one bears witness to new experiences, there are moments in which the mind, unknown even to itself, merges with the infinite, the divine. Having experienced the infinite, one becomes capable of discerning new hitherto untrodden paths and taking the first tentative steps. Gunasundari observed the household from her confinement. She also contemplated many things above and beyond this domesticity. She would often talk to herself thus: This was a novel experience, but what lies in store for tomorrow? Even in mundane everyday matters, a questing mind can find ideas to sustain itself, and thoughts and words like divine utterances can come together from unexpected quarters to nurture and enrich the mind. As she lay in her dark room of confinement, Gunasundari realised for the first time that in many ways, in many things, she was as inexperienced as her infant daughter, and she felt a new bond with her. The day after Manchatura’s show of temper Gunasundari’s friend Yashoda came to visit her. When they were alone, Yashoda told her about the rumours circulating in town. ‘It is being said that yesterday Vidya Chatura drove his sisters and sister-in-law out of the house. The old mother prevailed and got them back, but the mother and son had a bitter fight during which Vidya Chatura picked up the idols from her shrine and threw them away.’ Gunasundari was astonished and deeply hurt that her innocent husband had been blamed. She quietly narrated the previous day’s events to Yashoda. But in her mind, despite herself, she momentarily despised the entire family’s conduct. When she was left alone she lay down, pulled the covers over herself and cried for hours in despair. This gave her a fever, which too went unnoticed and unattended. Two-three days later a new problem arose. All the groceries were stored in a room on the first floor. Sundargauri was required to go up and fetch grocery whenever required. This poor widow had no other support but for Gunasundari. All the women were either jealous of her affection sustained her. That day all the women were eating their meal. The men had dispersed to their rooms. Sundargauri finished her meal quickly and went up to the grocery room to fetch some condiments to prepare Gunasundari’s medication. It was noon. Standing in the bright sun, the young widow’s fair complexion acquired a rosy hue. As she bent over to pick the condiments from a pot, her saree fluttered in the wind. The black saree covered her fair form as a dark cloud the sun. Her supple back was visible, arched like a rainbow. A lock of her hair had come to rest on her breasts. The heels of her soft bare feet were visible from below her saree. The dazzle of her body could have blinded any onlooker. Sundargauri was engrossed in her work and oblivious of such matters. Little did she know that eyes blinded by her beauty were watching her intently. Males consume and females are objects of their consumption. This is a trait shared by human beings and animals alike. Among animals, the female is pursued by the male like a hunter pursues his prey. The difference is that the hunter kills while the female is possessed and kept. The male preserves the female as one protects a goose laying golden eggs. This sense of protection and nurturance tends to be more refined among the higher species; human society exemplifies this. A daughter unknown and unloved to begin with becomes the most intimate of associates and one who is loved like no other. The tradition of marriage is an outcome of this sense of preservation and possession. As long as the human in us dominates our animal instincts, this sense of protection survives. But when the beast in us triumphs, men pursue women as prey. Such men become incapable of any consideration of right and wrong, for we lose this capacity for discernment when we lose our humanity. Nevertheless, there are exceptions; it is possible for this to unfold more subtly. Ravana captured Sita as if he were the hunter and she, the prey. And yet, he could never violate her. He abducted her in his bestiality, but his higher sensibility taught him: I do not approve of the union, even if successfully brought about, of two lovers, one of whom is ardent and the other heart-whole, it is better that an equally enamoured pair should ever pine away hopeless of mutual happiness.⟨fn:43⟩ All men are capable of being human and this enables them to be protective of orphaned and weak women. If all men were to acquire ‘chivalry’, the conduct of both men and women would become purer, and women would be freed from fear. When Sundargauri stood up and turned around, to her surprise she found Ganchatura standing right next to her. Ganchatura was satiated with food and seemed drowsy. Roused from his slumber by the rustle of her feet, he had come out and seen Sundargauri standing alone, looking ever so beautiful. The beast in him asserted itself as soon as he saw her. He lost his capacity for judgement. He did not consider morality or his relationship with her; he did not consider that the house was full of people. Ganchatura had the audacity to come and stand close to Sundargauri, but not the courage to advance further. He stood there petrified, his limbs refusing to move. Only the flicker of his eyes betrayed his base desire. Sundargauri turned pale at the sight of him. She was gripped by fear. She dropped what she had collected and ran down the stairs. She missed the last step and fell down, but was not hurt. She rushed into Gunasundari’s room, trembling as if his odious presence still shadowed her. Tears flowed from her eyes. Gunasundari had gone out of the room to eat. Sundargauri calmed herself with great effort but she was frightened. One has to constantly guard against the animal instincts. If they overpower us there is a danger we may lose our humanity for good, for the human beast is far worse than the animal one. The fear of this beast now pierced her heart like an arrow. Try as she might, Sundargauri could not rid herself of it. Her mind was in a flurry. She thought: Whom can I tell? How? How can I utter those words? Will I have the courage? Will anyone believe me? Why did this thought even occur to him? What will he do now? What will happen to me? What am I to do? How will I live in this house? Where else can I go? These and similar questions began to torment Sundargauri. Her response to each such question was a deep sigh and tears. Over the next few days, she found no solace even in household chores. Usually the last resort of the friendless is sleep, but even that eluded her. She withered, her face appeared sunken and withdrawn, joy and laughter became alien to her. Tears welled up in her eyes every time she spoke to Gunasundari. Only one observant would have noticed how often she sighed while speaking. It never occurred to Sundargauri that someone might notice these changes in her. Ganchatura noticed, but felt helpless in face of his lust. Gunasundari’s affectionate heart did not take long to see these changes but she did not understand the reasons for it. Why would anyone else in the house bother? Gunasundari asked Sundargauri repeatedly and pleaded with her. But Sundar’s response was the same every time, ‘No, it is nothing. Your suspicion is baseless. I am just not feeling well since the past few days. There is nothing else to it’. Gunasundari did not believe her. Ultimately Gunasundari asked Sundargauri to touch and swear by her newborn daughter. She also threatened to go on a fast. Sundargauri forced herself to smile and said, ‘Why would you do such a thing? But for you, who else can I talk to? Can we women keep a secret all our lives? I will do what you want me to, but you must also swear by me and promise to do what I ask of you’. Gunasundari agreed. Sundar said, ‘All right then, I will tell you. But you must not ask me anything about it until I tell you myself. Both of us are bound by a mutual pledge’. ‘Why can’t you tell me right now?’ asked Gunasundari. ‘There must be a reason’, replied Sundargauri. ‘As long as I am alive no harm will come to you.’ ‘I know that. Is there anyone else I trust or consider my own?’ ‘All right then, will you tell me this evening or tonight?’ ‘I will tell you when I feel up to it. Ask me after two or three days.’ The two went on arguing like this for a while, but Sundargauri was determined to say nothing; her heart would not allow a word to escape her lips. Gunasundari’s period of confinement finally came to an end. She had a ritual bath and could freely move about the house. She was not yet considered ritually pure and hence she could not touch anything in the house. But as she moved around and observed the goings on, the family drama became apparent to her.
chapters.summary: Gunasundari arrives in the well-governed Manoharpuri, where she becomes concerned by Sundargauri's mysterious changes, determined to uncover the secret troubling her friend.

chapters.title: Gunasundari (Continued)
paragraphs: Gunasundari (Continued) You are forever changing, O’ world.⟨fn:44⟩ Gunasundari was still ritually impure and not allowed to touch anything in the house. In some other families it was permissible to touch dry utensils and clothes. But Dharmalaxmi made no such allowances. Hence, Gunasundari used this time in other pursuits. She tried to fathom the minds of her family members. She spent time in Manchatura’s room, talking to him about his childhood and life thereafter. She tried to understand what shortcomings the old patriarch saw in the house, what his wants and desires were. Gunasundari tried to assuage his anger towards other members of the family and assured him that she and her husband would fulfill all the wants that they were capable of fulfilling. She also gauged if he harboured any discontent or resentment towards her and Vidya Chatura and what he thought of them. She anticipated his anxieties and vexations and she took preventive measures. All this she did quite cleverly and unobtrusively. Gunasundari’s intelligence, her patience and affection had its desired effect. Over time, Manchatura came to trust her. His anger subsided; he appeared to be largely content. His volatile anger was one of the reasons for his illness. Gunasundari soothed his mind and body. Not only Manchatura but gradually other members of the family, too, came under her spell one by one. Gunasundari would sit with Dharmalaxmi when she performed her rituals, spend time with Dukhba in the kitchen patiently listening to her woes, talk to Chanchal in the afternoons and converse with Chandika as well. She would gather the children around her and tell them stories, sing for them, read out to them, listen to their troubles, counsel them and enjoy their company. Gunasundari was an elder among the elderly and a child among children. In this way, like Manchatura, everyone else in the family opened up to her. They shared with her their frustrations, they saw her as their confidante, grew affectionate towards her and genuinely sought to make her happy. They even took care not to hurt her feelings. Before too long, Gunasundari became the thread holding all the dissimilar beads together. This apparently happy and tranquil dream was not without its shadow, however, nor was it everlasting. One afternoon when Gunasundari was alone, she sat reminiscing about the history of her own family. Happy and sad memories of her childhood flooded her mind. As an adolescent, unable to understand her husband’s aspirations, Gunasundari had felt distanced from him. This had distressed her; but it was her husband who had come to her aid and eased her distress. Vidya Chatura was a school teacher. She had little to do in the house. There were no other family members then. She had every opportunity to enjoy her husband’s company and affection. The two had not a care in the world. They were in the bloom of youth and as the world of senses opened up before them, they took as much delight in the pleasures of the body as in cultivating higher aesthetic sensibilities and sharing the myriad subtle pleasures of the mind. Abruptly crushed under the burden of a large joint family, these pleasures were now a distant dream. Gunasundari was of a sudden gripped by an overwhelming sense of despondency that her desires were to forever remain unfulfilled. This hopelessness took possession of her mind much as a cruel creditor lays seize to a debtor’s house. For five long months, she had not had one conversation with Vidya Chatura despite living in the same house. Tears welled up in her eyes and coursed down her cheeks. Kumud Sundari was lying in her lap. A few tears fell on her. Gunasundari wiped them and said, ‘Oh my child, how blissful you are! Will you too have to face all that I do one day?’ She lifted little Kumud up in her arms. Kumud smiled—it was her first smile. Overwhelmed with emotion, Gunasundari pressed her to her bosom. It was almost as if she had a premonition, that in future, despite their deep and abiding love for each other, Sarasvatichandra and Kumud were destined to live their lives as strangers. Gunasundari pressed her daughter closer to her heart and sobbed out aloud. Just then she heard the soft movement of someone’s feet. Someone had heard her crying. But who? She quickly wiped her tears and composed herself. That day, the family had been invited for a meal at Jarashankar’s house. Gunasundari, still not free of the impurities of childbirth, had remained at home. She was alone and had not latched the door from inside. Vidya Chatura was busy and was to go for the meal a little later. He had finished his work and come home. He opened and shut the door so softly that Gunasundari did not hear him enter. Finding no one else in the house, Vidya Chatura turned towards the parsal. He thought he had heard Gunasundari weeping. It was as if his heart had silently understood Gunasundari’s longing, her despondency and drawn him to her. When he entered her room, she had just wiped her tears. Gunasundari looked up and saw Vidya Chatura standing at her door. It was after many months that the two were alone. She had no patience even to gaze at his face. She forgot that she was not yet permitted to touch him. She put little Kumud down on the bed and she ran to him and embraced him. Like a ray of moonlight that envelops a cloud in its embrace, her arms entwined themselves around his neck. She lifted herself off the ground and hung from his neck like Lord Vishnu’s garland which reaches down to his feet. Vidya Chatura lifted her up in his arms and carried her to the swing. He seated her on the swing, which had become a pleasure boat, and sat down next to her. He picked up their daughter, lay her in his lap and asked Gunasundari with a smile, ‘What is the reason for such irrepressible joy?’ In response, Gunasundari kept a hand on his shoulder and with the other, she drew his hand and touched it to her face. She looked at him unblinking for moments, smiling. Then her eyes were drawn to some papers he was carrying. She could see something written in his hand on the back of an opened envelope. She took it from him and read it.

True love no time nor distance can destroy; And independent of all present joy, It grows in absence, as renewed delight, Some dear memorials, some loved lines excite.⟨fn:45⟩ She said, ‘My answer to your question is this: how did you think of this verse?’ He said, ‘These lines from the Meghdoot came to me all of a sudden while I was sitting in office, and I wrote them down.’ ‘But why did this very verse come to you?’ ‘Now you are cross-examining me like a lawyer, Gunial,’ he said, smiling. ‘Of course! Those who do not give straight answers need to be cross-examined.’ ‘All right. Ask whatever you wish.’ ‘Why did this verse come to you in the middle of office work? And even if it did, why did you have to write it down on an envelope that could have gone to some other hand? Have you lost your heart so completely? Come on, give me an answer. See, even this little girl is looking at you expectantly. She is a witness.’ Gunasundari’s eyes seemed to be laughing triumphantly at him. She playfully kept her hand on his shoulder again, as if the glorious morning sun had kept a rainbow against a mountain. ‘All right, Gunial. You win.’ ‘No, that is not sufficient. You are caught now, answer you must. I, too, have learnt something of your craft, you see.’ Vidya Chatura laughed. She continued, ‘You could, for instance, say that the feelings that took possession of me when I looked at you also possessed you when you thought of me’. ‘All right, yes, that is what it was. Anything else?’ ‘So your condition was the same as mine. If you ever ask me again about my feelings for you, you will be caught just like today.’

The husband and wife thus talked pleasantly for some time, moving joyfully from one thing to another. But their youthful emotions soon gave way to household concerns and they both turned grave. Vidya Chatura asked Gunasundari in detail about each member of the family. From her descriptions and responses, he also gauged how she felt towards each one of them. This allowed him to fathom the core of her emotional life. One by one, the layers of distance and silence that had grown over their hearts began to peel off, and he saw the startling purity of her heart. Just as the eyes feast on the beauty of the body, Vidya Chatura with his mind’s eye feasted on the unsullied beauty of Gunasundari’s heart. He saw in her heart a vast and unblemished love for him. He saw as much love and concern for the family as his father had, forgiveness like that of his mother, more industriousness than Chanchal, more delicacy than Sundargauri, a far greater capacity than himself to bear the entire family’s burden gracefully, and the childlike joy and innocence of the newborn. The beauty of her heart enticed him. Just as a lover tries to undo the knots of his beloved’s garments, he gently tried to loosen the knots of her heart and lay it bare. Bashful all at once, she tried to stop him, and then he could no longer contain himself. In a moment of desire he drew her to him and embraced her tightly, and these words escaped his lips: The bold presumption of her lover’s hands To cast aside the loosened vest, withstands; And, feeble to resist, bewildered turns Where the rich lamp with lofty radiance burns; And vainly whelms it with a fragrant cloud Of scented dust, in hope the light to shroud.⟨fn:46⟩ ‘Gunial, this is our Alakapuri. We could not speak to each other for five months. But haven’t we made up for all those lost months today? Speaking for myself, I am satiated, replete. Who else could have showered such nectar of love and joy on my family but for you? Men may try, but they can never look after the house as a woman does. You have cared for my old parents and my immature selfish siblings with such generosity of spirit. I am truly fortunate to have you, Gunial. But there is nothing at all that I can do for you. What have I ever done for you? The days when we took delight in sublime conversations and lofty thoughts are over. You are reduced to doing the work of a cook and a servant from dawn to night. Is this my gift to your many virtues? Am I lacking in means? Am I wanting in generosity?’ A deep sigh escaped Vidya Chatura. His hands no longer held Gunasundari’s, they clutched the chain of the swing. His face was lined by anxiety and concern. Gunasundari took Kumud from his lap and said, ‘No. The mistake is mine. I shared with you the goings on in the house and I had to hear your praise. You praise me but not yourself, which means that you consider me separate from yourself. Let us close this matter now’. With her adroit response, she attained two objectives: she cut short his praise of her, and she made him laugh. ‘All right, Madam Sahib. I realise my error. I will not praise you. Now do go on with your narration.’ Gunasundari continued with her narration which rolled on like an incessantly moving Persian wheel. Finally she came to the point. ‘I have spoken to everyone in the house. Firstly, you are doing so well but the elder brother has no work. This does not behove you. Pitaji is unhappy about this. Secondly, everyone but Dukhba is happy in the house, which does not look good. If you extend some help to Sahasrai, his days of running around in hiding will end and he will be able to come home and start some work; he is like a brother to you after all. Kumari is betrothed but there is no money to arrange her marriage. Dukhba is withering away everyday in this worry and she is unable to share it with anyone. Our child will have all the good things but Chanchalbehn’s children have no ornaments. This does not behove us. Even Mataji feels this is not right. She also wants a silver shrine for her gods; it is her heart’s desire. For the present, these are the wants. The rest I will tell you later.’ ‘There is more?! Tell me now itself.’ Vidya Chatura was stunned. He did not earn much. Moreover, he had to bear the brunt of expenses for the entire large household. The expenditure had greatly increased.

Gunasundari’s simant ceremony and feast cost a lot of money. All their savings were spent on it. Gunasundari realised what she had done. She said, ‘Those who have to bear the burden realise the weight of it. I did not realise your situation to begin with. You praise me but remain silent about the burden you bear. Why don’t you praise yourself? It is true that our hardships are apparent to all; but the burden you bear remains hidden. You tell me that you are unable to do anything for me. But what have I done for you? For the last five months I have not seen you have one free moment for yourself. I can share my worries, but you have no place to go and no one with whom you can unburden yourself. After so many months you came to talk with me. But the sinner that I am, I could not even bring myself to speak of things that would give you joy ...’ While she was still speaking, the door suddenly flew open and Sundargauri rushed in, panting. Vidya Chatura wore the pagdi on his head with a disappointed look and got up to leave for his meal. Gunasundari watched him leave, full of remorse. As he receded from view, she closed the door feeling close to tears. She turned around and saw Sundargauri trembling with fear and ready to burst out crying. ‘Sundarbhabhi, what’s wrong? Why are you trembling like this?’ Before Sundargauri could respond, the door burst open again and Ganchatura entered in some haste and caught the shoulder of the woman standing with her back to the door. He had expected to find Sundargauri, but he found he was holding Gunasundari’s shoulder instead. Realising his mistake, he immediately removed his hand. ‘Oh, it’s you!’ he said, ashamed, ‘I assumed it was your sister-in-law.’ Gunasundari, initially startled, was now enraged at his attempt to conceal a sin with a lie, and was about to retort, ‘Which sister-in- law?’ But before she could say anything, Ganchatura had rushed up the stairs and gone into his room. Gunasundari realised that nothing would be gained from whipping up the matter further.
