She composed herself and turned towards Sundargauri who stood shivering in a corner of the room, and gently said, ‘This must be the reason for your tears the other day as also the cause of your trembling today. Now I understand everything’.

Sundargauri could no longer contain herself. Her lips quivered from fear and shame as tears streamed down her eyes. She could not speak. She leaned against a wall, petrified. Her sari slipped from her head. She covered her face with her hands as leaves cover a flower. Even before Gunasundari could make a move to comfort her, Chandika rushed into the room in some rage. It seemed that something untoward had happened at the meal. She pounced on the terrified and weeping Sundargauri and pushed her further against the wall. ‘Rand! You revealed your true character today!’ she screamed at her. Gunasundari came to Sundargauri’s aid, pleading, ‘Bhabhi, what is this! Let her be!’ She somehow freed her from Chandika’s clutches. Chandika left the room in a huff, showering abuses on her as she went up to her room. She stood before her husband and beat her breasts and wailed as if she was in mourning. Gunasundari was stunned by Chandika’s rage and wondered: Did Sundar have a part to play in this? She corrected herself, No, there seems to be some misunderstanding. But before she could ask Sundar anything, the other women and children walked into the house. Gunasundari pretended as if nothing had happened. She asked about the meal. She waited for someone else to bring up the matter. Not wanting to draw attention to herself, Sundargauri got busy with household work. Gunasundari realised that no answers were forthcoming from anyone. Dharmalaxmi seemed angry; she sat with a surly face. Dukhba appeared nervous and, unable to find anything to do, she went and lay down on the swing. Chanchal busied herself with some work but kept muttering under her breath. Gunasundari watched the scene. For some reason everyone seemed to have lost their tempers that day. This was new for Gunasundari. Are they angry with me? Has someone been spreading false stories about me? Or are they angry with my husband? Oh God! I constantly watch their moods, I try my utmost to keep them happy, and still I am subjected to such things. Is this also a part of the burden of the household? Did I really do something wrong? Thousand such questions swamped her mind. Gunasundari looked at everyone’s face one by one but found no answers. She went to help Dharmalaxmi who snapped at her, ‘No, no, leave it. Let everything be as it is. I do not need any help nor do I want anything from you’. Gunasundari pretended she had not heard the rebuke and carried on with her work. Suddenly, Chanchal rushed towards her, visibly angry, took away the work from her and started doing it herself. Gunasundari went and sat next to Dukhba on the swing. Dukhba instantly got up as if Gunasundari’s touch would defile her and sat further away on the threshold of the parsal. Gunasundari tried to talk to her, ‘Motibehn, what has happened?’ Dukhba did not answer her straight. ‘Let it be. Why do you bother? You do what you have to.’ Spurned from all sides, tears welled up in Gunasundari’s eyes. She did not wish to respond to anyone in anger or hurt. She needed to be alone. Though the period of her ritual impurity was not yet over, Gunasundari took Kumud and went up to her room. Sundargauri saw her go up the stairs. Seeing Gunasundari upset, she forgot her own distress and thought: You need to please and plead with everyone, but no one needs to please you! How is this fair? Before she stepped into the room which she and Vidya Chatura used as their bed room, Gunasundari saw the state it was in. The room was dirty and in utter disarray. She was unable to care for it and no one had attended to it. She wondered how Vidya Chatura was able to sleep here. She could not bring herself to enter. A sudden desolation possessed Gunasundari. Forgetting her insult, hurt and anger, she stood on the last step of the staircase and gazed forlornly at their bed. She was nudged out of her thoughts by Sundargauri’s touch. They walked into the room. Gunasundari lay Kumud down on the bed and sat down beside her. Sundargauri held Gunasundari’s hand to comfort her. Wrapt in their own thoughts and silences, neither woman moved or spoke for some time. Finally, Gunasundari spoke. In this unsurpassable ocean of the world, I am sinking O my beloved and compassionate master, tell me who is my true refuge? The master replied: The great boat of the feet of Vishvesha, the Lord of the Universe, is the refuge.⟨fn:47⟩

As soon as she had uttered this verse, as if the master’s benedictions had reached her, her attention was drawn to Vidya Chatura’s books. She picked up a notebook of his personal jottings. She opened a page—it was the page on which he had written down Maharaja Mallaraj’s counsel. ‘Sundarbhabhi, come, take a look at this! The day your brother-in-law joined the Maharaja’s service, Mallaraj had counselled him. This is what he had said. Do take a look. How many duties of women has he enumerated! Men have even more obligations. Even we would benefit from this counsel.’ Sundargauri read it and returned the notebook. She said, ‘Bhabhi, all this is fine. We, too, are human. The others can feel bad if they want, but you should not feel hurt! Your husband earns and provides for all of us. You do all the housework and you also deal with everyone’s tantrums, complaints and taunts! No one cares at all for what you do or think. Not just that, they accuse you unjustly of all manner of things and you have no hope of getting a fair hearing. Is this the way of doing things? Is this at all fair? Even Mallaraj would not advise you to bear with so much!’ Gunasundari was silent for a while, her eyes on the ground. Then she said, ‘Sundarbhabhi, it is not how you take it to be. God places thousands of hardships upon us. It cannot be without a reason. A person is formed by suffering’. ‘Let your God go to sleep! What are you talking about? I have not experienced any joy, even a moment’s happiness ever. And I am certain that I won’t, not in this life at least. A widow’s lot is ignominy and suffering and relentless suffering until death relieves her of her misery. Bhabhi, where is my share of happiness? Don’t I deserve any? It is said that my present suffering is due to my deeds in my past life. That may be so, but all talk of redeeming our sins for the next birth is false. Hope brings nothing but dejection, misery and more suffering.’ ‘What you say is not entirely false, Sundarbhabhi. But if one believes in the validity of one’s past life, then why not in the next birth? It is an incessant cycle of eighty-four lakh births. A person does penance for the next life. The suffering we bear is a form of penance.’

‘How can it be called a penance? People who undergo hard penance do so voluntarily. But the suffering that befalls us is not what we asked for. It comes on us, and we bear it as God’s will. We have no choice.’ ‘But there are two ways in which we can deal with this suffering. One can complain and blame God. Or, one can believe that whatever God does is for the good. One way is to bear the suffering simply because it has befallen us. But the other way is to gladly submit to it and become willing servants of the divine will and consider this submission as our penance. Everyone in the family is displeased and angry with me right now. But soon, if not today then tomorrow, their anger will surely subside. We know this. But despite this knowledge if the two of us were to feel angry with them because they are angry, this is not fruitful. This momentary pain is insignificant compared to the lifelong suffering that is your lot. When the elders are angry with us, we should say: Let them be. If we, too, behave like petulant children, why should we then be called adults? To my mind, this is the only way to true happiness and inner peace.’ ‘True. Somehow, we have to teach the mind to compromise.’ ‘No, Sundarbhabhi, that is not quite what I meant. If by such submission, we can find a way for everyone to be happy, only then we should do so. If we see it only as suffering or joy, what is to befall our lot will befall our lot anyway. And if this be so, it is wise to consider even suffering as happiness.’ Sundargauri looked intently at Gunasundari. She felt her anguish somewhat assuaged, her misery somewhat more endurable. She took the book from Gunasundari’s hand, read something in it and said with a smile, ‘It is true. Your wisdom, your knowledge of life must come from my brother-in-law. What you have received from him has also proved beneficial to me. But not everyone is as fortunate as you. You must have worshipped the gods with true devotion, with all five fingers of the hand as they say, to have been blessed with a husband like my brother-in-law. And yet, despite everything that I endure as a widow, I am still better off than living with a husband like your Jethji. Listen to them, you can hear their farce being played out even from here.’

‘Let their drama be. But tell me whatever happened at Jarashankar Mama’s place? You must know?’ Gunasundari asked. So Sundargauri narrated to her the events of that morning. While talking to Manchatura, Jarashankar had enquired about the family’s wellbeing. Manchatura had for long observed the daily goings on in the family. He had also heard a few things from Gunasundari. He was exasperated and fed up beyond patience with everyone in the family. He brought out his anger on Dharmalaxmi. Manchatura had thought that Jarashankar would say a few words of censure to his sister, which would help restore some order in the family and improve matters. In this belief he enlisted all her shortcomings and berated and shouted at his wife in her old age in front of her own daughters, her daughters-in- law and her brother. Naturally, this was too much for Dharmalaxmi to bear. She was most grievously hurt. She felt Jarashankar would believe everything Manchatura said about her. Moreover, Manchatura had harsh words for everyone except for Gunasundari. This convinced Dharmalaxmi that it was Gunasundari who had carried all the tales to Manchatura. For instance, Manchatura knew that Dharmalaxmi wanted a silver shrine; he also knew what each of the others wanted and desired. Dharmalaxmi felt rage and revulsion for Gunasundari. When the women were alone, Dharmalaxmi complained bitterly to her daughters. ‘It is true—we eat what our son provides, which is the same as the daughter-in-law providing for us. We are helpless in our old age, so we are pushed around by a daughter-in-law. So be it. What else can she do? She has to bear the brunt of it. Why should and why would she have any affection or consideration for us?’ The daughters, too, added their bit, commiserating their mother’s hurt and helplessness and expressed their anger and righteous indignation at Gunasundari. Dharmalaxmi had tears in her eyes. Chanchal wiped them and said, ‘Ma, why are you so upset? The ways of the world are such that we have to sing praises of those who are ascendant’. Dukhba wept copiously and wailed, ‘All this is because of me!’ They had sat talking in the parsal of Jarashankar’s house. Sundargauri was also there, mixing mustard in the pickles. She recounted the entire episode to Gunasundari with a grave face.

Having heard her, Gunasundari said, ‘They are not to be blamed. The situation was such that their hurt is natural. I am not at fault, but that they should hold me guilty is not surprising at all. Pitaji has so much affection and compassion for me that he is forever finding faults with the others. What can I do so that he loves me a little less? Now I understand why I was being spurned by everyone. But Sundarbhabhi, you are promise-bound to tell me what happened with you’. Fair Sundargauri at once turned pale. Her lips froze. She stared at Gunasundari with eyes full of dread and a silent plea. Finally, she said, ‘Can it be that you do not ask me about it? If you forget about it, I shall be ever grateful to you’. ‘I do not want your gratitude. Tell me without any sense of shame or anxiety. Tell me like you would your own sister. Do I not share things with you?’ Sundargauri was about to relieve her heart of its burden, but she stopped herself again. ‘No. Let it be. I will tell you some other day.’ ‘No, we will not have this time together again. And I will find no peace until I hear about it. I swear upon this daughter of yours, if she is dear to you, tell me right now what happened,’ and saying so, Gunasundari picked up little Kumud and put her in Sundargauri’s lap. It was the widow who first realised the repercussions of this act. ‘Bhabhi, you are still not pure. Do you know that you have defiled me, this bed and the entire house!’ In her excitement, Gunasundari had completely forgotten about her state. In Vidya Chatura’s presence it was the outburst of joy that had caused her forgetfulness. And now it was the intense anguish, her own and Sundargauri’s, that had caused her to forget. Even Gunasundari was startled at her breach. ‘What can we do now, Sundarbhabhi? You go and take a bath, but can one bathe the bed? But you are digressing.’ Sundargauri replied, ‘I am helpless. I cannot bring myself to speak about it. Even to you. But until you know about it, I will also not be at ease. You know what it is in any case. So why do you ask me? I am required to go up to the store room every day to fetch grocery and other things. I do not know what has possessed him, but every time I go up, he comes and harasses me. So far I have managed to escape.

God has kept my virtue intact. But those who fetch water daily may slip and fall into the well one day.’ Gunasundari said, ‘From tomorrow onwards, you shall not go there. In any case I am to take my ritual bath tomorrow, after which I will myself go up and fetch things from the store room. But tell me what happened today? Why was Chandikabhabhi so angry with you?’ Sundargauri replied, ‘Please let us not even mention it. I am a widow, while she has a husband. I am a woman, and her husband is a man. That a wretch like me should be considered lowly is no surprise. What they say and do is right, and I must always be wrong. Why do you even ask me? If I could take my own life, why would I see such a day? I could jump into a well and drown or hang myself. But can I escape what is my destiny? I believe that if I take my life to escape this misery, the same suffering would befall me for the next seven births. If it were not so, would I have become a burden on my brother and now, on you? Yet, with all my sins I must have done something good, and so God resides in your heart and you take pity on me. Otherwise why should you do so much for me? What am I to you? But times are such that my own kin are not my own, and those like you take me for family. Bhabhi, I am incapable of taking my own life. Every time I go to the well, I pray I would slip and fall into it, but I don’t. And there is no one who would even give me a push. Why do you want to know what happened?’ Sundargauri could not go on she was trembling so much. Unable to speak any further, she put her head down in Gunasundari’s lap and sobbed, ‘Oh Bhabhi, you are truly like a mother to me! You gave me life!’ She was inconsolable. Racked by incessant sobbing and heaving, Sundargauri’s delicate body was exhausted; gradually she stiffened even as she kept trembling intermittently, and then finally she lay in Gunasundari’s lap still as a dead body. Gunasundari, too, had been weeping with her, clasping her to her bosom. She, too, was unable to speak and kept rubbing and caressing Sundar’s back, trying to comfort the widow. She suddenly realised that Sundargauri had stopped moving. She tried to lift her head, and failing in her attempt, Gunasundari cried out, ‘Sundarbhabhi! Sundarbehn! Please get up! I shall die if you feel so forsaken. I swear, this daughter of mine will die if you do not get up. Sundarbehn! Sundarbehn, please look up! Behn, take control of yourself. Don’t tell me anything if you can’t. I will not ask you anything more’. Sundargauri looked up and embraced Gunasundari even more tightly. ‘Bhabhi, you are more than a sister! More than a mother to me! Even my brother threw me out, but you gave me shelter. Who else but a mother would do that? Even a mother won’t care as much for a daughter’s pain as you have. If I don’t tell you, whom shall I tell?’ She wept aloud. Her cries could be heard downstairs. But everyone was still seething and self-absorbed with their individual woes and paid no attention to her weeping. Manchatura had just returned home. His anger had not yet subsided, and as he witnessed the farce in the house, it raised its hood again. He heard Sundargauri wailing in anguish and climbed up the stairs. The two women got up as soon as they saw Manchatura enter and tried hurriedly to wipe their tears and compose themselves. Manchatura enquired, ‘Why are you crying, Sundargauri? Gunasundari, what is the matter?’ Sundargauri was silent and would not lift her eyes from the ground. But Gunasundari could no longer control her anger. This was also a good opportunity to let him know the truth. She said loud and clear, ‘Pitaji, I do not know the cause of her tears, but I do know that she almost rushed into my room after the meal, followed moments later by Motabhai; but he ran up to his room as soon as he saw me. Sundarbhabhi has been crying ever since. She refuses to tell me what actually happened. I could ask the others; but it seems that even I have done some grievous wrong today as no one in the house is even willing to speak to me. Whom can I ask? If someone tells me what my fault is, I could assuage their hurt. But I am helpless when nothing is said to me. Sundarbhabhi, please stop crying.’ ‘I see. Now I understand everything.’ Manchatura was livid. He did not know what to say to either of them. He stormed down the stairs, striking each step with his stick as he went and speaking aloud for the whole house to hear, ‘That son of a rand! Couldn’t he find anyone outside that he wants to wreak havoc inside the house!

Bastard! Don’t you realise that she is like a mother to you! I suspected something all along!’ Manchatura climbed up to Ganchatura’s room and asked Chandika to leave the room. Ganchatura, taken aback, stared at his father. Manchatura raised his heavy stick and brought it down with all his strength on Ganchatura, who moved away, terrified. The stick struck the bed so hard that the bed cracked under its force. Manchatura had expended his energy; his anger had found a vent. He held Ganchatura by his shoulders and glared at his son, his eyes breathing fire. ‘Isn’t Sundargauri like a mother to you? Look here son, I will let you go this time. But if you ever bring her name to your lips or so much as glance at her again, I will finish you. I may be ill, but my body has strength enough for that.’ Manchatura turned to leave and on his way out, he said, ‘Remember, I will not pause to think that you are my own blood before I kill a son who is out to destroy the family. I am not afraid that the ruler will hang me. I gave you birth and truly, I will be the one to kill you with my own hands’. Manchatura had turned red with rage, his thick white hair glistened with perspiration as mogra flowers glisten with dew. His aged body throbbed with passion like waves in the sea. Dharmalaxmi, Chanchal and Dukhba had followed him as they saw him go up to Ganchatura’s room. Seeing him come out, they all filed down as quickly and stealthily as they had come. Manchatura slowly climbed down the stairs. Just as people are petrified to face a king in his wrath, the whole family silently lined up to see the patriarch enter his room. He flung his stick away and sat down on his bed, exhausted. Dharmalaxmi turned meek in the face of his wrath. She sent Chanchal to Gunasundari’s room. Chanchal, who had the rare ability to mask her true feelings, went in with a pleasant smiling face and brought both the sisters-in-law downstairs. Everyone hurriedly busied themselves in household work as if nothing in the world was the matter. Manchatura watched them all. Having done its work, his anger had subsided somewhat. He was satisfied. He twirled his moustache and smoothed it down with pale, wrinkled fingers. He said to himself: Good. I should be grateful that this was enough. In some other houses—God save them—there are people as thick-skinned as asses who delight in rubbing themselves in filth and mud. For them, all means would fail. For now, it looks as if He still keeps an eye over my house. Lord, I am merciful. Manchatura was happy to see Dharmalaxmi moving about trying to please Gunasundari. He thought: It is because of this old woman that everyone has gone back to their chores. Just as Shivji Mahadev lay down in the path of Ma Kalika as she wreaked destruction, this woman comes forward whenever I am in a rage. It is true—everyone gets what they deserve. Since my youth, I have a quick temper like that of Durvasa. She is patient and forbearing; even if I kick her, she would ask if my feet hurt! If I had not found such a deeply religious soul like her, I would certainly have murdered one or two wives by now, perhaps. Her parents helped her cultivate this disposition. May their souls rest in peace. This conversation with himself eased his fraught mind and helped Manchatura wash out the dregs of his rage. At peace with himself, he finally lay down to sleep. The rest of the day passed without incident. Everyone had had a heavy lunch and so were disinclined to have the evening meal. Only Gunasundari needed to eat, but she did not want a meal cooked only for herself. Once Manchatura went to sleep, the women began to make conciliatory gestures towards each other. They sought to explain and clarify their words and conduct and seemed eager to please, placate and show affection. Dharmalaxmi insisted that Gunasundari eat something. Chanchal offered to cook for her. Dukhba sat down with Sundargauri for a talk. Chandika sat on the swing and played with little Kumud, becoming childlike herself with the infant. The other children gathered around her and played. The constant daily friction, mistrust, resentment and conflict suddenly seemed to have passed just like an unpleasant dream. The family seemed peaceful and content once more, together and individually. Each one of them noticed this, but no one said anything. Ganchatura was the only one who could not partake of this newfound togetherness, tranquility and joy. He was not innately evil. He was also not stupid or bereft of a conscience. He was raised by Manchatura. He had spent time with his father travelling to various places and was a witness to his father’s debauched ways. The subordinates in Manchatura’s office would invite young Ganchatura to join them. They spoke freely about all manner of things in his presence. The office staff was also required to travel to remote interior parts of the country. The bored and weary staff members often took Ganchatura along with them and made him party to their lowly and debauched fun. The young lad did not have the discrimination or experience to see the follies of the elders; he, in fact, saw their unrestrained debauchery as a virtue. The elders took bribes, delighted in foul language; the bachelors among them would tease women in the neighbourhood. Unafraid of social stigma and unhampered by any sense of moral propriety, they sought out adolescent girls, pursued women who were in bad marriages, wives of naïve men, debauched women, women looking for company, barren women looking for men to impregnate them, women who used other women to get their way, wives of subordinates and friends who trusted them; they also sought out women who were under the influence of debauched mothers, friends or even brothers. A witness to such conduct, a young impressionable Ganchatura soon came to believe that these men were brave and manly and that all intelligent boys must be like them. He was brought up in this impure environment and when he grew up, he sought the same environment. Manchatura wielded lowly authority, earned money through dishonest means and spent it on all manner of vices. He had an appetite for debauchery and bawdy behaviour. Manchatura lorded over a company of vice. His subordinates were government employees, but he treated them as if they were his personal servants. The son naturally came under the spell of the father’s association. Manchatura, however, also had some rare qualities and extraordinary strengths which he forgot to pass on to his son. He had a tremendously strong personality. He was not servile to vice and debauchery and could keep these proclivities on a tight leash. He indulged in them when he wanted to; but when he was determined not to, even Indra’s divine consort Indrani could not entice him. Manchatura could will himself to be godly or satanic, and he took immense pride in this ability. He believed that religion and irreligion, merit and sin, his superiors and his subordinates were all inferior to him—and that he was servile to none. For him, manliness was to exemplify such behaviour. He was neither tempted by extreme happiness nor crushed by extreme pain; he was capable of laughter even when weighed down by immense sorrow. His passions were subject to his will; they surfaced when he desired and subsided at his command. He considered passions as insignificant as blades of grass. He enjoyed exercising power and displaying complete control—over his superiors, his subordinates, and over himself. If his superiors accepted his authority and gave him respect, Manchatura would use all the means at his command—intelligence, power and wealth— to help them in times of crisis and would not rest until he had succeeded. Some of his superiors had faced charges of bribery and similar misconduct; some had faced complex and knotty problems at work; some had to cope with criticism and machinations; some were sacrificed to the pride, vice or prejudices of their own superiors. Manchatura had shown them all a way out and saved them from a variety of complex problems by giving them real and timely assistance. Indebted and grateful, they all praised Manchatura’s intellect and would become servile to him. On the other hand, if a superior were to become opposed to him or create obstacles in his path, Manchatura’s intelligence and power were certain to trap him. He would consider it his great achievement in enticing the wife of such a superior and rest only when he publicly demonstrated his victory. The superior’s family was certain to be embroiled in strife; complaints would be made to higher offices. Such opponents would lose their social prestige, face criticism, ignominy and suddenly find that they had thousands of enemies, even amongst friends. Such a person was always under the threat of a beating either at home or outside. He would find no respite until, utterly harassed and cornered, he would admit defeat and beg and plead with Manchatura, appease him. Should it be a matter of surprise then if a man capable of bringing his superiors down to their knees was feared by his subordinates? Manchatura treated his subordinates like goats; he thought it beneath him to put them through any harassment or humiliation. He considered protecting them or helping them in need a sign of his superiority. He was also never taken in by their flattery. Manchatura had a motto: if one must cheat, one should cheat a king, and if one must kill, one should kill an elephant. He never took a paisa from the poor, nor did he take money from wealthy but good, god-fearing people; he did their work for free. But if a cunning man came to him, he would suck him dry of his money and do his work only after the man had pleaded with him. He would ensure that such a person remained beholden to him for life. Manchatura believed that to entice women within the family or of friends and relatives was a debased thing, and he despised those who did. He considered it an act of great cowardice and stupidity to entrap a woman whose husband had reposed trust in him. Associating with debauched women was not for him because in such relationships a man was ensnared by a lowly woman. In his view such men were effete. He felt that infatuation for a beautiful woman and spending money on her was akin to suspending one’s intelligence and a sign of utter stupidity. Manchatura’s debauchery was the result of extreme pride, ego and animosity. If these two forces were absent, his passions were also reigned in. If a woman were to insult Manchatura, within days she was sure to approach him and become his slave. Wise and virtuous women recognised his power and never acted haughty in his presence, instead preferring to address him respectfully as kaka, mama or bhai; Manchatura also never looked upon them with desire. Not only that, if such women appeared to stray, he would show them the right path and save them from debasement. But if a man were to lock horns with Manchatura or act haughty, his wife was certain to be trapped by Manchatura. Manchatura was a handsome man. Tall, broad, powerfully built and fair of complexion. In his youth, he cut his thick black hair short. They had a lustre all of their own. In his old age his hair turned grey but retained its lustre. He remained as attractive to women in his old age as he was in his youth. Women were drawn to him and submitted to his will. He spoke rarely, but when he did he spoke like a king, leaving his audience, even superiors, tongue-tied. He liked to exercise this ability of his, especially on women. Many debauched women infatuated with him would pursue him. He took advantage of their infatuation. Some who were not debauched but not strong-willed found him irresistible and willingly fell into his trap as moths fall into a lamp. Some intelligent women sought him out for his clever wit and conversation. Manchatura’s image and words would etch themselves upon the minds of women with refined sensibilities and intelligence, who would hover around him as bees swarm around a hive. Manchatura would permit them to pursue him, encourage their conversations and allow them to nurture false hopes. He enjoyed setting traps for them, but more than that he enjoyed not being entrapped by them. He truly believed he was not a slave to his passions, that such instincts danced to his tunes, and that the whole world was subject to his will. Manchatura believed himself to be like Shri Krishna who could remain unaffected by the world even when completely immersed in it. He put in practice such ideas and marvelled at his own ability to attain them. It was a source of both immense pride and joy for him. He would thus bring a woman to a point of total surrender, and at that crucial juncture he would not take the final steps. Of a thousand such encounters he would bring only one to fruition, but give hope to the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine women that they could have been the lucky one. Though dejected they would not lose hope. The arrogance of his youth did not entirely disappear with old age. But life taught him a lesson towards the end. At a time when he had almost given up his debauched ways, he contracted a disease from some woman, which proved incurable. All her life, Dharmalaxmi had borne with forbearance his vices and his wilfulness. She had remained silent hitherto. But in her approaching old age, she lost her patience. She sat weeping by his bedside and lectured him on moral conduct. ‘Oh, I am ill-fated indeed! Some overeat, some steal, while others pursue women. If you were one of them, I would have said that like them you, too, are lowly. Just as we cannot control our bodies, the lowly and the inferior cannot control their instincts. The wretches may even recognise that they do wrong and repent, but fail to reign in their passions. But you, you have absolute control over your passions. You are capable of the self-control of an ascetic. Whatever you do, you do on purpose. Those who do wrong on purpose commit twice the sin—they cannot even repent.’ She heaved a deep sigh and continued. ‘We are partners in sin and merit in equal measure. I am and I desire to be religious—to be born a human is not easy and it does not happen repeatedly. But is my knowledge of any use? I realise this and you do not. It is like trying to put gloss on dust. You sin, and I too must share in your sins. The merit that I garner through my good deeds is washed away and the sin of others attaches itself to me. I will have to bear the burden of your sins even in the next life. I have borne this burden since my youth. I have never uttered a word or done anything, nor once chastised you. Did my heart not burn at the sight of your other women? Once, you suspected me of some wrongdoing and felt much the worse for it. Think of how they must have scalded me, how they singed me. May God keep you well. I shall undergo my share of suffering in this life. Good. If I have suffered enough, I will not be born again to suffer. But alas! What can I do? Everything flashes before my eyes—I see nothing but darkness. It breaks my heart to see you thus. Shiv! Shiv! Shiv! Oh my strong, clever and capable husband, won’t realisation come to you even now? Won’t these grey hairs of yours force you to reflect? Won’t this illness teach you anything? I do not know how much more suffering is fated for me!’ She was quiet for a while collecting her thoughts, then continued. ‘By now you would have reached a pay of five hundred rupees. But we have to make do with little because of this one bad habit of yours. The body is here today and gone tomorrow. I am no longer worried about myself. But you have saved nothing. What will the children do? The younger one grew up with my brother and because of him, he earns something today. But the elder one has grown up in your shadow. You have found him a job and he carries on somehow. But your shadow is cast upon him. The merits and sins of parents must be borne by children as well. All your vices have flowered in him. He has neither your intelligence nor your abilities, but he imitates you. One day that boy is certain to fall, and that day there will be no one to help him rise. If I die before you, I would consider myself fortunate. But what will this boy eat? You are not going to leave him an inheritance. And whatever little is lying around in the nooks and crannies of the house will be spent on musical evenings or the children of debauched women will enjoy it. Throw it all into fire and let it burn to ashes! Each one must face what is destined for them. Even you will be born again. Have you ever considered what will become of you? Think about it. I am alive today but may not be tomorrow. This life will cease in a fraction of a second. Until then, I am bound to you by my destiny—thereafter what happens is not in my hands!’ Dharmalaxmi sat by Manchatura’s bedside and kept talking, wiping her tears intermittently. When she started speaking, Manchatura’s anger rose and he was about to tell her: Rand! Is this the time to say such things? But he stopped himself and waited for her to finish. As Dharmalaxmi narrated how his impure life had cast a shadow over his family, how his elder son had followed in his footsteps, like a warrior who leads his forces into the hands of the enemy by his own wilfulness and folly and comes to despise himself for it, Manchatura, too, began to despise himself. For years, he had deluded himself that what he had done was an act of courage and defiance. But as he realised that his actions had also planted the seeds of a noxious weed in his own family, his anger gave way to repentance. Shaken by disease and remorse, his conscience rose as arrogance and pride made way for thoughts of morality. His mind opened like the doors and windows of a house uninhabited and locked up for years. Just as one cleans the house with a lamp in one hand and a broom in another, Dharmalaxmi’s words on moral conduct entered his mind and gradually began to cleanse it and change it. These changes taking place within him were evident in the crease on his forehead, his eyes that blinked rapidly, in the colour of his face which turned crimson and then pale in succession, in the involuntary movement of his lips and in the unease of his body. As he realised his wife’s infinite forbearance and forgiveness towards him since the days of their youth, Manchatura recognised his evil, and he burnt within like a hair singed to its roots. It suddenly came home to him that he had no recognition whatsoever of any wrongdoing, and that his achievement was limited to wounding the hearts of women. In the dark night that his mind was in, Dharmalaxmi’s patience and forgiveness flashed like lightning. He knew that he deserved no mercy from her. Manchatura had never shed a tear since he was a young boy. A few tears now glistened in the old man’s eyes. He looked up at her finally and said, ‘You speak when it is too late. You give me counsel when I am on my death bed. Of what use is it to me now? Why didn’t you say this when you first came into this house as a young bride? Why did you decide to dig a well only after the fire was well and truly raging?’ His sleep-laden eyes were wide open as he spoke. They remained open as he kept looking at her, as if to capture her response with his eyes. His hand came to rest in Dharmalaxmi’s lap, as if seeking forgiveness. Dharmalaxmi took his hand in hers. ‘I know this is not the best time for me to say these things to you. If I were certain that you are never going to be cured of your disease, I would have said nothing. But my conscience tells me that tomorrow morning you will leave this bed. I am not so ill-fated. I am destined to die with all the auspicious signs of marriage intact on me. All that I have said today will prove beneficial to you once your health is completely restored. Hitherto, I never said anything because even if I had, you would have discarded it as useless. And if I had waited for you to get well, you would not have heard a word from me. I am old now, my desires have died; but your passions will be rekindled. Right now your eyes are open, and hence you are willing to see what I show you; your ears are alert and hence you hear me out. I know I cause you great pain by saying these things, but if I do not say them now, then when? Have you ever granted me the right to speak for your good and my good and the good of our family? How could I have said anything to you before now? This right which I have given to myself will last only until the day you get well. After that I will lose this right. This pinprick will save you from the agonies of death and ignominy—it is only in this hope that I have wounded you with barbs. My words must hurt, please forgive me! This is the most opportune moment for me to say these things, because it will protect your dharma and mine, and our family’s welfare. If I miss this opportunity, a second one of this kind would not present itself during my lifetime. I have seized the moment and I have been harsh to you. Please forgive me!’ The pious, devoted and loving wife capable of great forgiveness clasped her husband’s feet and wept, ‘Forgive me, please forgive me! I am hard as vajra and heartless as a sword. But what else can I do? I am married to a man as strong-willed as you. In my life I have come across many men big and small; but I found them all to be weaklings with little or no self-control. They all talk wisely until the moment of trial arrives; but at the first available opportunity, all men without exception are shaken from their resolve like children tempted by the sight of a toy. They entice innocent and virtuous women and are driven mad by their passions. The mind of man is effete, it melts in a moment, it rolls away like mercury. Men have no shame, no religiosity, recognise no relationships; they are not in possession of their senses, they do not understand the feelings of others; they relate to women only through bodily passion and desire, they seek nothing but the fulfilment of their desires. I have observed men who follow social customs and perform religious acts. I know well the conscientiousness of men of conscience, be they men of learning, ascetics or devotees. The authority of high officials is confined only to their offices, their power is only in their words. They are all slaves to their passions. Their greatness is false. And then there are those who come to us with their English learning. They say one should not accept bribes; they decry religion and insist that truth is the only religion. They criticise our religion and observances as mere superstition. We women are a thousand times better than these men who have received English education. You, too, are not ignorant of their base intentions with regard to women. If one were to even lightly squeeze a wet cloth, water would drip from it—their resolve is only as firm as that water. I have seen you make such men dance as if they were your puppets. Men are weaker and lowlier than women. I have hitherto seen only one man truly powerful and possessed of firm resolve and will. I have that man for my husband. I am proud of his manliness. I am proud that I am the wife of such a man. Women sing during the garba: My husband is equal to fifty-two brave men. At such moments, I am delighted. For I say to them, albeit in my mind, that all of you are lying—only I have such a husband. You possess the self-restraint to disregard a woman whose beauty entices the world as if she were disfigured and ugly. You can control your desires. I know from experience that all other men are made of straw; you are the only true man!’ As she praised her husband from her heart, Dharmalaxmi was filled with gladness. Her tears dried. The pride and joy she had once known in her youth came back to her in her old age. Manchatura, too, was overwhelmed to hear true praise from his wife. He sat up erect, looked at her affectionately and said, laughing, ‘All right, I understand everything that you have said. Now tell me what is it that you want from me? I will grant your wish. Tell me what is your desire? All your life you have kept my word, my honour, my whims and wishes. Do you think I am incapable of granting you this one wish?’ Dharmalaxmi quietly said, ‘Once you decide, the matter is entirely within your grasp. I only want you to make up your mind about things that are already within your grasp. The rest of mankind may resolve a thousand times but will not be able to keep it. But you, my husband, have only to make a resolve, and I know you shall keep it, always’. ‘All right, from today onwards I make the resolve.’ With these words Manchatura lay down again and closed his eyes. Dharmalaxmi felt that his pledge was a fulfilment of both his and her life. She knew that his pledge would not be false. This certainty gave her peace at last. She felt reborn and closed her eyes to fully experience the profound peace and joy that she felt within her. The devoted wife softly asked, ‘Is it a firm resolve?’ ‘Yes, it is a firm resolve,’ he spoke like one in deep slumber and his right hand raised itself as if in promise and fell into her lap. Manchatura had fallen asleep. She held his hand for some time, gazing at his imposing features, his closed eyelids and his silver moustache and hair ruffled gently by the breeze. She carefully placed his hand back on his bed and got up noiselessly. She stood there thoughtfully for a while, a hand on her heart. She willed and prayed with all her being that her husband’s body be restored to complete health by the power of his newfound purity and resolve. Thus reassured, she left him in the care of sleep. As she came out, quietly closing the door of his room behind her, Dharmalaxmi engrossed herself in domestic matters.

Pious Dharmalaxmi reformed Manchatura; but their eldest son was not to be reformed. Ganchatura possessed not even a fraction of his father’s will and self-restraint. He was incapable of grasping the power of his father’s intellect. Bereft of Manchatura’s formidable mental strength, the vices magnified a hundred fold in Ganchatura; they crushed all sense of discernment and forced their way just as the Niagara falls forcefully make their way through rocky terrain. Dharmalaxmi considered Ganchatura to be a lowly being. Tired of trying to reform him, she eventually gave up and left him to his fate. She would tell Manchatura that their son’s vices were because of him and that he should reform him. This was not easy. The father tried every trick he knew, but succeeded only partially. Manchatura was never fully cured of his disease, though he recovered enough to rejoin his post. He worked for three or four years. Then the disease that lay dormant resurfaced. Finally, he resigned from his post and came to live with his younger son. During these years, many opportunities came his way to tempt him to break the pledge he had taken at his wife’s insistence. Several women who had relations with him previously tried their utmost to lure him back into a relationship. He had many occasions to wield what he had hitherto considered to be manliness. But Manchatura now sought fulfilment and channelised his not inconsiderable energies elsewhere. He now considered it a blot upon his manhood and a sign of weakness if Dharmalaxmi were to believe that he was once again lured by lust. He was eager to demonstrate that he was not weak, and that he had the power to uphold his pledge. In his old age, he was enthused and possessed by the idea of being faithful to his devout and virtuous wife and of leading a pure and blameless life. He wanted above all to prove that he could control his demons and passions effortlessly, that his willpower was so strong that nothing was impossible for him. Dharmalaxmi had told him, ‘You have only to make a resolve, and I know you shall keep it’. Manchatura proved that her faith in him was not misplaced. Dharmalaxmi’s pride in her husband grew even stronger. She told everyone that her husband’s fidelity was as steadfast as Shri Krishna’s detachment and the asceticism of Rishi Durvasa. She felt that her husband had at last broken free from his cage of lust. She saw him like a lion break free from bondage and roar to celebrate his newfound freedom. It was as if the joys of old age had repaid all the agonies and uncertainties of youth. Dharmalaxmi had only one more aspiration. She told Manchatura, ‘Ganchatura is caught in a trap even stronger than yours. But he possesses not an iota of your strength. You have only one more duty to perform—set him free from his bondage’. Old Manchatura, experienced in such matters, made a great many efforts to reform his son. Initially, he tried to keep Ganchatura so occupied with work that he would not have the time to indulge his vices. But Ganchatura found the time as easily as water slips through a sieve. Manchatura found for him good friends; but he made his friends take to his ways. Manchatura tried to isolate him from his friends; Ganchatura met them secretly and cheated on his father. Manchatura tried to show him that a life of vice may result in incurable disease and the poor physical condition that he himself had been reduced to. Ganchatura was aware of the dangers of disease, but he was blinded by lust and could not free himself from this ghost. Manchatura pointed out other dangers; he told Ganchatura he might lose his job, face criminal charges, ignominy, bring disrepute to the entire family and meet an untimely and gruesome death. He pointed out thousands of such dangers, but to no effect. Manchatura pursued his son with determination. He spread rumours that the women Ganchatura associated with were diseased, that the husbands of some of these women had hired killers to murder Ganchatura. He even sent hired thugs in pursuit of his son who threatened Ganchatura in the name of the husbands. He had armed men chase Ganchatura right up to his bed room; they would return without harming him and report that Ganchatura had a lucky escape that day. Manchatura would berate and abuse him saying, ‘Rascal, don’t you know you are being pursued by your death!’ Frightened for his life, Ganchatura grew weary. In face of extreme fear, his lust seemed to subside. Manchatura felt that his ploy had paid off at last. Ganchatura lost his job and some modicum of sense seemed to dawn upon him. His body grew feeble, which also affected his lust. Jobless, he was forced to seek shelter with the younger brother, which he resented. He felt confined and dependent. His lust seemed to evaporate. But Ganchatura was innately weak of mind and so the impulses that lay dormant suddenly raised their head. He did not have the discrimination to recognise that Sundargauri was his brother’s widow. Moreover, he had also kept his hand on Gunasundari’s shoulder—that was the ultimate mistake. Everyone in the family now knew what they should have never known. He had crossed his limits and consequently, Manchatura’s patience had also run its course. To add insult to injury, his wife Chandika had wailed and beaten her breasts before him as if he were already dead. After his father left with a dire warning, Ganchatura was left all alone in his room. He felt that death was preferable to a life of such disgrace. He was incapable of earning his livelihood and everyone, including his wife, was behaving as if they were strangers. Ganchatura thought: I have no one I can call my own. With what face can I go to my family? Who needs me anyway? Besieged by such gloomy thoughts, his mind was in a whirl. He sat alone in his room from two in the afternoon till late in the night. No one thought of bringing a lamp up to his room after dark. No food was cooked, hence no one came to ask him if he wanted to eat. Ganchatura felt that the neglect was intentional. As he sat brooding in the dark room, hours passed. He thought of ending his life by pulling the sacred janoi around his neck. He folded the thread three or four times to strengthen it, looped it around his neck and pulled. But he lacked the courage to pull it hard enough to strangle himself. He tried to muster the will to end his life. Just then, Ganchatura saw a light reflect on the wall opposite his room. He could also hear the footsteps of two persons. Who were they? What was their purpose? Manchatura had gone to sleep after giving Ganchatura a tongue- lashing. The women had patched up and were busily chatting away and working. Ganchatura was the only one who could not forget what had happened. That evening after dark, Dharmalaxmi went to talk with Manchatura. Gunasundari, Chandika and the others were in the courtyard. They could overhear snatches of the old couple’s conversation.

A worried Dharmalaxmi asked Manchatura as to what had really transpired earlier in the day. She wanted to know what he intended to do with Ganchatura. As he narrated to her the details, Manchatura’s voice rose in irritation. ‘I cannot reform him. Even if he could be reformed, I shall make no further attempts. I am tired of him. I give up. His vices will only go with his death. Only his wife could have reformed him. When a woman goes astray, her husband must be blamed; likewise when a man takes to vice, his wife, too, is to be blamed. If for nothing else, they are to be blamed for not attempting to reform the other. I am not going to live as long as he does. He will never realise his options; hence he will never reform himself. What can we do? If he does not mend his ways, his wife will have to bear the brunt. Therefore, if she knows how, she should try and change him. If she does not know, it is her funeral. Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari, in the goodness of their hearts, provide for Ganchatura and Chandika—but can they do so all their life? You changed me, didn’t you? Similarly, Chandika should try and change him. Or else the two of them can go jump into a ditch.’ Manchatura said nothing more. Dharmalaxmi did not want to excite him any further. She got up and came away. Chandika heard this conversation from the courtyard. She was somewhat foolish, but she was naturally jealous of Ganchatura’s affairs with other women. Like Dharmalaxmi, she too had faced these experiences ever since her marriage at a young age. But she did not have Dharmalaxmi’s patience and forgiveness. Lifelong jealousy and insecurity had turned her into a cantankerous nag. Over time, jealousy and a perpetual irrational irritability became part of her nature. Chandika was well aware of this, but she lacked the strength to fight back envy. She was envious of Sundargauri because Gunasundari was fond of her. She burned with envy because Gunasundari had a house, a good husband who loved her, while she lacked both. She would beat her breasts and lament when alone; she would berate and abuse Ganchatura, beat her children. She would not extend any help to Gunasundari with household work and feel pleased whenever Gunasundari encountered any problem. If someone scolded Chandika, she would pay no heed. If Manchatura praised Gunasundari, she would make faces at him. If Gunasundari did something for their mother- in-law, Chandika accused her of sycophancy. The only person she was not envious of was Dukhba—because Dukhba had nothing that Chandika could be envious about. When she overheard Manchatura say that she was also to be blamed for her husband’s vices and her own misfortune, it was the last straw. Chandika lost her temper. But she could not respond to Manchatura, so her anger and distress found no outlet. Not knowing what to do, Chandika went to Gunasundari and suddenly broke down. She said, ‘Bhabhi, did you hear that? Even this fault lies with me! What can a wretch like me do! How can I reform others of their vices? I would accept the charge if I had done wrong. They should pity me and my wretched plight. Instead, they call me vile! All right, let them say what they want. I was ill-fated to be married into this house, so everyone’s wrongs become my fault. That must be so. Why did I not die!’ Gunasundari knew that what her worldly wise father-in-law had said was not without substance. But if she were to point this out, Chandika would have turned against her. Chandika had hitherto always remained distant and cold. Now she had come to her of her own will, unexpectedly opened her heart, wept and sought advice. Gunasundari knew that another opportunity like this was unlikely to present itself to gain Chandika’s affection and trust and to draw her nearer. She said to console her elder sister-in-law, ‘Bhabhiji, let it be. Don’t cry. What are we to do? He is an elder of the family. How can men understand the workings of a woman’s mind?’ They spoke for about an hour. Gunasundari wisely allowed Chandika to unburden herself first. Chandika felt new affection for such a patient listener. This was the real achievement of this small gesture of Gunasundari. At length, she also showed Chandika a way out of her predicament. Chandika’s envy slowly made way for trust and affection and she listened attentively to Gunasundari. ‘Bhabhiji, it is within your power to reform Motabhai. Let me tell you how. You should fulfil his desires. You know him well; you should anticipate his wants. Once you take him into your hands, you can pull the strings like a puppeteer. It is not something you cannot do. Once you fulfil his desires, he will be your slave.’ Chandika snapped, ‘No, that is not possible for me! He wants that I should ignore all his philandering with lascivious women. I cannot do that—absolutely not!’ ‘Why do you fume and fret? What we want is to cut these women off. I will show you a way. Motabhai will not even look at them and you shall be the focus of all his attention.’ ‘That will only be in my next life for sure!’ ‘Bhabhiji, the way those women please him, you should, too. You should keep him under your control to the extent that he won’t set eyes on anyone else.’ ‘My attempt to control him would inevitably result in a quarrel.’ ‘No, why should it be so? You should act wisely and calmly and always be sweet of tongue. He can get angry only if you lose your temper. We are concerned here with the fruits of our actions. You should willingly agree to all his suggestions, but get him to do exactly what you want.’ ‘I do not know how to do these things.’ ‘Bhabhiji, but you are intelligent and most capable! Tell me, is there anything that you cannot do if you really want to?’ Gunasundari said with a laugh. Chandika was surprised and pleased to hear her own praise; no one had ever praised her before. Gunasundari chatted pleasantly with her, distracted her with jokes, and they went up to her and Ganchatura’s room. The three of them spent a few hours talking. Gunasundari generously praised Chandika and gave her due respect, acting as if she were subservient to her elder sister-in-law. And like a mother who overlooks her son’s follies, she also pretended to have forgotten Ganchatura’s transgression. In the few hours that she spent with them, Gunasundari sucked out the poison of envy from Chandika. They became like friends. Even Ganchatura, who until a little while ago had felt utterly alone, unwanted and bereft of family, began to look upon Gunasundari as a motherly figure. By the time Gunasundari finally went down, happy and content at what she had been able to achieve, it was almost midnight. Everyone else had gone to sleep. Sundargauri had slept off on the floor of the store room with her head resting on the raised threshold. Gunasundari gently woke her up and sent her to bed. Then she lay down in her own bed. But sleep eluded her. The next day, her period of impurity was going to end. She thought of all the many tasks and challenges that awaited her. She must reorganise the household, keep everyone happy and be a source of joy for her husband. All these thoughts did not allow her to sleep. The clock struck twelve; then one; then two, but there was no trace of sleep in her eyes. So Gunasundari talked to herself. Oh God, guide me through this ocean! Until the other day, I believed that a joint family was a boon, a source of endless joy. But this is no joy—only conflict and endless blood-boil! Each one has a mind of their own; their true colours are different. Each one has a bad habit as large as a tree; and when their bad habits are curbed, I get all the blame! I have to care for all their desires, but there is no one to care for mine. No one considers what my feelings are. My condition is like that of a washerman’s dog that belongs neither to the washing ghats nor to the washerman’s house. This world has been likened to a stormy sea, and the comparison is not futile. I have already had such varied experiences. Who knows what more lies in store for me. Pitaji, Mataji, Chanchalbehn, Dukhba, Chandikabhabhi and Motabhai Ganchatura—all of them have one quality and one vice. This Sundargauri sleeps so soundly! Sleep, my sister, sleep. You are far happier compared with me. You need worry only for yourself. But I must worry for all of you. And now this girl! Who knows what concerns she will bring me once she grows up? But my beloved Chatura, you have far greater worries than I do. And I cannot share them. Oh, how his face withered today! Just a word from me, and his face fell. He had come to spend just a few moments of joy with me after months, and he went away looking dejected. Who knows what he thinks and feels? Wretch that I am, I did not even ask him. But what do I need to ask? It is apparent. He is worried about the family. He says nothing. But he has eyes and ears, he sees and listens. And he is concerned about me as well. He earns little, but the expenditure is huge. He would be less concerned if all these problems were to disappear. If I cannot even manage that much, then I am of little use, am I not? Pitaji is stern and prone to fits of rage. He could turn even a wedding celebration into a funeral. But apart from him, who else takes pity on me or even thinks of me? But of what use is his compassion to me? I do not want to be honoured and feted and praised. What I do is for the love of God. The family of my Chatura is my family. However they might be, whatever they might be, can he get rid of his family? Hence, what is his is also mine. Pitaji will care for me. My Chatura will care for me. But how am I to care for him? He must have gone to bed with who knows how many worries. It is true that an irritable, nagging nature turns one into a beast. Chandikabhabhi almost crushed Sundarbhabhi in her rage. She also silenced Motabhai. But how can one blame her? What a source of infernal pain her husband must be! How can she just watch in silence? But Jethji truly knows no limits—how his lust has blinded him! How lascivious, how weak can a man be? How he must repent now. He has been punished. But how much more punishment must lie in wait for him. Lust is a terrible thing, and however strong we are, we all submit to it. Oh my Chatura! We were barely together for a few moments. So be it. This social practice of segregation after childbirth is not such a bad thing after all. A rain-laden cloud finds no relief in solitary thunder. Similarly when we are alone together, mere talk does not satisfy us. All passions are bad, be it lust, anger or any other. When passions rule, humans cease to be human and become animal. They can think of neither their own nor of the good of others; a person loses sight of everything else. Or else why would Motabhai mistake me for Sundargauri? Poor Sundar, her condition is a hundred times worse than mine. Isn’t she a human being? Doesn’t she have needs and desires? But God snatched away what He gave her, and so young. I am blessed. His blessings upon me are far more generous than on Sundar and both my sisters-in-law. Or else, my Chatura, without you ... Without you ...! Why did such inauspicious words, why did such an inauspicious thought even occur to me? What if they were to come true? How desolate my life would be! How could I live without my Chatura? How would I pass the days? Sahasrai is alive, but without him Dukhba has turned sour. Is it surprising that Dukhba’s nature has become what it is? What state would my Chatura be in if I had died? Gunasundari imagined herself dead and pictured a lonely and vacant Vidya Chatura. Tears filled her eyes. She tried to shut her eyes and go to sleep. Infant Kumud suckled at her breast; with her mother’s milk she also drank her melancholy thoughts. Gunasundari sought refuge in the wooden plank of the bed. She slept close to it, touching it. When at last she fell asleep, she murmured in her sleep and wept softly. The night progressed quickly. The whole house slept. As the hours moved on stealthily, the night was no longer young. And just as old age creeps in after youth, dawn was about to break. The morning dew cooled the world. Gunasundari was an early riser. She opened her eyes and sat up in bed. The silence was total—not a whisper could be heard in the house. She stared at the lamp that still burned. The myriad concerns of the previous night sprouted in her mind like seeds. She was to take her ritually purifying bath and take over the reins of the household today. She eagerly thought of ways to put her experiences to good use. In a short while, she had thought everything through. She asked herself: What was there to think of? It was simple—I must take all responsibility. I must get the daily provisions so that Sundar is not required to go up and face Ganchatura. The provisions, which were required often, should be stored downstairs. I must prepare well before sitting down to cook. The one who serves food has the position of a queen who provides; someone else must be given this responsibility. All other sundry tasks should be completed while others take their meals. Cooking does not require the use of speech; hence all instructions to servants and children should be passed on while I cook. Sundar will look after my daughter; this will also keep her happy. I must rest for an hour after lunch—only if I care for my body will I be able to care for others. If I keep feeling sorry for myself like Dukhba, suffering will attach itself to me for life. Why would I want that? I must also get back to my studies—my Chatura would be very happy for it. After studies, I must go to the temple and take the children with me. This would give me exercise and help digestion. On my return, I must prepare for dinner. In the evening, I should spend time with the family. And the night shall belong only to me and my Chatura. Until then Gunasundari had not seriously thought of what to do. That morning she applied herself and found a way out. Sometimes one has to remind oneself to think. Gunasundari had understood how to economise on her work and learnt how to work without taking help from others; she also knew the advantages of being large-hearted. Through her diligence and acumen, Gunasundari quickly set the household smoothly on sail. Her quiet forbearance stitched shut all bickering tongues. Her generosity gave no scope for envy to flourish; starved of fodder in a short while envy died out. Her cheerfulness and affection ruled over the family. She set everyone free and accepted regimentation for herself. Her virtues enslaved everyone and they regarded her as superior to themselves. Vidya Chatura regained his peace and his happiness. He credited Gunasundari for this. Gunasundari’s responsibilities did not end with assigning all the work to herself and apportioning her time accordingly. It enabled her to run the household efficiently without having to ask or expect any help from anyone. Gunasundari took upon herself the burden of the man of the house, that of alleviating difficulties for everyone without their having to ask for it. She aspired to serve everyone selflessly and gain their trust. She hoped to keep them happy and entertained. She also aspired to lead them on the path of noble virtues. The expert in household economy sought to minimise expenses and maximise happiness. She read the Ramayana and the Mahabharata during the day and in the evening. She gradually weaned the conversation away from domestic matters and gossip to introduce the insights of seers like Valmiki and Vyasa. She would narrate interesting and illuminating episodes from these texts and explain them, enabling the others to share and appreciate their teachings on life in this world as well as the next. In her role as teacher, there was a newfound respect for her in the family. Gradually a situation developed that people were hesitant to speak vengeful, angry or distasteful words that might hurt others. What others fail to achieve by anger, deceit, force and punishment, Gunasundari achieved through her kind and gentle words. People felt hesitant to act contrary to her wishes, albeit unspoken, and if they did, they were rebuked by someone else, not her. Ganchatura was without work. Vidya Chatura did not know what to do about it. He tried to get him a job wherever there was an opening, but failed. Many a times he requested Jarashankar to find his brother a job. Jarashankar had grown weary of Ganchatura’s vices. Every time Vidya Chatura broached the subject, Jarashankar was quick to retort, ‘In the rule of kings like Mallaraj, his employees have to be as careful as one is while walking on a sword’s edge. Your brother’s vices are such that he would rob us all of our jobs and food. The wise thing therefore is for you to provide for him from your earnings so that the rest of us can feed our families and retain our employment. In a few years he would be considered too old for employment. Your father earned his “pension” and left his job, but this one lost both his pension and his job. If you are looking after one, then look after the other as well’. Vidya Chatura was unable to share such responses with anyone else. No one knew of the real reasons for his failure to find employment for Ganchatura and remained dissatisfied with him. Gunasundari took upon herself what her husband had failed to do. One day with this intent she visited Jarashankar Mama’s house. She spoke to his wife and with her help broached the subject with him. Jarashankar was amused that Gunasundari should plead the case of her elder brother-in-law, but his response was the same as he had given Vidya Chatura. Gunasundari had an answer ready. She said what her husband had been unable to say. ‘Mamaji, what you say is true. But just as the ignorance of adolescence is remedied by old age, the remedy for vice is experience. A person does not remain unchanged for ever. My plea to find Jethji a job is not because I want them to leave my house and set up their own. Being gainfully occupied reforms even those who have taken the path of vice—Jethji is already on the path of reform. Mamaji, you cannot escape your responsibility. Children may turn against us, but can parents decline to be parents?’ Jarashankar laughed at her advocacy. ‘Beta, you may give your jeth a ‘certificate’ of good behaviour out of your generosity and enthusiasm, but I do not believe it. If Ganchatura is not reformed, do you take the responsibility of reforming him? If you accept to be a guarantor for him, I may consider.’ Gunasundari was prompt to respond, ‘Is that all? All right, I take it upon me. But you have given me your word, Mamaji, and you must be true to it.’ Jarashankar could not refuse Gunasundari. In a few days, a position appropriate to Ganchatura’s abilities was found for him in Ratnanagari. Some days later, Jarashankar’s wife told Ganchatura and Chandika how the job was found for him. Both of them felt beholden to Gunasundari and repented their past behaviour towards her. Ganchatura was deeply ashamed that he had inadvertently touched Gunasundari. If the earth had opened up and accepted him, he would have willingly disappeared into it, such was his guilt and repentance. Ganchatura wanted to change Gunasundari’s opinion of him, especially with regard to his conduct towards Sundargauri—this became his primary objective. The man who could not be reformed by his own father was changed by Gunasundari and by his own sense of shame. Gunasundari was destined to do more for him and his wife. There was a time when Chandika would haughtily say, ‘What do I need Gunasundari for?’ But times changed. Gunasundari had to look after Chandika’s children, too. Chandika’s elder son Hariprasad was a good-natured boy; his wife Manohari was older than him. When Ganchatura had lost his job, Manohari had gone to live with her parents. Manohari was tall, intelligent and beautiful. She was in the bloom of adolescence while her husband was still childish; he was also less intelligent than her. She was youthful and passionate and her beauty attracted a lot of young men. It was well known that Manohari and Hariprasad were a mismatch. Some lascivious men saw this as an opportunity. People sang bawdy songs about Manohari. Her name was scribbled on public walls. Every time she ventured out, lewd comments would fall on her ears; she could sense eyes staring at her. Every time she danced the garba a crowd would gather around; some even threw pebbles at her to attract her attention or pulled at her clothes. If she walked alone, some men would brush against her on purpose or follow her while others would walk ahead and turn their heads to watch her. Manohari was exasperated and frightened by such harassment. She would ignore such advances and unwanted attention. People sent anonymous letters to her and her husband. Even at the temple, people never missed a chance to say a few lewd words to her, and if she was in a crowd, some took even greater liberty with her. When she joined the community feast, people spoke in whispers about her; some spoke openly. Over time, Manohari, too, became brazen. She was no longer bothered by these remarks and lewd gossip. The gossip was not without substance either. She invariably had a tryst with all the romantic men who passed through town. She reasoned that with a husband like hers, she had a licence for some promiscuity. She wanted her husband to grow up so she could be freed from such promiscuous tendencies. Hariprasad invariably got to hear of all the gossip about his wife. In anger, he took to beating Manohari. But she became immune to his beating and sometimes she would even hit back. Sometimes she would mock him and say, ‘Come on, beat me. I take your beating because I want to. Or else you can’t even raise a finger at me’. Manohari had driven Chandika mad. The mother constantly egged on her son to reform Manohari and suggested various ways of doing so. Manohari felt that her mother-in-law was turning her husband against her and so she tended to disregard everything her husband said. Sometimes she complained about Hariprasad’s beatings to her paramour, who would beat up Hariprasad either in the school or in the streets and would take an undertaking from him that he would not beat Manohari in future. Chandika was hugely relieved when Manohari decided to go and live with her parents. But when she chose to come back and live with the rest of them in Vidya Chatura’s house, Chandika grew anxious and apprehensive. God knows what new woes await me now, she thought. One day all the women had sat down for lunch. Gunasundari was busy with something and had not joined the others for the meal. Little Kumud was in Manohari’s care. Manohari sat playing with Kumud on a swing on the first floor, singing aloud as she swayed on the swing. Going, going ... going away This youth of mine is going Like trickling water Like the arc of a star My youth is wasting away A woman with a boy husband Is in an ill-starred match— Her youth wastes away Like she whose husband is away She is married yet a widow— Oh, her youth wastes away The mother-in-law nags her The husband is mother’s pet— Oh, her youth wastes away Such a wife weeps; the widow weeps, too Oh, their youth wastes away The song infuriated Chandika. But what could she do? Manohari was sharp of tongue and quick to retort. Everyone else laughed when they heard the song and exchanged furtive glances. Gunasundari also heard the song. Manohari began to sing a new song more suggestive than the previous one. She sang lustily and full-throated in rhythm to the swing. I can’t bear it, I can’t stand it I can’t bear this youth of mine I see all my friends carousing and I can’t stop these eyes from staring This mismatch has made of me a A jealous woman: my boy-husband holds no charm I’m promised that in four years, he’ll become a man But by then I will be an old hag My untamed youth won’t wait But I contain myself somehow

Chandika could bear it no longer. She left her food and got up. Gunasundari realised that she had lost her temper. To prevent a confrontation, she quickly intervened, cajoled Chandika and sent her back to her meal, promising she would speak to Manohari herself. The song had stopped. Manohari was playing with Kumud, holding her high up in the air, rocking her in her arms and showering kisses on her. Gunasundari came up and silently stood watching. Manohari had her back to Gunasundari and so was not aware of being watched. Seeing her mother, little Kumud smiled, extending her arms and kicking her legs, wanting to go to her. Manohari realised that Gunasundari had come up and that she might have heard the bawdy song. She felt somewhat ashamed then. She got up from the swing and came towards Gunasundari, her cheeks flushed. Seeing that Manohari still possessed a sense of shame, Gunasundari felt that all was not lost and she was pleased. Gunasundari was hardly five or seven years elder to Manohari. Despite being an aunt-in-law to her, Gunasundari could take advantage of her age and talk as friends. Sometimes the advice of peers is most effective. Gunasundari felt that Manohari may have taken to bad ways, but that she was intelligent and could grasp the message quickly. If Gunasundari were to speak to her affectionately as an equal, Manohari could be influenced and reformed. Gunasundari thought: If I were to confront her and point out her errors she is sure to take affront; she is still a child, wilful and petulant. Hence, the best way would be to befriend her and make her realise her follies herself. I should say nothing by way of advice but wait for her to admit her mistakes. This mismatch is the outcome of social custom. She is young and her youthful passions have found an outlet. Her child husband behaved childishly and Chandika’s responses are characteristic of her nature. What can poor Manohari do? No one guided her to the path of virtue, so she took the path that her youthful passions dictated. As Manohari shyly approached her, Gunasundari quickly thought of a response. She sat down with her on the swing and said appreciatively, ‘You have a good voice. What is it you were singing?’ Manohari blushed and looking down at Kumud who was in her lap, replied, ‘Nothing, just a few lines’. Manohari could retort brazenly to her mother-in-law, but in presence of Gunasundari who was her aunt-in-law she was tongue-tied. She felt restrained. She thought: Why did Kakiji have to hear my song? What am I to tell her? Intelligent and capable of recognising goodness, Manohari was aware of Gunasundari’s virtues. Chandika had none of Gunasundari’s qualities and therefore her attempts to reform Manohari had only made her more defiant. Manohari got up from the swing. She played with Kumud, kissed her and pressed the child to her bosom and said to divert Gunasundari from any talk of her singing, ‘Kakiji, how did this little one recognise you? You are not even paying attention to her. She is delicate as a petal. She compels us to love her’. As they sat talking on the swing, Gunasundari slowly coaxed Manohari to open up. She also advised Manohari during the course of the conversation, but in a manner that it did not clash with the girl’s nature. When Manohari finally spoke up, it proved that Gunasundari’s advice had found its mark. ‘Kakiji, tell me what wrong have I done? But ask my mother-in-law how often she has filled his ears with stories about me? It was my fate that I should be in such a mismatched marriage. He is just about to grow out of childhood, but his mother wants him to be completely devoted to her. I am young, am I not? I might have some desires, too, isn’t it? But she can’t bear it even if he buys me a comb worth a few paisas. She calls him weak and unmanly. If he comes up to my room in the afternoon even for a glass of water on his return from school, she calls us shameless and brazen in the presence of outsiders. My husband is after all her son—why should she be envious of us? It would be another matter if I were to talk to someone else. She behaves as if she has forgotten her own youth. Kakiji, you do all the household work, all the drudgery; Kakaji does the work of the state. But when you are alone for a few moments and spend time gazing into each other’s eyes, it would not be a sin, would it? And if someone were to object to that, their eyes should be plucked out, isn’t it!’ Manohari gesticulated animatedly as she spoke, made angry faces and pursed her lips. Gunasundari was amused and laughed at the sight. Young Manohari who kept the company of lowly people did not realise that she should not be saying such things to Gunasundari. She was slightly taken aback by Gunasundari’s laughter. The girl realised that her words were inappropriate, and that if she had spoken such words to her mother-in-law, by now they would have quarrelled.
