Gunasundari said in jest, ‘You are clever, one has to admit. You thought if you take my example, I would have nothing to say. But your mother-in-law is your elder; she knows something more of the ways of the world than you. She must have thought that she should teach you the ways of our family. And hence she would have told you certain things. I will try and see to it that she does not speak harshly to you henceforth. But Manohari, your conduct should also be such that she has no opportunity to say anything unpleasant to you’. Manohari replied, ‘All right, but you will see that she will not be able to restrain herself. If she does not scold me, she will scold her son. Kakiji, you do not know her nature. If I spend time with you, she will tell me to carry my complaints to you and say that she has nothing more to do with me. You do not know that her eyes are full of envy. You will realise it only when you yourself face it. Nandi the bull knows the true nature of Mahadev; similarly only a daughter-in-law knows the true character of her mother-in-law.’ Gunasundari realised there was some truth to what loquacious Manohari had said. She affectionately placed her hand on Manohari’s head and said, ‘All right, but what if she were to stop saying things about you to Hariprasad or anyone else?’ ‘So what? How do I know what she likes? She does a thousand vile things which I can neither imagine nor tolerate. I am not her slave. I will never be her slave,’ said Manohari with a toss of her head. Gunasundari gently persisted, ‘Let that be, but you will do what I ask of you, won’t you?’ ‘All right, I will. But Kakiji, let us be clear, I am not going to follow my mother-in-law’s dictates. That will never happen, never ever. I don’t even like looking at her face. She has stopped short of nothing while harassing me. I will do what you ask me to do because you know my pain. If you tie me with a cotton thread, I will gladly accept that bondage. But if she were to tie me with thick ropes, I will wriggle free and make a scene to top it all!’

Gunasundari gradually took Manohari in her hands. She also spoke to Chandika and she told her a thing or two. She taught Chandika to be happy at the joy of her son and daughter-in-law and to set them free, within certain limits. She proved that young ones cannot be reformed by scolding. She told Chandika that she must always praise Manohari in presence of her son. She gave Chandika the assurance that she would reform Manohari and that Chandika would have her way with Manohari, but only through Gunasundari’s mediation. It took a lot of effort over many days for Gunasundari to accomplish this. She ensured that Manohari spent as much time with her as possible; she took her with her whenever she went out and urged her to dress up; she fulfilled some of her youthful desires. Manohari began to understand which of her desires could be fulfilled and which she would have to learn to suppress for the time being. Gunasundari did not prevent Manohari from expressing her youthful desires but taught her to impose limits on herself. If Manohari were to speak about men, Gunasundari would cleverly change the subject to Hariprasad and his qualities. Gradually, Manohari, too, grew fond of her husband. She did not become completely submissive, but her haughtiness was restricted to her dealings with outsiders; she was quick to pounce on anyone who spoke ill of her family. Gunasundari kept Manohari’s youthful exuberance under control until Hariprasad attained maturity. As the couple become more compatible in age, body and mind, Gunasundari made it possible for them to cohabit happily. Chandika used to take pride that she was not beholden to Gunasundari for anything. But Gunasundari’s conduct made Chandika profoundly grateful and obliged to her. Earlier Chandika had fought hard to retain her pride; now pride was replaced by repentance and humility. Though she was younger, Gunasundari had proved more mature in terms of her abilities and qualities and had assumed the role of the elder between them. Chandika often went to Gunasundari for help and succour. ‘How shall I ever thank you?’ she would say. ‘Your Jeth has completely changed—it is as if a man who could not live without meat now drinks only milk. It is easier to capture and subdue a snake, but Manohari could not be subdued by anything. Even if she were confined to the nether world, she was capable of jumping up to the skies. But you have made her as compliant as a snake charmer’s snake. How will I ever repay your gratitude? My own temper was so harsh—and let me admit, I was given to envy as well—but you have changed me. What praises can I sing of your virtues? The one who gave you such an apt name truly deserves praise.’ In response, Gunasundari would simply smile and change the topic. If she had to respond she would say, ‘How have I done anything at all? You have all these qualities and hence you have taken these things positively. If you have changed, it is because of your own abilities and efforts’. Gunasundari’s responsibilities to the family were not yet over. She was concerned about the condition of her two sisters-in-law. Dukhba was a permanent source of heartburn to her parents. Her husband Sahasrai wandered from place to place and never even wrote a letter to Dukhba. Their daughter Kumari had attained marriageable age. Over time, Gunasundari befriended Dukhba. But the resolution of her problems required money. Vidya Chatura’s limited income was entirely spent on his large household. Gunasundari knew this well. She found a way out from resources that were within her means. One day when she saw Vidya Chatura in a balanced frame of mind, she broached the subject of Dukhba’s problems. He heard her out. He, too, felt that something should be done and sought Gunasundari’s advice on the matter. Gunasundari looked around to make sure they were alone, and said, ‘Kumari’s marriage must take place. There is no option. No one speaks about it, but don’t we know of its necessity? If we don’t take the responsibility, who will? I feel that to incur a debt is not right. You deposit my gold and jewels as security and borrow money against it. We shall save money over the next four years or so and reclaim it on payment of dues. We shall be able to invite Sahasrai for this occasion. All the money will not be spent on the marriage; what remains can be used to repay his debts’. Vidya Chatura could not help but smile. He said, ‘Gunial, you speak as if gold and jewels are just lying around waiting to be picked. What will you do once your ornaments are pawned?’

It was a question about the future. A ponderous question. Gunasundari thought about it for a moment, trembling inside. Then she put her hands on her hips, looked up at him and said, ‘If I am ill-fated, what use would ornaments be for me? If my destiny turns against me, what is the guarantee that these ornaments will also not prove unlucky? If I am destined to suffer, how will human effort help? But if I have trembled at the thought of sin, even God will not forsake me in times of sorrow. Don’t I have Sundarbhabhi’s example before me? Therefore please do as I ask you. As long as you are there with me, I possess the equivalent of countless priceless ornaments. Why should I even think that you shall not be with me for ever? Won’t I have the good fortune to die before you? Why should we think of our own future while doing good to others? So rise, my Chatura!’ Vidya Chatura was reminded of the generous Raja Bhoj, and of the king’s response to his minister who urged caution as Bhoj prepared to make generous gifts. Save wealth for difficult times, o King. But Minister, how can the wealthy have difficulties? My King, if one squanders wealth, one will eventually lose all accumulated wealth.⟨fn:48⟩ Vidya Chatura posed another question to test her. ‘All right, let us forget about the future. But have you thought of the present? I have not been able to give you a single ornament. You have nothing except what you came with from your parent’s home. If you give away all the ornaments from your body, what will you wear?’ He assumed that even educated and wise women tend to be fond of ornaments, and that Gunasundari would be no exception to this. ‘Oh! I did not know that you have failed to know me hitherto. This is a failing on your part, my Chatura.’ ‘What is it that I have failed to know?’ ‘You assumed that like other women I, too, am married to gold and silver. No. Not in the least. Why does one wear ornaments? So that others look at us and feel happy? No. Can we see the ornaments that we wear? No. Do I wear ornaments because there is a lack in my beauty? Do I want to please my Chatura with ornaments?’ ‘Ah! So you do not feel obliged to please me any longer?’ ‘How can I say that I do not feel the need to please you? But we have to help Dukhba, it is our joint duty. And I know well that nothing would give you more pleasure than the performance of our duty. Now tell me, my Chatura, aren’t you caught? You must admit you have been defeated and I have won!’ ‘Does defeating the husband also form part of a wife’s duties according to you?’ ‘Not in everything, but certainly in love and play. Don’t you remember what Rati said? Dost thou remember, O Cupid, my binding thee with the strings of my waist-band whenever I was addressed with a wrong name by thee, or my beating thee with lotuses used as ear-ornaments, hurting thy eyes with pollen-dust dropping from them?⟨fn:49⟩ ‘Even without the lustre of ornaments, I am your Rati and you are my Kama. I must win over you and I must also bind you! Now do you understand, my Chatura? I win over you every time I utter your name.’ They moved from domestic matters to their mutual love and desire. Their conversation delighted them. Vidya Chatura immensely enjoyed conversing with his learned, intelligent and comely wife. For an instant, he distanced himself like a witness and gazed upon her face unblinking. He remembered the saying: An ideal wife will have these six virtues—she will be like a counsellor in dealing with various situations, like a maid servant in serving her husband, like Goddess Lakshmi in beauty, like earth in patience, like a mother in giving love, and like a courtesan in the bed chamber.⟨fn:50⟩ ‘O’ bharya, the one who bears burden, you took my family under your care, you held them close to your heart. Gunial, only you could have done this. It is because of you that this family is together and happy today. But for you, it would have been a bed of thorns.’ This one thought proved to be a distraction in their joyful conversation. Gunasundari found it pleasant to be a distraction. Vidya Chatura resolved that he must help find a way out of Dukhba’s woes. He asked his wife many things during their conversation which helped him make up his mind. He also posed to her many questions to ascertain her capacity to negotiate hurdles. He never hesitated in having a frank discussion with her and delighted in gauging the depth of her intelligence and also if she were really capable of following her words with action. Vidya Chatura decided he would be guided by Gunasundari in this. Gunasundari decided that she would arrange Kumari’s marriage, and with the consent of her husband, she took the entire family into confidence. Everyone was pleased and praised her decision. But not Manchatura; he was in fact greatly annoyed. Sahasrai was wandering about who knows where. Vidya Chatura was already shouldering a huge burden of responsibilities. Manchatura was not pleased at this further addition to his burden. I am not anxious that some old woman would die, he thought, but this is like showing Yama the road to their house! Moreover, Manchatura did not want this to become a habit with everyone. Chanchal’s children were also unmarried. Manchatura made his displeasure known to Gunasundari in no uncertain terms. ‘Gunasundari, you have no mercy for yourself. You are still childish. You will have other children of your own. Vidya Chatura does not earn so much that we can spend lakhs. If you take on new responsibilities, you will not be able to fulfill them in times to come. And if you are unable to bear these burdens in future, whatever you have done in the past will also be abused by others while their expectations will forever remain unfulfilled. Hence, do not take on this responsibility. If Sahasrai is not concerned about his daughter, why should you be? You want to take credit for your good deeds—but credit can also become a noose around your neck. Credit is not going to bring food to your house. If you are so concerned, ask Dukhba to call Sahasrai. If you are going to feed the brahmins by keeping your children hungry, you and I will not get along. If daughters are so dear to their mothers, mothers would rob their sons to fill their daughters’ houses, and the sons-in- law would get all the good things while the daughters would come back and sit on our heads. By doing this you will endear yourself to your mother-in-law. But if you want my affection, have some pity on my son who works hard day and night to feed the house. Your sister- in-law has a right to be fed in your house. But Gunasundari, if you take on the responsibility of arranging the marriages of their children, even the gods will turn against you.’ The whole family, including Dukhba, was present when Mancha­ tura expressed his annoyance. Dukhba could not bring herself to tell Gunasundari, ‘Why do you worry so much?’ She was meek; her sorrow had made her greedy and self-seeking. She had not parted with one piece of her gold to help Sahasrai in all his troubles. Instead, she opted to live with her brother and sister-in-law. But Dukhba had no sense of gratitude towards them. She believed that they had the means to arrange for Kumari’s marriage and therefore they were doing it. She heard her father, but she could not bring herself to say, even insincerely, to Gunasundari, ‘But why should you take on this burden?’ She felt if she were to say anything of the kind, Gunasundari would do exactly what her father wanted. Dharmalaxmi did not like the charge that she was robbing her son to fill the houses of her daughters. She kept quiet because she knew that Manchatura was angry. Everyone eagerly awaited Gunasundari’s response. They all looked towards her. Gunasundari gravely listened to her father-in-law. Then she spoke with a smile, ‘Pitaji, have we ever disregarded your words? Why would we, the women, trouble ourselves about where the money for Kumari’s marriage will come from? You are there for it; so is Sahasrai, and so is everyone else. You will do what is appropriate. You have no objection if we call back Sahasrai. You also have no objection if we look for a suitable groom for Kumari. Once the marriage is fixed, the celebration will take place in whichever house you decide. You do not discriminate between your five fingers. The expenses will be borne by whosoever you decide. Why should we think of that now? Pitaji, now tell me, do you still object?’

Manchatura was thoughtful for a while, then said, ‘No, there is no objection in doing that much. But I know your tricks. Be careful. And know that for me all fingers are of varying length; some are longer than the others. Each one does its work. Don’t bind me to it. And don’t take this as an assurance for the future’. Gunasundari replied, ‘Pitaji, how can we tie you down to anything? Is it appropriate for us to seek assurances from you? We needed your permission, which you have given. The matter ends there’. Gunasundari busied herself with household chores. Everyone else also went their separate ways. Left alone, Manchatura thought to himself: This daughter-in-law of mine is virtuous and equally clever. I will not be able to have my way with her. She has made up her mind and she will conclude this her own way. She got me to agree to those things about which I cannot possibly object; the rest she has kept hanging. Who knows what shape she will give it when the time comes? Was I right in saying what I did? She works so hard. The rest are like animals; they don’t lighten her burden even for the sake of form. Sahasrai has incurred big debts; he is unlikely to return for the asking. How is he going to spend on the wedding? He knows quite well that Vidya Chatura will spend for his nieces and nephews. He must have written to Dukhba. And Dukhba must have got Gunasundari to agree to the idea. Gunasundari wants credit. But she does not know that the axe will fall on her feet. She is not so dumb that she wouldn’t understand this, but God has made her generous and forgiving. If my son were the Karbhari of Ratnanagari, her generosity would have brought him even greater glory. Manchatura’s anger gradually subsided as his mind turned to more positive thoughts. A search was mounted for a suitable groom for Kumari. Dukhba liked an old but rich man. She was tempted by his wealth. There was another proposal, but that was an obvious mismatch. And with Manohari’s example before Dukhba, she was against such matches. Manohari also chipped in, saying, ‘Only the ill-fated would agree to such a match’. Gunasundari was against the marriage with the old man. ‘We cannot decide by looking at the old man’s wealth,’ she said. ‘A man’s body is fit to enjoy the pleasures of marriage for long years, but by the time men turn fifty they become useless. In this Kaliyug one lives only for sixty years. So when a man turns fifty, he should be considered as good as dead for some things. His wife should also forsake worldly pleasures. From the age of fifty to sixty, our daughter will be a closet widow, and after sixty she will be widowed in any case. Therefore, this idea must be dropped.’ Unknown to Gunasundari, Manchatura overheard this conver­ sation and his eyes widened in surprise as he thought: How does she know of all this at her age? But Manohari could not restrain herself. She burst out laughing, caught hold of Gunasundari’s shoulder and loudly butted in, ‘Wait, Kakiji, wait! How do you know all these things? I don’t deny that you speak wisely. But please tell me from where did you learn all this? Now you are caught good and proper. Tell me, please, you have to! I won’t let you speak of anything else’. Dukhba caught hold of Manohari and said, ‘Go away! Why do you interfere in things you don’t understand?’ ‘Why, Foiji? Can’t I even ask? Kakiji doesn’t mind in the least. So what is your problem?’ Manohari sharply asked her elder aunt-in-law. Dukhba persisted, ‘No, Gunasundari merely keeps quiet, so don’t assume she doesn’t. And think before you speak, Manohari. All you can do is bark! Do you even have the brains for anything else?’ Manohari saw her point and kept quiet. Gunasundari turned to her and smiling, said, ‘Even those who are yet to marry have attended marriages. I might have asked someone knowledgeable like you, and therefore I know these things’. ‘Happy? Got your answer? What did you gain by butting in? Even my tongue grew weary of warning you not to take on your Kakiji. Now take what she dished out to you and hold your tongue!’ Dukhba said. Manohari felt sheepish. ‘Foiji, I am still a child, so I can ask such things. You said it is inappropriate to ask these things, so I won’t ask again. But I don’t know what it is about Kakiji that every time one opens one’s mouth, she responds so sharply that we have to shut up. But what Kakiji said is not wrong at all. A woman soon to be widowed by marrying an old man has no future. But the kind of problem I have was short-lived. By the time we are twenty-twenty-two, these problems vanish. And with an old husband, one gets some pleasure till he turns fifty, after which the woman has to roam around, doesn’t she? Will his money satisfy our hunger? I am much better off!’ This was not something that should have been said openly. Manohari was immature and brash, but what she said reflected her own experience. The other women blushed at her blunt talk and laughed her off. But Manohari nevertheless brought home to them the truth of the matter. Eventually, Kumari was betrothed to a boy ten years her senior and of average means. Sahasrai returned. Kumari’s marriage was fixed. Some days prior to the marriage Gunasundari took out all her ornaments and gave them to Vidya Chatura. Vidya Chatura did not accept them. He reasoned with her, ‘If I take away your ornaments now, someone will come to know of it and there will be a lot of unnecessary discussion. Also, on the day of the marriage if you are seen without any ornaments on your person, it will look bad. We are going to bring the necessary things on credit. I will need money only when the accounts are to be settled. We shall take a decision then’. No one asked the question of money and expenditure until the time came for the accounts to be settled. No one even mentioned it. Sahasrai had assumed that Vidya Chatura would bear all expenses. Gunasundari had assured Manchatura that, ‘You will not have to pay’. Manchatura’s response was, ‘We will see’. Only the two of them were worried about the expenses. Gunasundari was worried that Vidya Chatura might hesitate while taking her ornaments. Manchatura was worried that eventually Sahasrai will wash his hands off and Vidya Chatura will have to bear the entire expenses. Gunasundari’s assurance to Manchatura was some comfort to him; but he was still apprehensive that ultimately Gunasundari will be cheated and Vidya Chatura will have to pay either out of social compulsion, or out of pity for Dukhba and Sahasrai. Gunasundari had indeed said that Manchatura will not have to pay. What she had not said was that: ‘I will pay—I will give my ornaments’. Manchatura had not understood what she had deliberately left unsaid.

Some days after the marriage, the creditors brought the accounts to Vidya Chatura and sought payment. Neither Gunasundari nor Manchatura were unaware of this development. Gunasundari went up to her room and confronted Vidya Chatura, ‘Have you thought of a solution?’ Vidya Chatura laughed and said, ‘You have to think of a solution. Why do you ask me?’ Manchatura was quick to realise that Gunasundari had gone up to her room to arrange for the payment. He got up. Hitherto, he had never spied upon his son and daughter-in-law. But that day he stood at the bottom of the staircase and overheard their conversation with eager anticipation. Manchatura found Vidya Chatura’s question rather strange; he failed to understand it. Just then Gunasundari said in response, ‘My dearest Chatura, today you have finally said the right thing. Kumari’s marriage was a source of great joy. Dukhba is relieved. And I, too, shall feel relieved once my promise is fulfilled. I am fortunate that my ornaments will at last be put to some good use’. Manchatura was shocked. He chewed his lower lip, pulled on his moustache pensively and muttered: So the expenses will be paid from Gunasundari’s jewellery! Vidya Chatura was heard speaking in disconcerted tones, ‘I don’t know if this is good fortune or ill fortune, but I have no cash to spare at present. I undertook this responsibility only upon your insistence and your steadfastness, Gunial’. Manchatura slapped his forehead and stamped his foot in anger. Shame on a son who accepts his wife’s ornaments! Oh, such is my fate that not one of my sons proved worthy of anything. I was wrong in my estimation of this son as well. This daughter-in-law is the light of the family. All the rest bring me nothing but discredit and pain. ... Her ornaments! But Gunasundari’s response did not allow Manchatura to express his anger. She said, ‘You speak to me in honorific terms. You sound depressed. This is new’. Vidya Chatura forced a smile. ‘No, it’s nothing, really. What can I do? If I go out to seek money on loan, it might be refused. We would also lose our prestige. Till date I have never asked anyone for anything.’ ‘Why do you need to do so now? It is almost night. Tomorrow morning I will give you the ornaments. Go and sell them off; you will have all the money you want and you won’t need to ask anyone for a loan.’ ‘But everyone will notice if there are no ornaments on you. We will lose our prestige either way.’ ‘You will earn merit if the ornaments are used for a good cause. This merit will bring good times and I will have a hundred fold more jewellery to use. If we give our jewels for your sister, our prestige will increase by a hundred-thousand fold.’ ‘But if I try to sell them, I will get a lower price. Instead of a hundred rupees, I will get only sixty.’ ‘God will make up for such losses.’ ‘It is not a sign of wisdom to invoke God in practical matters.’ Gunasundari could not help but laugh. ‘Should we then invoke God only in useless matters?’ Vidya Chatura was defeated. ‘I think that we should pawn the jewellery, not sell it.’ ‘Then do so.’ ‘But it is not a good thing to pawn jewellery.’ ‘Why so?’ ‘The world will call us foolish.’ ‘Let the world go to hell. We are not doing this to earn praise.’ ‘If someone were to know about this in the family, they would never let us do it.’ ‘We should not worry about that now. They will know only after the matter is resolved.’ ‘It is neither my duty nor my morality that I should take away your ornaments. I will find some other way.’ ‘Do you consider me separate from you?’ Gunasundari asked, pain writ large over her face. Vidya Chatura got up. ‘No, I don’t. But we shall see.’ He began to change his clothes. Gunasundari, still seated, held on to his hand and stopped him. ‘If this is not separateness, then what is?’ He wriggled out of her grip and began to wear his angarkha. ‘No, no. Why do you think such ill thoughts? I have to go to the palace soon. Everything will be fine, Gunial—all at the right time.’ Gunasundari got up and brought him his pagdi. She placed it on his head and said, ‘There is no such thing as the right time. Everything must be done by tomorrow. I will not allow you to have your way’. ‘We shall see,’ Vidya Chatura said, moving towards the staircase. But Gunasundari held on to his angarkha and stopped him, ‘No, there is nothing more to see. Give my life or your word’. ‘Let me go, Gunial. Pitaji is downstairs, he will see us.’ Gunasundari let go off him and said, ‘All right. You are going away just now. But I will have my way ultimately. There is a night to pass before tomorrow comes’. Vidya Chatura hurried down the stairs thinking to himself: Such a good wife is an act of God’s grace. But a woman who is virtuous and also cares for the family is so rare to find! Gunial, your thoughts are lofty and do well unto others. Your steadfastness and strength with regard to your own aspirations for others defeat us all. You always get your way. You win over everyone with your virtues, intellect and deeds. I have you for a wife, and that is a sign of God’s grace on me. Why should I, a husband of a jewel like you, not take pride in you and prize you more than wealth or a position in the state? He recalled the lines of a poem. Sweet stream, that winds through yonder glade, Apt emblem of a virtuous maid— Silent and chaste she steals along, Far from the world’s gay busy throng; With gentle yet prevailing force, Intent upon her destined course; Graceful and useful all she does, Blessing and blest where’er she goes; Pure bosomed as that watery glass, And heaven reflected in her face.⟨fn:51⟩

My Gunial, too, is a heavenly blessing, thought Vidya Chatura as he left the house. Gunasundari followed after him. But Manchatura accosted her on the way and asked, ‘Gunasundari, these creditors have been doing the rounds. Who is going to pay them? Your sister-in-law or her husband? You had said that we won’t have to bear the burden’. ‘No, of course not. You will not have to pay.’ ‘Then who is going to pay? Are all the creditors just going to give up their claims?’ ‘Pitaji, you will know when it is done. Even if Dukhba and her husband do not pay, the burden will not come upon your family.’ Gunasundari did not want to answer any further questions, so she quickly went inside and got busy with chores. Manchatura stood there stroking his chin thoughtfully. She is determined to give away her ornaments. They are those that she got from her parents’ home at marriage. That is why she said the burden will not fall on my family. Gunasundari spoke the truth. She can’t be accused of lying. She spoke the truth and she tricked me as well. How was I to imagine that she would give away her own ornaments? What I could not imagine she is intent on doing. Her virtue is limitless. It is something without a precedent. That a daughter-in-law would give away her own ornaments for the marriage of her sister-in-law’s daughter! My old eyes will see something unseen! I am not going to let this happen. She is capable of such generosity, and these asses in my family are so selfish they can neither comprehend nor appreciate it! I have now understood. And if I pretend otherwise, I would be labelled the leader of a pack of asses! Our ancestors made this custom of giving gold ornaments to our daughters for their own protection, so that if widowed, they would not be left without means. And this wretched rand of a daughter of mine! Her husband is hale and hearty and yet she is a burden on her brother. What would she not do if he were to die! But Manchatura checked himself, he did not want to pursue such inauspicious thoughts and consume his energies needlessly. What is Dukhba going to do with her ornaments, he wondered. She will keep them. But Gunasundari will give away hers to pay for Kumari’s wedding! Oh, the absurdity of it! Darkness seems to have descended on Brahma’s house. If Gunasundari were to starve to death someday, will Sahasrai find it within himself to give her even a pie to buy poison? What is Dukhba doing with her gold, rubbing it on her boils to soothe them? No. I am not going to let this happen. Such a practice should not be encouraged. Even Chanchal has children who need to be married. God, will these children ever bring any light to my family? Gunasundari is still young. Poor thing, she is accursed! Manchatura withdrew to his room. After everyone had gone to sleep after dinner, he called Sahasrai to his room. He told him of Gunasundari’s decision to give away her ornaments and scolded him. Sahasrai was ashamed to tears. He said, ‘What am I to do? I don’t have money enough to buy myself poison. I feel ashamed. I will do whatever you suggest’. Manchatura suggested that Dukhba’s ornaments be pawned to pay off the expenses. Sahasrai sighed deeply and said, ‘As if that is within my power. When I had asked for it to save my pride and prestige, she refused to part with it. If I could have used her gold, I would not have come to such a pass today. My creditors are generous; they are even willing to settle for less. If I had Dukhba’s ornaments, I could have re-established my business without anyone’s support’. Manchatura felt pity for Sahasrai. His dislike and anger for his meek yet unfair and selfish daughter intensified. He called Dukhba and told her of Gunasundari’s decision. He berated her more harshly than he had Sahasrai and shamed her, saying, ‘Wretch, at least now make an offer, however false! She is not the one to accept. But you are found wanting even in pretence! Where have you kept your ornaments?’ Dukhba said nothing. ‘Oh! So you won’t say anything? Anything at all?’ Manchatura barked, nearly hitting her. Suddenly he said, ‘Sahasrai, get up. I know where she has kept them’. Dukhba was frightened. She quickly went and stood with her back towards the tin case where she had kept her ornaments. Manchatura realised that she had hidden her ornaments in that case. He suddenly leapt up, caught Dukhba by her throat, clenched his teeth and said with eyes bulging in anger, ‘Will you hand them to us, rand, or shall I take them?’ Terrified, Dukhba opened the case and gave all her ornaments to her father. Father-in-law and son-in-law went away. Dukhba spent the whole night crying. She did not sleep. Early morning, Manchatura and Sahasrai went into town, pawned the ornaments and got the money. Around the same time, Gunasundari took off all the gold ornaments from her body and handed them to Vidya Chatura. He kept them safely in his case. He looked at his wife, completely bereft of any adornment. ‘Gunial, is there not even a trace of unhappiness in you? Sorrow has cast a shadow over your face, pain is writ large on it. You finally had your way. You gave your word without really meaning to, but you did keep it. You make a brave show of being unruffled. So be it. But I am glad that you kept your word. You may deny it, but I know it pains you deep within. I don’t want that. I am happy with your gesture. Take them, put them on. You don’t look good without them.’ Gunasundari smiled in response. ‘If my state was really the way you describe it to be, your words would have singed me. I have done nothing to please you. I had decided to do something. I did. That is all. Kumari’s marriage has been celebrated, and I have given my ornaments to you. I had resolved to do this. This was not done to please you. You may be right that I don’t look good without any embellishments. Ornaments enhance the beauty of a woman bereft of both virtue and beauty. But my Chatura, you are so clever and yet you make a mistake. We were married as children. You did not marry my beauty, my virtue or even my ornaments. You were married to me. Ugly, foolish or without virtues, you only have me.’ Whatever I am, I am yours Ocean of compassion, bear with me Gunasundari looked alluringly beautiful as she sang and danced joyfully to the song. Her only adornment was a bangle on her wrist, a sign of her married status, a simple clean sari wrapped around her, and a crescent moon-shaped mark on her forehead. Her long black hair gleamed. Not just her face but her entire fair unblemished body seemed to smile at him enticingly. Her radiant forehead, her bright mischievous eyes, her dimpled cheeks, full smiling lips, pearl-white teeth; her bare neck seemed longer without ornaments, her bare arms delicate and smooth as lotus stems looked even more beautiful for she had not worn a blouse; her breasts trembled ever so slightly under the translucent cloth like a pair of love birds, enticing and inviting; her flat stomach, her firm legs visible from under the cloth and even the delicate soft heels of her feet radiated a sensual joy. Vidya Chatura, who had enjoyed the pleasures of that virtuous body, forgot everything else and drank in her beauty without restraint. Gazing into her laughing eyes, he put his arms around her shoulders and sang to himself. Clad in a white silk raiment, decked only with ornaments indispensable to auspiciousness, ... her hair marked with the holy durva grass, [she] appears to be reconciled with me from her very person, with its haughty deportment given up under the pretext of (the observance of) a vow.⟨fn:52⟩ He held her in a close embrace for moments. Then he led her to his cupboard, opened it and showed her a bag full of money. He looked at her and smiled. ‘Gunial, all this was done to see the limits to which your virtue extends. I also wanted to see your beauty without any embellishments. God has given me enough money for the wedding expenses. Now put on all your ornaments.’ Gunasundari bashfully hid herself in his arms and gave no response. Eventually she went down, but without any ornaments. Manchatura called Vidya Chatura for a talk and gathered all the information about the wedding expenses and the amount due to each creditor. After lunch, Vidya Chatura went out. Manchatura and Sahasrai went to each creditor and paid the amount due to them on behalf of Vidya Chatura. The accounts were settled. Surprised that his creditors had not sought payment of dues from him, Vidya Chatura made enquiries. He was then told that Manchatura and Sahasrai had made all the payments. Manchatura had his way. His ego was satisfied. Everything that happened was conducive to his nature. Gunasundari performed all her familial duties as always. The life of the family settled into a routine. Occasionally, there was some friction. If Gunasundari got something for herself, it was invariably exhausted in sharing with the family, but her generous heart never failed to take delight in it. Manchatura was the only one who disapproved of such generosity. He was reminded of the proverb: A good daughter-in- law cooks and a worthy son goes to a foreign land to earn. He clearly foresaw that Gunasundari will never be able to experience the real joys of life as long as she was entrapped within this family web. He believed it was a sign of ingratitude to keep her embroiled in family affairs at such a young age. Manchatura thought: I have enjoyed my youth. She must also have some desires. Gunasundari is generous to a fault and does not take the deprivation to heart. A string of flowers meant for her hair were claimed by Manohari; she got a ring which Dukhba took away; a bed meant for her went to Chandika’s pleasure suite—that rand has grown up children and still desires a new bed! She got glass chandeliers which the old woman claimed for her gods. Everyone needs everything. Old and wise Gunasundari needs nothing—she has no desires! Ganchatura does not realise that he now earns and he should lead his own life and reduce his younger brother’s burden. They all want to crush their brother to the ground. That Ganchatura thinks if he were to have his own house, it would look bad in society! Not any longer. Sahasrai has re-established his business; I will pack off Dukhba to her husband. And I will drive all the remaining asses to Manoharpuri and live there. It is a village, expenses will be less there, and this one here will get some respite. Yes, that is my final decision. If I don’t understand her plight, who will? Manchatura went about his task tactfully and adroitly. First, he sent Dukhba off to Sahasrai. Manchatura argued that it was difficult for Sahasrai to live alone in a foreign land. Sahasrai had learnt some useful tips from Manchatura. His business was doing well; he could easily bear his wife’s additional expense. After this Manchatura convinced Ganchatura to start living independently. Gunasundari objected but Manchatura brushed her objections aside. A house adjacent to Vidya Chatura’s was rented for Ganchatura and Chandika. Gunasundari shifted from her house as much furniture as could be fitted in that house. Manchatura did not keep very well. He used that as an excuse and went for a change of climate and fresh air to Manoharpuri. Dharmalaxmi also moved to Manoharpuri along with Chanchal and her children. Thus, just as birds go their separate ways at the break of dawn, one by one everyone left Gunasundari’s house. Only Sundargauri stayed on. Bereft of family, Gunasundari felt lonely in that vacant house and initially she even wept for them. She visited Manoharpuri often. As the days passed, Gunasundari gained in experience. Two years after Kumud Sundari’s birth, another daughter was born to her, Kusum Sundari. She had no more children after that. For some years, Gunasundari had desired a son. But Vidya Chatura helped her to alleviate this discontent; her own good education and intellect also helped her. Then came those years when one after another members of the family died. First Dharmalaxmi, followed by Chanchal, then her children, then Dukhba, followed by Ganchatura and finally Chandika, they all passed away. Gunasundari dealt with their illnesses and deaths and subsequent rituals. She had to make her heart stony. At the present juncture in our narrative, Gunasundari and Vidya Chatura lived alone in Ratnanagari. Kumud Sundari was with her in- laws in Suvarnapur. Manchatura, despite all these hard blows, lived on. He continued to stay at Manoharpuri. Sundargauri, almost on the threshold of old age now, lived with Manchatura and cared for him; she had adopted a widow’s garb and shaven her hair. Hariprasad had given up studies and taken up a job. Manohari, now caught in the  responsibilities of family life, no longer behaved petulantly. They lived in another town. Manohari occasionally wrote letters to Gunasundari as a daughter would to a mother. Gunasundari’s heart had grown a thousand-fold more tender and loving with all these myriad different experiences. The rich memories of days gone past came before her often, and they prepared her for the barrenness and loneliness of death.

That loving mother was now anxiously waiting to meet her daughter at Bhadreshwar. Standing on the high raised platform of her rest house at Manoharpuri, for a moment Gunasundari forgot that she was the wife of the Prime Minister of Ratnanagari. As her eyes strained to look beyond the village outskirts, her heart was filled with memories of family life. She wondered: So many have left me for good. Which of them will stay with me forever? What lies in the fates of my two daughters? Her eyes brimmed over with tears. All the people who had gathered to receive and welcome her seemed to float in her tears.
chapters.summary: Gunasundari's gentle wisdom unites her new family, culminating in a tender reunion with Vidya Chatura, as their deep, unspoken love finds solace and expression.

chapters.title: A Night in Manoharpuri
paragraphs: A Night in Manoharpuri Compared to other houses in the village, Gunasundari’s house in Manoharpuri was spacious and comfortable. There were separate rooms for Manchatura, Sundargauri, Gunasundari and Chandrakant. Each of these rooms had all the required conveniences and the rooms were well furnished. There was a kitchen, a dining room, a water room and a bath room. There was a veranda through which one entered the house. There was some land at the rear of the house which was fenced. From the time that Sarasvatichandra lay wounded in the forest till dusk with Aarthdas for company, Gunasundari remained in the veranda of her house, her eyes riveted on the road that led to the village. The sun had not yet set. In the distance, the taad trees caught the last rays of the sun. Leaning against a ladder for support, Gunasundari was responding to the queries and concerns of the villagers who had gathered to meet her, but her mind was elsewhere. Her attention moved from the road to the history of her family. The sun finally set. As darkness descended, Gunasundari saw two riders approaching the village. She followed their progress as they made their way through the curious crowd. Even from a distance, their dress identified them. As they came closer, it became clear that these were the two armed guards—Abdullah and Fatehsinh—who had been sent to Suvarnapur. They rode up to the veranda and Fatehsinh, still astride his horse, handed a note to Gunasundari. She quickly tore open the cover and read the letter.

Mother, pious as a shrine, may the auspicious signs of your marriage remain forever. I shall leave this evening and embrace your feet tomorrow morning. The riders will give you other news as well. My revered father-in-law has become the Karbhari of Suvarnapur. The old administration has changed. Mother-in- law and sister-in-law invite you here. I am happy here. But today my heart feels heavy. I will unburden myself when I meet you tomorrow. Please convey my dandavat pranam to Dadaji and Kaki. My blessings to the sister. Father must be in Ratnanagari. Dandvat pranam of Kumud, the dust of thy feet. Chaitra Sud Bij As Gunasundari read the letter, Manchatura, Sundargauri, Kusum Sundari and Chandrakant came and stood around her in anticipation. Kusum took the letter from her mother and read it out aloud. Each of them took turns to read it, including Chandrakant. He had last seen Kumud’s letters in the hands of Sarasvatichandra; that memory now caused a desolate sigh to escape him. Gunasundari was worried by the words, ‘... my heart feels heavy. I will unburden myself when I meet you tomorrow’. She speculated over what Kumud could have possibly meant. She put many queries to the two riders, asking them about Suvarnapur, Buddhidhan’s family, her son-in-law and her daughter. Finally, Abdullah and Fatehsinh sought her permission and left. Night descended upon the world. The lamps were lit, spreading their light. The villagers also sought leave of Gunasundari and left for their homes, talking amongst themselves about the goodness of their minister’s wife. For some time their chatter, and the sounds of children playing their last games before being called home, pierced the falling dark. Everything became quiet after that. Only the dark of the night persisted. It was time for dinner. Manchatura decreed that everyone, including the women of the house, should sit down to dinner together. He wanted to savour the togetherness. Everyone sat down. Gunasundari had raised an orphan girl who lived in Manoharpuri; she, too, sat down with them. Manchatura was fond of hearing village songs. He asked her to sing. As the others ate their dinner, the girl sang for them. ‘Gunasundariba,’ she said, ‘Listen to this message sent by a daughter from her in-laws’ house.’ Go tell mother and father that, Banished to a faraway marital home, Their daughter is dead Sister-in-law taunts me; mother-in-law gives me grief, My husband, his mother’s boy, tears my heart to shreds To whom do I unburden my soul? I’m confused: do I jump into this well or that pond? I have no more will to live, mother But I long to see you again, mother Why have you forsaken me? Kumud Sundari’s letter still fresh in her mind, the simple plaintive village song pierced Gunasundari’s heart. Tears welled up in her eyes. She grew restless. She turned to Sundargauri and said, ‘Such is the plight of a daughter sent to her in-laws. She has no one to share her pain with. Sundarbhabhi, my heart is not in my control ever since I read Kumud’s letter. Sing, my daughter, sing!’ The girl said, ‘Gunasundariba, listen. A girl sits at a window in her in-laws’ house. Her gaze is fixed in the direction of her parents’ house. She heaves deep sighs and sends messages with passers-by. Listen ...’ Gunasundari listened, absorbed, and the morsel of food remained uneaten in her hand. This road leads to my house But my eyes can’t see that far Today my heart longs for home O’ traveller, if you go by my house Tell my mother, tell my father That their daughter yearns for them Gunasundari suppressed a sob. The girl continued her song. O’ sky farer, go take wing: you will Find shelter in my home; stay there awhile At break of dawn, go sit on my roof My parents will be in the courtyard Waiting

When father goes to the village square Mother will tell him: Ask is she well and happy? Having told him so, she will weep Gunasundari could no longer contain herself and she cried out: ‘Speechless bird, watching this even you shall weep!’ The girl said, ‘Gunasundariba, just the other day Kumud behn and I were sitting in the veranda and singing this song. I said to her that you, too, will go away to Bombay and leave your parents’ home.’ The atmosphere turned solemn and sad. Gunasundari was reminded of Sarasvatichandra. She asked the girl to sing the last two lines again, and she wept her heart out. Kusum Sundari had also sat down for dinner with her mother. Hitherto, she used to eat with her grandfather. She was thirteen now. Her body had begun to change. Her mind, too, was maturing. Her marriage had not yet been fixed. This did not prevent youth from dawning upon her adolescent body. As a child she had been naughty, unabashed and independent. Her parents had given her an education. Kusum proved to be an intelligent and keen learner of new skills and arts. She taught herself through observation. She heard attentively, watched carefully and imitated to perfection, resting only when she had mastered the skill she had set her mind to. Kusum was still innocent and she neither knew nor recognised passion. And yet, unknown to her, Kama the God of Love had not failed in his duties to teach her his art. She still had naïve and romantic notions of love and was too young to know anything of the art of lovemaking. And yet, unseen and unknown passions flowed through her veins, through every hair on her body. This change had gone unnoticed. People who saw her were still under the impression that only her body was changing, not her mind. No one could discern the intense new energies flowing through Kusum. A new sense of shame restrained her. She tried to hide her growing body. Shame made her dress differently, walk differently. Those who observed her and believed that Kusum had not changed at all were not entirely misguided either. In the grip of something she could neither understand nor control, she held on fiercely to her childhood, to what she knew, swaying under the pull of dual forces. Kusum was seated between Gunasundari and Sundargauri. She saw her mother weeping. She turned to Manchatura and said, ‘Dadaji, did you see, Gunial has tears in her eyes and she is crying.’ Her unexpected question broke the spell. Old Manchatura smiled and told his granddaughter, ‘Kusum behn, your prestige is at stake. You are with her, and still she weeps.’ ‘No, no, that is not true. When we were in Ratnanagari, Gunial was critical of Sarasvatichandra. She said he was childish and that he should not have been so offended at a few harsh words from his father. And now Gunial is weeping at a song that describes a daughter’s plight. Is Gunial not being childish? Sarasvatichandra’s hurt was personal, but she is crying at a song! I was telling Gunial the other day that before criticising Sarasvatichandra, we should consider what we would have done if we were in his place.’ ‘You intend to say that you have won the argument and that Gunial has lost, isn’t it?’ ‘Of course! Not once but a thousand times over.’ ‘Kusum, we shouldn’t desire to defeat our mother,’ Sundargauri said gently, caressing Kusum affectionately. ‘No, that is not true, Kaki. The young always win over their elders. You have often told me that Gunial would win over everyone in the family and to such an extent that no one, not even Dadaji, not even Moti Ba nor any of the aunts could contradict her. If she won over everyone, why should I not win over her?’ Everyone, including Chandrakant, laughed. Chandrakant felt like joining issues with Kusum. He asked her with a smile, ‘Behn, how can you take sides with someone that your mother is critical of?’ Part of Kusum Sundari’s face glowed in the light of the lamp while the rest was in shadow. Chandrakant’s eyes were focused on the part of her eager and joyous face lit by the lamp. As he looked at the girl who still defended Sarasvatichandra, Chandrakant’s mind was filled with mixed emotions. He said to himself, but more to his absent friend: Sarasvatichandra, Kumud Sundari is meek. This one is a more suitable match for you. Because she will be equal to you. She will change your grave and peculiar character. But when will that day come? Chandrakant sighed and looked at Kusum expectantly. Chandrakant was a stranger. Kusum was not accustomed to talking to such men. She was a little taken aback at his unexpected question. She felt shy and looked down. Then assuming a gravity beyond her years, she said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, Sarasvatichandra left my sister. But you, a friend of his, still have affection for Kumud’s family. Why is that so? Just as you have affection for us, we are also partial to Sarasvatichandra. This is also a heartfelt relationship.’ Chandrakant was won over by her response and choked with emotion. ‘You are right, behn. May such feelings last forever.’ He again thought: Sarasvatichandra, you deserve her. But where are you? Manchatura butted in, ‘Kumud was raised by Sundar, and Kusum by Manohari. If Manohari cannot be defeated by words, how can Kusum be? Isn’t it so, Kusum?’ Gunasundari changed the topic. Buddhidhan had become the Karbhari of Suvarnapur—this was important news. There was much speculation about Sarasvatichandra’s sudden departure from Suvarnapur and his probable destination. Chandrakant was worried. There was much talk of the presence of outlaws. Kumud Sundari was scheduled to travel the next day. Everyone grew increasingly anxious about her safety. They talked through the meal and finally retired to their respective bedrooms. Chandrakant was to share Manchatura’s room. They continued to talk late into the night. Manchatura asked about Sarasvatichandra’s decision to leave home. Chandrakant spoke at length. As he described Sarasvatichandra’s qualities, his achievements, Chandrakant’s narration grew animated. He described Sheth Laxminandan’s feeble-mindedness, Guman’s jealousy and insecurity, Dhurtalal’s machinations and the tragic outcome of these forces. His hatred for them was evident. His voice was sad as he described his friend’s disappearance. He also spoke at length about Vidya Chatura’s disapproval of Sarasvatichandra. He did not care that the one listening to his narration was none other than Vidya Chatura’s father. Chandrakant refuted Vidya Chatura’s charges with passion and eloquence. Such levels of eloquence and lucidity eluded him during intellectual debates in Bombay. He did not realise that Gunasundari had entered the room. His love for his friend had made him articulate and he argued like the lawyer that he was. He asserted that ministers and high functionaries of native states were way below the calibre of his friend Sarasvatichandra who possessed qualities which were unique to him. Chandrakant’s ardent speech had the desired effect on Manchatura, Gunasundari and others who heard him. Gunasundari repented that Vidya Chatura had been so harsh in his criticism of Sarasvatichandra. Young Kusum leaned on Sundargauri’s shoulders and listened with bated breath as Chandrakant passionately defended his friend against the world. Old Manchatura heard him indulgently as if it were his duty to solace a wounded heart. He drew upon his past experiences to sit in judgement upon his own son, clarify his own position and absolve Sarasvatichandra of any wrongdoing. In conclusion Manchatura said, ‘Chandrakant, all things considered, Sarasvatichandra’s decision was not wrong. There can be no doubt that Kumud would not have been happy with a mother-in-law like Guman. Vidya Chatura is unlikely to understand such things. He is fortunate to have Gunasundari as his wife. She has always shielded him from the lashes of the world. He cannot even imagine how the world can hurt you. By now Gunasundari would have forgotten. She was just twenty-two or twenty-three years old then. Our family was more or less harmonious, but still there were daily dramas. I still clearly remember how she, even at that young age, worked tactfully to bring peace to the house. That girl of just twenty-odd years bore the burden of the whole family as lightly as if she were carrying a flower. That burden would have crushed even mature experienced elders under its weight. But her dainty frame moved around the house as swift as a silver lamp—she spread her light in every corner. Her patience, her equanimity was praiseworthy. An old man like me found it difficult to keep my temper in check, but she would never utter a word. And when she spoke, she spoke slowly, in a calm voice. She soothed everyone. Not only that, she never took anything to heart. There are some people who feel the hurt but conceal it. But this young girl was something else. If someone came to bite her, she loved them even more. She would not confront them but would be accommodative and win them over, as if nothing was the matter.’ Manchatura’s praise made Gunasundari coy. She was about to give an appropriately modest response when Manchatura, shrewd as he was, sensed it and was quick to stop her. Looking at her fondly, he laughed and said, ‘Gunasundari, don’t be so impatient. Don’t feel so proud at my praise. It is not you that I praise. Many years ago there was a girl called Gunasundari in this house. It is her I praise. You may not even have seen that girl. Tell me did you ever see another girl like her? It is possible that you may have seen her in the mirror.’ Everyone laughed at this. ‘You I am going to criticise. And that you will have to hear patiently. When an elder criticises, one must listen, isn’t it?’ Gunasundari smiled beguilingly and said, ‘Yes, of course. Whatever the elders say must be right’, and she touched her forehead as a sign of deference. Manchatura continued his narrative. ‘Chandrakant, what shall I tell you? The house was full of people. Someone must have said something untoward, spoken something by way of a taunt, would have been ungrateful, refused to bear the burden, even made her dance to their tune. Someone would have taken things away from her, harassed her, accused her wrongly, and all this went on for years. But Gunasundari never uttered a word. She also ensured that Vidya Chatura knew nothing about it. She kept him completely ignorant of everyday domestic matters. She never allowed the poor man to experience the pains of being in a family—not even in his worst nightmares. What is this? Is this conduct worthy of a woman? Any other woman in her place would have wept daily and robbed her husband of sleep. She would have given him an object lesson in the pains of domesticity, and the man would have repented the day he married. A woman is one who makes her husband an equal partner in her sorrows. But our Gunasundari was extremely selfish. She bore all the suffering, did not share it with anyone, she drank the poison alone. She wanted all the suffering for herself. Do you understand? As a result, throughout his life Vidya Chatura was denied any knowledge, any experience of suffering. And so he failed to understand Sarasvatichandra’s pain. He could not understand the anguish of harsh words spoken by a father ensnared by a younger woman. And the reason for Vidya Chatura’s failure to do so is our Gunial. When I talk about it, she feels coy. How is she to share her failings? She gave my Vidya Chatura only joy and denied him any share of pain. No other woman should ever do such a thing. A woman who does not allow the husband to experience pain, does not harass him by weeping and complaining is not a woman. Therefore, Chandrakant, you should disregard what my son said to you and blame it all on Gunasundari that she did not allow even a whisper of suffering to reach him. All these are her failings. ‘Yes, my son’s fault is that he assumed that every house has a Gunasundari. Because he had her for a wife. He assumed that it was child’s play to be a Gunasundari. Those who eat sweets know nothing of the plight of those who eat coarse grains. But I have experienced more than he has, and understand these things well. Sarasvatichandra was anguished by Laxminandan’s harsh words. And rightly so. He is delicate as a flower. How can a flower like him withstand snowy blizzards? His assumption was also not faulty. My meek Kumud would have been oppressed and tormented by Guman and she would have died suffering. Even my Gunial cannot withstand a Guman, how could poor Kumud be a match? Guman needs someone brazen— someone like my Kusum. What do you say, Kusum? Will you put Guman in order, or will she straighten you out?’ ‘You think I am so gutsy?’ Kusum said. ‘Dadaji, you are very clever. You praised Gunial again!’ ‘Is there anything wrong in being clever?’ ‘No, why should it be so? If the grandfather is clever, the granddaughter must be clever, too. We got diverted. Let us hear you.’ Manchatura took up the thread once again. ‘All right, I will neither praise your mother, nor will I point out her follies. But Chandrakant, even you will admit that Sarasvatichandra’s diagnosis was correct, but not his remedy. He left home and became a wanderer. His intellect failed him. He should have lived independently from Laxminandan.

If you ask me, I see much wisdom in the customs of the white Sahibs. They have the wherewithal to maintain a separate household. They marry and live separately. Our customs are not all wrong, but they work only when everyone lives together with affection. It works as long as there is harmony. Among the Sahibs, they have the joys of a couple, but they know nothing of the joys of our family life. My family is around me. We have so much fun together. I know and appreciate these joys, and so does my Gunial. But the Sahibs cannot imagine them even in their dreams. Among the Sahibs, the wife’s mother and sisters are welcome but the man’s old parents have to fend for themselves somehow. Among us, an old man like me and a poor widow like Sundar have insurance without ever having the need to take out insurance. Our blessings are with Gunasundari and she will always be happy. Old, lame, unproductive people like us have been a burden on Gunasundari for years, even when Vidya Chatura earned a low salary ...’ ‘What are you saying, Pitaji! Have some pity on us!’ Gunasundari interjected. ‘Listen to me. What I said is not without substance. It is also true that we might have been of some help to you at some point, your service will bring you glory in this and the other world; but till such time comes, the person who can endure the burden is only one, and that is Gunasundari. And this Gunasundari is in this house—she is matchless, not found anywhere else. What could be crueller than being dependent upon the income of poor and struggling sons, to belabour good and industrious daughters-in-law to the bone, to imprison them by our presence in a way that their youthful aspirations find no expression, and to suppress their intelligence and creativity? I speak from experience that many parents and parents-in-law have either consciously or unconsciously acted in a way that is cruel. Everyone knows the sufferings of daughters-in-law who speak out and fight back. The world knows of the misadventures of worthless sons. But there is a saying among us that a good daughter-in-law cooks while a worthy son goes to a foreign land to earn. If we were to go by that, who knows about the plight of sons and daughters-in-law who do not complain?

It is the duty of parents and parents-in-laws to know the plight of such children and not subject them to punishment; it is not good to uproot trees that bear sweet fruits. Parents do not subject their children to punishment wilfully, but even when it is done unconsciously the one that is crushed is as delicate as a flower. I speak from experience. I believe it to be the duty of parents and siblings to work for the freedom of others. One may not always have the means, but gradually one must work towards separation and independence. If Laxminandan had worked out an arrangement whereby Sarasvatichandra could have lived separately and yet maintained togetherness, such a day would never have come. It is a sign of wisdom and foresight to work out the separate arrangement when the family is still harmonious. One should not wait for discord to set in. It is foolish to consider possible social disapproval. Eventually, every generation and each branch of the family has to live separately, but to do so at the right time is a sign of social wisdom. Sarasvatichandra could not even conceive that he could have lived in his own house, separate from his parents. This inability proves that although learned, he was not made wise by experience. Was this a big issue? It is the societal norm that eventually each one must live separately, why must one hesitate? Sarasvatichandra felt ashamed of taking this decision because he is still fundamentally a child. I have set forth some principles. The first of which is at no point should two women be made to live in the same house. The second is that everyone—man or woman—should be allowed to live their separate lives in their own households. For my own self I have adopted the model of the sun. The sun is far away from the earth and provides light and heat, but the sun does not bother as to what humans do under the roofs of their houses, nor does it want to see what we do in nooks and crannies where its light does not reach. I should be the sun of the family. The happiness and welfare of all will be secured by this. This is the duty of elders, and all elders must abide by this duty if we truly love our families and desire happiness for all. If the elders follow this norm, their old age will be as happy and fulfilling as mine. But those who act contrary to this will have to abuse their sons and sing that song: Who sent me old age? All of you will attain old age someday. And therefore,

I say this to you. There is a lesson in it for your conduct in the present as well. If some action is imperative, do not act like Sarasvatichandra, or like a woman ask yourself: How can this be done? Do not hesitate or be shy. Do what appears to be correct; act patiently, deliberately and consciously. Do not harbour any hesitation or doubt. Those who are frank about food and social conduct remain happy.’ Gunasundari was not in the habit of interrupting her father- in-law. She heard him out patiently and then asked, ‘So this was the reason why Jethji was sent to his own house notwithstanding all my protests? And this is why you came to live here, pretending that you needed a change of air and water?’ Manchatura looked up straight at her and twirling his moustache, smiled a wicked smile and triumphantly said, ‘Yes.’ His monosyllabic answer silenced Gunasundari. Chandrakant had felt enraged at Vidya Chatura’s criticism of Sarasvatichandra. Manchatura’s forceful, even if somewhat inconsistent argument, drawing upon his diverse experiences left Chandrakant spellbound. He was surprised and stunned by his sharp intellect. He felt that Manchatura was much sharper than his minister son and he found himself in awe of the old patriarch. It was late into the night. Everyone retired to their bedrooms and sooner or later, they fell asleep. But Gunasundari’s natural and characteristic patience and calm deserted her. She was anxious and apprehensive. Kumud Sundari’s letter and her impending journey filled Gunasundari with trepidation. Sleep eluded her. At some point Sundargauri woke up and found Gunasundari awake and weeping silently to herself. Sundargauri gathered her wits about her and asked, ‘Gunialbhabhi, what happened? Why do you cry?’ Gunasundari rested her head on Sundar’s bosom and wept. ‘Sundarbhabhi, today I have a sense of foreboding and I cannot but cry. Kumud’s letter fills me with apprehension and pain. I can no longer bear it.’ Kusum Sundari, ever so alert, also woke up. As she was about to get up from bed, someone was heard knocking at the door and calling out, ‘Gunasundariba, Gunasundariba, please open the door!’ They strained their ears to ascertain the voice. Kusum recognised it and said, ‘That is Fatehsinh’s voice! Gunial, shall I open the door?’ Gunasundari nodded and Kusum opened the door. Fatehsinh entered with a lantern in hand. He kept the lantern on the floor and sat down at some distance from Gunasundari. He held his sword in his hand and spoke, ‘I could not have shared this with others. Hence, I have come back.’ Everyone grew anxious. Fatehsinh informed Gunasundari of what Kumud Sundari had told him regarding Sarasvatichandra. He also told her that the outlaws had abducted Sarasvatichandra and that Harbhamji had gone in search of him. ‘What! Sarasvatichandra was found and then lost again? Have the outlaws abducted him? Oh, Sundar! He was a guest of Buddhidhan. Do you now understand the meaning of Kumud’s letter? She wrote about unburdening her heart. What else could it be? Shall we wake up Pitaji and Chandrakant and give them the news?’ Fatehsinh said, ‘No, no, there is no need to wake them up so late in the night.’ Sundargauri interjected, ‘But Chandrakant is a friend of Sarasvatichandra. He has come only in search of Sarasvatichandra.’ Gunasundari tried to calm herself. She thought for a while and said, ‘What news is to be given to him? He has finally gone to sleep, tired. Let him sleep. What can he do even if we wake him up now? If he hears this, he will lose both his sleep and his peace. And nothing can be done until Harbham comes back with some news. Fatehsinh, you can go now. We will wake up the others only in the morning. But bring Harbham as soon as he returns and wake us up.’ Fatehsinh left. Kusum latched the door. Gunasundari said, ‘Who knows what news the morning will bring. Chandrakant will never see Sarasvatichandra’s folly. Oh why should Sarasvatichandra bring such things upon himself?’ Sundargauri replied, ‘It is his destiny. What can he do?’ Kusum remembered the lines from a song: What is destined cannot be altered. Sundargauri hugged Kusum. Just then there was a knock on the door. They were startled. ‘Who is there?’ asked Gunasundari. The silence of the night was pierced once again.

As soon as Fatehsinh stepped out of Gunasundari’s house, he saw two human forms approach. He could not ascertain whether they were thieves or good men, ghost or human, friends or foes. Fatehsinh walked on, his hand ready to draw his sword. He called out loudly, ‘Victory to Maharaja Maniraj! Who goes there?’ From a distance both forms responded in unison, ‘Victory to Maharaja Maniraj!’ They recognised each other’s voices. The outlaws had met under the banyan tree where the three roads met. It was the first quarter of the night. Harbhamji, hidden in the tree, had heard their plans. He had rushed to meet Mukhi Patel, the village headman, and they were now on their way to inform Gunasundari and Manchatura when they met Fatehsinh. It was dark, faces could not be discerned. ‘Is that Harbhamji?’ ‘Yes. Is that Fatehsinhji?’ ‘Yes. Who is following you?’ ‘Mukhi Patel.’ ‘Good. Gunasundariba awaits us.’ Fatehsinh led the way. So it was he who knocked on Gunasundari’s door once again that night and replied, ‘Ba, it is us, Harbham and Fatehsinh. Please open the door’. Even before he had finished speaking, Kusum appeared carrying a lantern. The masculine faces were brought into focus by its light. The three came in and closed the door behind them. Gunasundari and Sundargauri sat on a cot. Kusum squeezed in between them. The lantern was kept on the floor. The three men sat at some distance on the floor. Harbhamji sat on his haunches and narrated the sequence of events. He informed them in detail about the outlaws and their plans to capture Kumud Sundari. He said, ‘Ba, do not be afraid. Buddhidhanbhai’s authority is immense. The world trembles before Maharaja Maniraj’s power. Anyone who dares lay his hands on Vidya Chatura’s daughter will have no future.’ The three women were terrified. Sundargauri wept. Kusum Sundari trembled. Gunasundari finally overcame her numbing fear and said, ‘Fatehsinh, wake up Pitaji at once’. They rushed towards Manchatura’s room.

Manchatura and Chandrakant woke up by the rustle of their feet. They opened the door and came out. Manchatura asked, ‘What is it, behn? What has happened?’ Gunasundari hurriedly appraised them both. Chandrakant went cold the moment he heard that the outlaws had captured Sarasvatichandra. But what had happened to Sarasvatichandra was no longer the primary concern. Right now, it was far more important to save Kumud Sundari. Concern about Sarasvatichandra’s plight faded from their minds just as the moon fades at the first light of dawn. Chandrakant’s mind churned in helplessness and fury. He was furious at his obdurate friend and he berated himself for his own stupidity: I sent him that letter, and that is why he left Suvarnapur! Now where on earth shall I look for him? Until Kumud Sundari reaches home safe and unharmed, how can I even speak of a search party for Sarasvatichandra? Questions like these circled relentlessly in Chandrakant’s fraught mind. But outwardly, he remained concerned about Kumud Sundari’s fate. Manchatura put some quick questions to Harbhamji and consulted the Mukhi Patel about possible courses of action. He heard the Mukhi and the two soldiers, considered their suggestions and thought quietly to himself for a while. Then he began to issue rapid instructions: ‘Mukhi Patel, you claim there are about forty riders ready in the village. That is fortuitous. Make the following arrangements. We will divide them into five groups. We shall send the maximum number of soldiers to the spot where they intend to capture Kumud. One group should be stationed in the village; another group should patrol the area where the three roads meet. A third group should be positioned near the bridge on the river; they should hide in the ravines. Where shall we keep the fourth group? Yes, they should be on the other bank of river Subhadra which is where the forest is. They should be as close to the Suvarnapur border as possible. The last group should meet Kumud and her group on the way and escort her to safety. ‘Mukhi Patel, you have extra responsibility. You are familiar with all roads. Therefore, you should patrol the terrain between the banyan tree and the river. You should move about with your men with due pomp and show. The outlaws must realise that you are alert and prepared and the rascals won’t dare to make any mischief. I am certain that you will be more than a match for Chandandas and Vaghji. The group that will stay on in Manoharpuri should comprise ordinary men, but they should remain completely alert and ready.’ Harbhamji agreed, ‘Yes, this is perfect. No one can point a finger at Vidya Chaturabhai’s security arrangements. The entire area is in awe of Maharaja Maniraj’s power. And in Manoharpuri we already have an army of people, so there is no need to deploy soldiers. Even so, it is good to have a few men guard the village in case of any eventuality; they could be anyone from among the troops.’ Manchatura was pleased to hear his son’s praise. He said, ‘Harbham, Mukhi Patel will keep watch over the entire stretch between the tree and the river without any trouble’. Manchatura wanted Harbhamji’s opinion on this; but he also wanted to test the Mukhi’s courage. Mukhi’s hand went to his sword at once; he clenched his teeth which sparkled in the light of the lamp. Manchatura saw this as a good omen. He continued, ‘Fatehsinh, you will hide in the ravines and keep a close watch over Bhimji and Pratap. That is something you will do easily’. Fatehsinh twirled his moustaches in response. ‘Harbham, the most important task will be assigned to you. Will you be able to do it?’ ‘Thundering clouds do not rain,’ replied Harbhamji. ‘Do I need to thunder?’ ‘So be it—go and pour over them! You must right away ascertain the whereabouts of Sursinh. You and your group must ensure that Sursinh’s associates are unable to send him messages. You should not allow him to cross over to the other side either by the river or by the road. He should find you as his shadow whenever he turns, wherever he goes.’ Pleased at this responsibility, Harbhamji promptly responded, ‘Consider it done! But you still need to deploy one more group.’ Manchatura said, ‘You are so impatient, Harbham, that you don’t let me finish. Abdullah will lead that group.’

Harbhamji said, ‘Abdullah is an expert swordsman. But we need someone with intelligence. Pratapsinh is certain to try and snatch Kumud behn away. He will play some vile tricks. Abdullah will not be a match for him.’ Manchatura’s chest expanded with pride as he said, ‘I will go with Abdullah and his men’. Harbhamji replied, ‘Yes, that is best’. Gunasundari grew alarmed and immediately said, ‘No, Pitaji, you cannot take that risk! Your body is old. This is not your work’. Manchatura laughed. ‘Gunasundari, just watch your father-in- law. You were not even born then. The Sahibs had just entered the country. At that time I used to wield a sword along with the Rajputs. My Kumud is in danger, and am I to be a mere spectator? If that happens my life itself would be futile. Harbham, now pay attention. Abdullah and I will leave forthwith. We and the soldiers will cross the Subhadra and keep going till we meet Kumud. We shall escort her back. She will also be accompanied by a few soldiers. We shall go now and come back fast, having made all the arrangements. Gunasundari, have someone take out a pyjama from my old clothes. I will tell you what other clothes I will need. Fatehsinh, find me a good sword and fetch a rifle as well and ...’ Before Manchatura could say anything more they had all dispersed, eager to carry out his orders. The women went in to get his clothes. In the olden times, before the advent of the British, the entire country used to carry arms for protection against thugs and bandits. Even brahmins and women were required to be prepared for self- defence. Manchatura had passed his youth in such dangerous times. He was often required to use arms and was skilled at wielding a variety of weapons. The country was disarmed following Nana Sahib’s revolt. But the courage, valour and expertise required for the use of arms had not deserted Manchatura. It was after many years that he had this opportunity. A lion awakened from sleep is still a lion—Manchatura felt his old valour reinvigorated and new blood flow in his old veins. He turned to Chandrakant and said, ‘You stay at home. You will be safe here with the women. The English Bahadur took away our arms. So along with women, men like you are freed from this burden.’ Chandrakant, deep in his own thoughts, was startled by this statement. He felt angry at the British government for having disarmed the country. Manchatura continued, ‘Don’t worry. I am not going to get into a debate with you right now. You will achieve nothing by coming with us. The outlaws will have no patience for your legal debates. I could give you a gun, but you can’t stuff books in it and fire. It needs gun powder. I have no time for further talk. I am going fully armed and prepared. By the time I return, do write an essay about it’. And without waiting for a response, Manchatura disappeared outside to oversee arrangements. Angry, ashamed and stunned, Chandrakant kept sitting there. Soon, many more people assembled outside; he could hear their urgent but low voices indistinctly and the clink of their weapons. Finally he heard Manchatura’s rousing command, ‘Let us go!’ Once the armed contingent had set off for the encounter, the night turned silent once again. Chandrakant realised that he was left alone with the women of the house. He sat there, trying to collect his disparate thoughts. At about three in the morning he at last fell asleep, exhausted.
chapters.summary: Amidst a night of poignant songs and family debates, Chandrakant finds himself pondering Kusum Sundari's spirited nature and her potential connection to Sarasvatichandra.

chapters.title: Forest, Dark Night and Sarasvatichandra
paragraphs: Forest, Dark Night and Sarasvatichandra Aarthdas, who was moved purely by self-interest, was incapable of comprehending Sarasvatichandra’s selfless generosity. He disappeared with the ring that Sarasvatichandra offered him without once looking back. The night was upon them. The sky seemed to be in the throes of labour, uneasy and on the verge of losing consciousness. Sensing the liminality of the twilight hour as if by instinct, birds small and big flew back to earth and disappeared into the branches of trees that sheltered them. The play of light and dark, the moving shadows and the shroud-like silence of the forest were capable of unnerving a lonely, forlorn heart. A distant feeble moon rose uncertainly in the sky. The moon seemed frightened by the world and wished to hide with the sun and the constellations in the dark caves of the mythical Astachal which lay in the west.
