It was at that twilight hour that Sarasvatichandra regained consciousness. As he lay on his back, his open eyes took in the sky, the forest and the shrieking night. The last vestige of human presence, Aarthdas, was nowhere to be seen. Sarasvatichandra sat up and looked around, his eyes searching the swiftly falling dark for the path that Aarthdas would have taken. He realised that he searched in vain. He looked up at the night sky. All around him, the forest breathed and rustled in the wind as if it were alive. Sounds of wild animals coming from deep within the forest startled and frightened him. He stood up at once, his heart pounding. His agility suggested that he was neither hungry, nor feeble, nor even melancholic. The faint moon had disappeared as if in fright. Darkness, impenetrable, soft and heavy, descended as suddenly as a tiger jumps on its prey and it enveloped Sarasvatichandra. Face to face with that all-encompassing dark, his heart stopped beating for moments. He cupped his hands over his ears to stop the blood rushing in his ears. Suddenly, his eyes began to glow with an intense delight. He cried out aloud: Oh, at last!—the vision of the Great Night that I have long sought! Oh, Kumud, at this moment I erase you from memory. You belong to the world of day, and I to the world of night. This vision allows me to imagine the dark night of death. Chandrakant, you had wanted to save me from this vision, to redeem me! Gumanba, all this was possible because of you. Pitaji, you stopped loving me and freed me from the bondage of love. Today I stand freed of all bonds—of illusion, society, family, love and wealth. Free at last, I can experience this ultimate sublime state. I am surrounded by this dark, dense forest bereft of any human presence except myself. Here I am amidst the beasts of the night. God is my only succour. I have attained the condition that one attains at the end of one’s life. I have moved from being a millionaire in Bombay to a destitute guest of Buddhidhan. And now I stand in this blind forest. It is certain that I shall go further down. While the sound whirls around, Down, down! As the fawn draws the hound, As the lightning the vapour, As a weak moth the taper; Death, despair; love, sorrow; Time, both; to-day, to-morrow; As steel obeys the spirit of the stone, Down, down! Through the gray, void abysm, Down, down! Where the air is no prism, And the moon and stars are not, And the cavern-crags wear not The radiance of Heaven, Nor the gloom to Earth given, Where there is One pervading, One alone,

Down, down! In the depth of the deep, Down, down! Like veiled lightning asleep, Like the spark nursed in embers, The last look Love remembers, Like a diamond which shines On the dark wealth of mines, A spell is treasured but for thee alone. Down, down!⟨fn:53⟩ Sarasvatichandra was unaware of his own speech. The forest echoed his words back to him like so many answers. As he stood there in that impenetrable darkness, his arms crossed over his chest, he felt a profound silence surge within him, a sense of contentment. He felt at peace with himself. Not one thought clouded his mind. He stood there motionless, as if waiting for the light that would pierce the dark and the song that would drown the sounds of the forest. At that moment when Sarasvatichandra stood still, almost lifeless, lost in a dream world in a deep meditative silence, like him the night, too, broke free of all constraints, it erased all concerns of the world, all its joys and sorrows and desires. It stood lifeless, eternal and vast— extending itself from one end of the universe to the other. It destroyed all sense of duty and obligation, right and wrong, good and evil. Under its inexorable sweep, those who wore crowns submitted to the charms of women; diligent scholars grew stupefied with sleep; those under oath of celibacy and asceticism were enticed into the world of dreams; those who were rational and clever came under its sway and behaved irrationally. The world gripped by night was bereft of light, of consciousness, even vesture. People lay lifeless like dead bodies in a crematorium. Owls and jackals howled as eternal solitude burnt on the pyre of time. Darkness enveloped all ten directions. Forests, hills, cities and beasts were enfolded by the unseen limbs of darkness. The night merged the world of consciousness into the unconscious.

The roars of lions and tigers were part of its dream world. The myriad machinations and decisions of the day were swallowed by the unfathomable dark. Sarasvatichandra’s mind became imbued with the presence of something omnipresent—and the darkness merged with it. He had abandoned home, wealth, father, friend, Kumud, and love itself. As all these veils were lifted one by one, Sarasvatichandra could see the unseen. He stood surrounded by the infinite night and the forest in a state of absolute thoughtlessness. But this condition did not last long. Soon, like rocks that break the flow of a mighty river, the body reasserted itself—it broke his solitude. The mind grew aware of the body once again. When a resurgent body asserts itself, even the power of yoga pales before it. Hunger devoured his mind; his mind turned blank and thirst lodged itself in his parched throat and drank up knowledge and Sarasvati herself. His eyes rendered useless by the dark closed as his frail body could no longer bear their sightless weight. Sarasvatichandra fell to the ground and lost consciousness. Intellect that produces remorse lost anchor; consciousness that experiences fear and sorrow was lost. Arrogant men make lofty claims but lose courage the moment they are to be tested. But not Sarasvatichandra. Many submit to their passions, act thoughtlessly, and later, as hindsight prevails, try to undo what cannot be undone. It was no longer possible for Sarasvatichandra to undo what he had done unto Kumud Sundari—this was his only regret. And so he had run away from Chandrakant and sought refuge in the forest; he had sought peace and meaning in a rootless wanderer’s life. The curtains came down on this strange drama quite abruptly. Sarasvatichandra could no longer consider if he had acted foolishly or wisely and attained some higher purpose. Time and space also did nothing to awaken him. Darkness like an army moved swiftly and brought all ten direc­ tions under its sway. The night was filled with sounds like those of galloping horses. The branches of trees swayed and grazed and collided with each other like the clashing of swords. The wind rustled and whistled through the trees, branches and leaves like so many arrows from the bow of a great warrior. The shrill buzz of insects filled the forest air like clarion calls fill a battlefield. Deer, rabbits and other defenceless creatures captured by predators cried out in anguish of death. Their cries and moans were like those of fatally wounded soldiers who lay waiting for death, trampled under the feet of their warring comrades. Predators and prey ran amuck in the forest; teeth and claws tore into warm flesh. Jackals howled like cowardly soldiers deserting the battlefield. Tigers moved swiftly and stealthily through the forest like mighty warriors on their steeds. A lone lion, just by his roar, stamped his authority over all other beasts. His roar—like the deafening thunder of clouds or cannons firing—silenced even tigers and elephants; wild buffaloes and deer ran helter-skelter; monkeys chattered and shrieked excitedly; birds asleep in the trees woke up startled, squawking. His roar reverberated through every nook and glade of the forest and reached the caves of the distant Sundargiri mountains. His fiery eyes glowed like embers, mocking anyone who dared approach him. The undisputed king of the forest roared time and again, silencing even the constant buzz of forest insects. As the lion sat alone and regal in one part of the forest, Sarasvatichandra, master of his own mind and destiny, lay lifeless in a place where any other heart would tremble and palpitate with fear. No human being would have the heart to enter the forest at that hour. Even the bravest of the brave would not dare face the predators of the night. Even when the outlaws met, they preferred to meet under the banyan tree on the way to Manoharpuri. The spot where Sarasvatichandra lay was at some distance from the banyan tree. As he regained consciousness and opened his eyes, his senses were once more assaulted by the dreadful darkness saturated with the roars, cries and howls of the wild. Even the distant stars in the sky seemed to him frightful like countless fiery eyes. The awe-inspiring grandeur of the wild would have driven a feeble-minded person mad. All thought deserted him; poetry did not dare come near; all knowledge was swallowed by oblivion and amnesia; parents, Kumud Sundari, Chandrakant—he could see no one in his mind’s eye. At the hour of death, one is utterly alone and lonely. Sarasvatichandra lay orphaned, face to face with mortal danger. Like in a nightmare, he lay paralysed without the strength to move, get up or call out. Running away was out of the question. Where could he have run to? The forest was dark, dense and unfamiliar. Death seemed intimate and near. If hunger and thirst did not claim him first, some wild beast certainly would. He felt it was time to bid this world farewell. A pained visage of his father, of Kumud, of his dearest friend Chandrakant now flashed before his eyes; they all seemed to be weeping inconsolably. Sarasvatichandra could not speak but his soul cried out, he sought their forgiveness, he pleaded with them. He remembered that he had slain Kumud’s love, a crime as heinous as the murder of a brahmin. Tears flowed from his eyes and were absorbed by the dust. He felt cold convulsions rippling through his body. If he had any strength left, he would have cried aloud, but he couldn’t. His limbs went numb. Laxminandan, Kumud Sundari, Chandrakant—these three names got caught in his breath and his chest heaved as he tried to exhale. He opened his mouth so his breath and, with it, his life could escape his body. A fire raged in his belly. He heard footsteps, footsteps of the messenger of God of Death. There was no one to cremate his body, no one to mourn him. The forest enveloped him just as a tiger pounces on his prey, ready to devour it. Just then a sound came from the bushes and a great black cobra came out hissing. It moved rapidly towards Sarasvatichandra, unstoppable as the waves of the sea. Its hissing and sinuous movement infused his numb and feeble body with some energy and he moved his neck to watch death approach him. He took his eyes away and stared up at the sky. In a flash, all thoughts of near and dear ones, all remorse, sorrows, tears and all other worldly matters vanished. Sarasvatichandra prepared himself for the most auspicious moment and waited with bated breath for the cobra to bite him. For him the world was about to end. He was filled with peace. In that moment of calm, the fear of death also disappeared. The only thing left in him was the ‘instinct of self-preservation’. This instinct taught him that it was better to appear dead and allow the cobra to pass over his body. As it came closer, Sarasvatichandra stopped breathing. The cobra slithered up to him, saw an obstacle in its path, went around the inert body and finally climbed on top of him. It was thick, black and about five to six hand-spans long. The serpent coiled itself over Sarasvatichandra’s chest and raising its hood, began to sway to its own slow deathly rhythm. Its gleaming round eyes and the white pattern on its hood glowed like jewels in the light of the stars. Sarasvatichandra’s patience had its limits. Numb with fear, he felt crushed by its weight. The cobra seemed to grow heavier with every passing moment. The knife-sharp agony he experienced was akin to the bite of the cobra itself. His lips, nails and teeth must have turned black with fear, but this was difficult to discern in the dark. His body went cold as ice, his ears turned deaf, the blood stopped flowing in his veins. Only the soul remained a mute witness in his lifeless body. The cobra remained on his chest for five to seven eternal minutes. Then quite abruptly it turned around, lashing its tail on his face as it did, slithered down the length of his body and went away. At that moment, Sarasvatichandra felt the pain of the cobra’s bite, which fearful possibility flowed through his veins like venom. His heart stopped beating and he lost consciousness. The forest was unchanged. The darkness burnt like a body in funeral pyre. The forest, the wild animals wailed in mourning. Their cries pierced the sky. The lion roared but his roar was like the wail of death, powerful enough to melt the stoniest of hearts. All other sounds drowned in this roar. As Sarasvatichandra lay in the lap of death in the forest enshrouded by night, there was no reason to believe that there was any other human being present even in the vicinity of a few miles to witness his final journey. The forest, the earth, the sky and all the ten directions called out to the ebbing life. Sarasvatichandra! O’ Sarasvatichandra!—this cavernous wail escaped the tall forest trees and pierced Chandrakant’s heart in Manoharpuri. They reached Suvarnapur and drove out sleep from Kumud’s eyes and filled them with tears. Pramaddhan’s bedroom, his abode of lustful pleasures turned as desolate as a crematorium for her. At an hour when it was impossible to hear a foot fall in the forest, Sarasvatichandra lay lifeless. The wild beasts roared even louder as the owls and jackals joined them with their dreadful calls. The dogs of Manoharpuri barked furiously in response. Except for a lone wisp of cloud that had lost its way, the night sky was studded with stars, but their solitary light filled one with trepidation. Dew had started to form. It clung to the frightened world like beads of perspiration. The night was cold. The world shivered. It was about eleven. Just then, some ghostlike apparitions seemed to materialise from the east. They were not the outlaws, who had long dispersed after their meeting. Some of them carried torches of bamboo. These long torches burnt without oil, their orange-red flames leaping and dancing as they strode briskly through the night. These torches looked like the flaming tops of the surrounding trees in the dark. When the burning bamboo splintered, sparks and embers would fly. Each member of this group had long black matted hair coiled into a large bun or left to hang like snakes from their shoulders. This was a group of ascetics. The cobra had heard their footfalls and, sensing lights approach from a distance, had vanished into the safety of darkness. This group of sadhus soon arrived at the spot where Sarasvati­ chandra lay. There were thirty or forty of them. At the centre of the group was a carriage, not pulled by bullocks but by the sadhus themselves. Some carried a variety of musical instruments which they played as they walked. Some were torch-bearers. Some carried unsheathed swords, alert and ready to protect the carriage. One of them carried a large saffron flag; the red and ochre of the flag glowed in the light of the torch flames. They had smeared ash, sandalwood paste and vermillion on their bodies; their torsos were laden with beaded necklaces; their dark, sinewy bodies gave an inkling of their strength; their song was robust and could match the piercing roar of the lion. They walked effortlessly to the rhythm of their song. This group of carefree ascetics who had vanquished the forest presented a sight no less fearsome and awe-inspiring than the sight of lions and tigers. They walked with long strides. Their voices boomed. Fire leapt from their torches. Each of them carried long black tongs which gave the appearance of black snakes hanging from their bodies. A boat- shaped vessel for seeking alms was slung over their shoulders. Each of them also carried a saffron cloth bag. They looked like a group of tigers or the dreaded gana of Shiva as they approached Sarasvatichandra.

The man who walked in front suddenly saw a body lying inert in his path. Startled, he stopped. The entire group halted in its tracks, stunned into silence. Vishnudas, their leader who rode in the carriage, shouted, ‘Mohanpuri, what is it?’ A group of sword-wielding ascetics surrounded Mohanpuri and the unconscious body. Mohanpuri bent his stout frame, examined the body in the light of the torches and replied, ‘Guruji, there is a human body lying here as if dead. If you permit, I could ascertain by touch if he is alive or dead’. They examined the body and resolved that he was neither killed by animals, nor was he in fact dead. Guruji closed his eyes in silence for a moment, then commanded, ‘Child, lift him up! Our Lord Shri Jagadish desires that this man will be the saviour of our Sundargiri muth and that the sadhus will one day follow him. Child, protect him with your life. He shall be a great soul one day and be worshipped even by sadhus’. Vishnudas was said to possess knowledge of all three times—the past, the present and the future. This unexpected declaration stunned them. Mohanpuri lifted the unconscious Sarasvatichandra onto his shoulders as easily as one would a child. And the group walked away, singing. Some distance away a forest fire raged. A dense thicket of bamboo had caught fire; the bamboo cracked and split and the flying embers spread the fire. Animals large and small, predator and prey alike ran amuck to escape the flames. Birds asleep in their nests were caught unawares and charred to death. They gave one last shriek of horror before being silenced forever. The skies were filled with smoke. The night sky itself seemed to be afire. The group of sadhus made their way through this inferno, disappearing right into the scorching heat and tree-high walls of fire. Sarasvatichandra lay lifeless on Mohanpuri’s broad shoulders. For a fleeting moment the terrible heat caused him to open his eyes. He thought he was looking at a painted dream. He asked no questions, he thought no thoughts, and his eyes closed once again.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra, lost and alone in a dark forest, finds profound peace before collapsing, then mysterious ascetics find him amidst a raging fire.

chapters.title: Kumud Sundari Leaves Suvarnapur
paragraphs: Kumud Sundari Leaves Suvarnapur Navinchandra was none other than Sarasvatichandra himself, and Chandrakant would take him back to Bombay where he would live a life of glorious fulfilment. These and similar other thoughts had filled Kumud Sundari with hope and joy. But the morning had crushed all her hopes. Sarasvatichandra left Suvarnapur. And all she could do was to helplessly watch him leave. She was not allowed even a word with him. Could any pain be more agonising than this? This unseen wound was inflicted upon Kumud at a time when Buddhidhan’s household was waking up to celebrations. She had fallen down unconscious in presence of everyone, as you may recall. Dear reader, this part of the story we know. Kumud Sundari decided to share everything with her parents. She resolved to find Sarasvatichandra. She was determined not to fail. She sent Harbhamji, Fatehsinh and Abdullah back to Manoharpuri with this news. Her departure for Bhadreshwar was delayed by a day. Krishna Kalika and Pramaddhan rejoiced at Kumud’s decision to visit her parents. But Buddhidhan had been informed of their liaison. This spoilt their joy. Pramaddhan was gripped by fear when he realised that Buddhidhan was intent on punishment. Navinchandra refused to be of any assistance. This was also a cause of worry. There was no one else who could have advised him; therefore Pramaddhan sought Krishna Kalika’s counsel and he called her to Rajeshwar Mahadev. She in her wisdom suggested that he should accuse Kumud Sundari of an amorous alliance with Navinchandra. She further advised that Pramaddhan should present her as a witness and also suggest that the accusations of his illicit conduct were of Kumud Sundari’s making. Pramaddhan went home, but on second thoughts realised that no one would believe his accusation. He paced up and down in his room searching for a plausible defence. His eyes fell on some tiny scraps of paper lying under his desk. Kumud Sundari had torn and burnt all her letters, made marmadarakbhasma of them and kept the remains in a bottle labelled ‘Soul Ash’. But some tiny unburnt pieces lay under the table. On piecing the scraps together, Pramaddhan immediately recognised Navinchandra’s handwriting. He deciphered a line which read: ‘I once had wealth, a father, a beloved and a friend’. Pramaddhan was overjoyed at this discovery. Navinchandra wrote the word beloved! What more could be required as proof? His joy swiftly turned to anger as he thought: Such are the ways of the educated! I never knew that you were Navinchandra’s beloved. At that instant Kumud Sundari entered the room. Observant as she was, she immediately discerned a change in Pramaddhan. But before she could ask anything, Pramaddhan went berserk, ‘So my wise, most clever and learned one, ultimately this is who you turned out to be!’ Kumud Sundari was already numbed by her grief. She was also still weak from her faint. But this unexpected shower of flower petals startled her. She looked at her husband, calmed her nerves and asked in a soft yet steady voice, ‘What is it?’ Pramaddhan shot back at her in even greater rage, ‘What is it? Why, you were the one who was a beloved of that fellow Navinchandra, isn’t it so? Read this and pluck out your eyes!’ He flung the scraps of paper at Kumud Sundari who stood trembling. Poor Kumud Sundari! It was as if fuel was added to raging fire. It was a blow to one already fallen. Her face grew lustreless, her legs threatened to give way, she broke into a cold sweat, her gaze was fixed to the ground and tears flowed from her eyes. In that moment, five hundred different thoughts flashed through her overwrought, unhappy mind. Her heart wrenched. She thought: To whom shall I tell the truth? Who shall believe me? All that I lacked was this dark blot upon my character. Am I to tell a lie? How can I deceive him? My condition is like that of Damayanti whose necklace was stolen, and worse. Dear God! You know the truth. I submit to You. Do what You must with me. Guide me to the path that is destined for me. I have done no wrong. And yet I am not entirely blameless. What can I tell him? She said nothing and returned the scraps of paper to Pramaddhan. Pramaddhan was enraged. ‘What? Do you admit that this is true or not? Tell me!’ He slapped Kumud Sundari hard. She did not raise her hand to shield her face. Her tears dried up. She stopped sweating and no longer trembled. She looked up calmly at her husband and said, ‘Why do you hesitate? Why end it just with a slap? Oh my warrior, lift that sword from the corner and put it to my neck. Why get into this futile exchange of words? If you kill me, I will find redemption. When else would I get a death by your hands?’ She fetched the sword and placed it by his side. She stood before him, lowered her neck and quietly repeated, ‘Do not hesitate. Lift the sword. It is my good fortune to receive this death from your hands’. Kumud Sundari believed in earnest that her enraged husband would kill her and free her from all her agony and misery. She stood there with her head lowered, waiting anxiously for the sword to fall. She kept waiting. After a while she looked up and found herself alone in the room. Stunned and taken aback by this gruesome suggestion of Kumud and not knowing what to do, Pramaddhan had pocketed the scraps of paper and silently walked out. He was at his wit’s end; he had no courage to say or do anything else. In deep quandary and in anguish, Kumud sat down on a chair and wept. Pramaddhan immediately went in search of Krishna Kalika and told her what happened. She counselled him, ‘It is not advantageous to prolong the matter with Kumud Sundari. Tell her that this was only a drama to test her. Tell her that you are assured of her good character, show affection for her, deceive her and quickly send her off to her parents. Once she goes, a thorn from our side will have been removed. If she suspects that you harbour any suspicion at all, she will not go and come in our way. If your father brings up the matter about us after she is gone, show him the scraps of paper and tell him that Kumud spread the rumours about us to conceal her illicit liaison. But all this is to be done only after she is gone’.

Pramaddhan liked the suggestion and executed it to perfection. Kumud Sundari was deceived. Late that night, she sat in her carriage ready to depart for her journey, escorted by the soldiers sent by Gunasundari and few others assigned by Buddhidhan. Her mother- in-law and sister-in-law embraced her and wept. Buddhidhan, too, choked with emotion. Everyone except for Pramaddhan was sad to see her leave. As the carriage slowly began to move, her family tearfully bid her farewell. ‘Kumud Sundari, come back soon! Bhabhi, please don’t stay a day more than fifteen! Daughter, your parents will be overjoyed, but my house will be vacant without you. Come back soon, my daughter, take pity on your mother-in-law. Bhabhisahib, take care of yourself and return soon! Go in God’s care.’ Buddhidhan, Saubhagya Devi and Alak Kishori stood at the threshold with tears in their eyes along with the household servants, watching anxiously as the carriage disappeared into the night. Inside, Kumud Sundari, too, sat weeping. The night was dark and still. In a while, the creaking of wheels and the trotting of horses could no longer be heard. Even the light of the torches carried by the soldiers grew smaller and finally disappeared. No one in the household of Suvarnapur’s new Karbhari went back to sleep that night. They talked among themselves, sang praises of the wise, virtuous and affectionate daughter-in-law. Pramaddhan was hugely relieved. He happily went up to his room and dreamt of Krishna Kalika. Before Kumud Sundari’s carriage had left the town, it was brought to a halt near the outskirts. By chance, Vanleela had witnessed Pramaddhan’s meeting with Krishna Kalika and had heard their entire conversation unobserved. But she did not tell Kumud about it, not wanting to add to her distress. She also had no opportunity during the day for a private conversation with her. But finally when she realised that there was no way that Kumud would know unless she herself told her, Vanleela could no longer keep it a secret. She wrote down all that had transpired on a piece of paper. She had stayed awake and kept a watch from a window. Unknown to anyone else in the family and unobserved, Vanleela had followed the carriage at a distance. Once it reached the outskirts of

Suvarnapur, she caused it to stop and got into it. She gave the letter to Kumud Sundari and asked her to read it at daybreak. ‘Kumud behn, I cannot ever forget your affection. There is no one else I can talk to. I will write to you—do respond. Oh, this love is not a good thing—I just can’t bring myself to leave you! You have imprisoned me by your qualities. Convey my regards to Gunial. Do not forget me, dearest Kumud behn, and do not stop loving me.’ Vanleela said many such things as she held Kumud tightly in her arms. Both of them wept unabashedly. ‘Oh, my Vanliladi, I could have relieved my heart of its burdens if I had just a night to spend with you. But now what is to happen will happen. Come to Ratnanagari. How can I ever forget you! Keep loving me. And go back home safely,’ Kumud said to Vanleela, embracing her. At last they separated. Vanleela, still weeping, walked back to her house. Kumud was unaware of the grave nature of the letter; she assumed that it contained some light-hearted banter and rumours going around the town. She kept it inside her blouse without another thought. The carriage moved on. Thoughts of her parents, of Sarasvatichandra, Pramaddhan, her parents-in- law and sister-in-law crowded her mind. Finally, exhausted from all the exertions and excitement of the day, her fragile body and tired mind surrendered to the rhythmic movement of the carriage and she fell asleep. Even as she slept, tears streamed down her cheeks. Her innocent and hurt mind had only a momentary respite from the machinations of the evil world when the world of dreams caught up with her. Sleep like a mother took pity on this virtuous daughter and drove away all her nightmares. At last, Kumud Sundari fell into a deep and dreamless sleep. The soldiers moved alongside the carriage, talking softly amongst themselves. The night was dark but stars shone in the sky. The torches they carried spread light. It was pleasantly cold. They emerged out of the gates of the capital and moved onto the forest path. Even the wild animals took pity on this young woman harassed by the world of men. As the last quarter of the night moved towards day, the animals became quiet; the forest was free of fear for Kumud. The wind rustling through the leaves and dry blades of grass brought with it the sweet fragrance of wild nocturnal flowers, the coolness of ponds, streams and the vast star-studded sky. It gently ruffled the curtains of Kumud’s carriage, driving out all her dreams to soothe and to calm her troubled heart as she slept.
chapters.summary: Accused falsely by Pramaddhan, Kumud Sundari tearfully departs Suvarnapur, unknowingly carrying a secret letter from Vanleela that could expose a hidden truth.

chapters.title: Preparations for the Morning
paragraphs: Preparations for the Morning To go from Suvarnapur to Manoharpuri one had to cross a bridge on river Subhadra. The river flowed under the arches of this stone bridge. The sea was near. Hence, even during the summer months of Chaitra the water in the river was deep, almost as high as a full grown man. The river was even deeper around the pillars of the bridge. The water came rushing down to be halted by the arches of the bridge only to emerge with greater force, cutting through the deep ravines on either bank. A stranger to these parts watching the river from the top of the ravines was quite likely to fall and drown in the river if not extremely cautious. The force of the flow was such that even expert swimmers dared not swim across the Subhadra. Since midnight the stone bridge had been the focus of stealthy but urgent human movement. Exactly at midnight Shankar Maharaj was seen running towards Suvarnapur, carrying his long thick staff in hand; he was heading for a village within the territory of Suvarnapur. The brave brahmin warrior feared neither wild animals nor Sursinh; anyone watching him would imagine that he too was a tiger or lion in human form. A few hours later a group of riders from Manoharpuri were seen approaching the bridge. They halted at the bridge and divided themselves into two groups. One group led by Manchatura and Abdullah moved on while Fatehsinh stayed back with the rest. Three or four of them got down from their horses and got busy preparing large fires. The men sat around these fires, exchanging stories of past valour among themselves, alert to the slightest movement and sound. Within a quarter of an hour, the riders from Manoharpuri had covered the entire area from the banyan tree to the stone bridge and beyond. As they went, they shouted out: ‘Victory to Maharaja Maniraj! Run! Run, all enemies of Maniraj, run!’ The forest and the skies reverberated with their calls. On the southern end of the bridge the fires crackled merrily, their crimson flames leaping up to the skies, dispelling the dark, while on its northern end, Maniraj’s victory was hailed aloud. All this hectic nocturnal activity was not witnessed by other people. But the forest was silent as if in awe of Maniraj’s power. Even the lions and tigers had retreated to their lairs as if to signal that a new day was upon them. The gushing waters of the Subhadra reflected the glow of the fires and the echoes of the soldiers hailing victory to Maniraj. They removed all shadows of inauspiciousness from Kumud Sundari’s path. On the other side, Sursinh’s men had also taken up their positions. Each group with its leader had reached the remote villages located on the peripheries of the forest. Some of these villages had no human presence except for abandoned and denuded houses, some were sparsely populated, but none of them had the wherewithal to resist and deny shelter to the outlaws. The outlaws slept where they could. Some slept on the floor, others managed to make beds of hay, a few even managed to get sheets to cover them with; they rested their heads on stones or the shields that they carried. Each man kept his weapons within reach as he slept. Their swords hung by their sides, bows and arrows next to them and spears and clubs at their feet. Pratapsinh, Vaghji, Bhimji and Chandandas accompanied by their men tried to catch a few hours of disturbed and anxiety-filled sleep while remaining vigilant. Some of them lit small fires and sat around them, smoking, alert to the slightest movement or sound. They chatted among themselves to keep sleep at bay. As the night progressed, they looked up at the stars to determine as to when they should wake up their companions. On either side, the men were anxious, impatient and sleepless. Sursinh’s men were somewhat more carefree as they had no inkling that someone had overheard their plans. They were prepared for any eventuality, but they did not anticipate the kind of organised resistance that awaited them.

One of the principles of Vidya Chatura’s statecraft was that he ensured that he was kept apprised of all matters. Those who were assigned a given task were required to apprise themselves of all issues relating to the task at hand. It is often the case in native states that subordinate officers are untrustworthy; hence their superiors do not repose any trust in them and do not give them any autonomous responsibility. The tendency of the subordinates, too, is to deny all responsibility. They are often seen eager to please their superiors instead of doing the task assigned to them. No minister or ruler can do all the work by himself, work that ought to be done by subordinates. Consequently, work suffers. Ultimately, some lifeless wretched individual is blamed for the disorder. The British administered areas had vast territories and were thickly populated. It was not possible for the rulers to keep all functionaries under close observation; therefore, reliance upon laws and administrative hierarchy became imperative. But in smaller native states, it was possible to keep all functionaries under observation, to assign them responsibilities, and thus create conditions that permitted a certain degree of autonomy in exercise of authority even at the lower levels of administration. Vidya Chatura was convinced that it was possible to create such a mechanism of governance. He was also convinced that a state administered on these lines would far better secure the people’s welfare as compared to a state under British rule. Vidya Chatura believed that it was equally inappropriate for rulers to either mistrust all functionaries as also to repose full faith in all of them. This principle applied not only to the ruler but also to his ministers. Vidya Chatura’s own conduct, therefore, was in conformity to these principles. His counsel to young Maniraj was: ‘O’ glorious King! Why should we not be able to find trustworthy men? Those whom we cannot trust are not fit to be in your service. If they are worthy of our trust, they also deserve the autonomy to serve you well. We are concerned with work. We should not expect our servants to rise and sit at our command. Everyone in your service should know as to what ways and means are undesirable to you. It is your and, in turn, my responsibility to find capable, intelligent and independent persons who can accomplish the tasks assigned to them efficiently using good means, while keeping their distance from undesirable methods. Servants unworthy of trust and incapable of independent action work without enthusiasm. Lack of enthusiasm achieves nothing; it only spoils the work. When people are given the freedom to work, they work with a will and develop their intellect and capabilities, and intelligent servants are capable of recognising what is unacceptable to their superiors. Even ordinary men are capable of ascertaining the true worth of gems. It is a king’s duty to ascertain the true worth of his men. Gems adorn the king’s crown and his ornaments, but priceless and rare individuals are the true gems of a kingdom; such men bring light to a state, cause poverty to disappear and their light dispels darkness. Maharaja! No state can be without such sterling men, but only wise and intelligent rulers can find them, test them and nurture them.’ Vidya Chatura counselled Maniraj without taking away anything from the king’s authority. He not only gave him advice but put it in practice by his own conduct. Just as a magnet attracts even the tiniest of metal pieces, Vidya Chatura found capable men from remote parts of the state, observed them minutely and gave them prestige and responsibility commensurate with their abilities. He trusted them, gave them autonomy, and they in turn proved true to his trust. Every servant of the state could take pride in knowing that he was a pillar of strength for the state; and yet he also remained free of false pride in his dealings with his superiors. Both superiors and subordinates learnt from each other and accomplished the assigned task. They grasped the norms of righteous and good statecraft through example and discussion. Just as an army moves at a signal from its chief, Vidya Chatura’s administration functioned similarly. His administration itself was a place for learning. The plan prepared to protect Kumud Sundari was also a result of such experience. Fatehsinh, Abdullah and Harbhamji were low- level functionaries of the state but well-versed in the task assigned to them. It would not be an exaggeration to say that the qualities and capabilities they possessed were to be found in most officers of Ratnanagari. Vidya Chatura had not personally appointed them, but the chief of police, following his minister’s principles, had selected them. They were assigned their responsibilities and shown the way, but the decision as to how they should implement them was left to them. Their judgement was trusted. Their superior officers ensured that this trust was not misplaced. Thus, the reins of power were in the hands of all functionaries of the state—together they wove the tapestry of statecraft. The alert servants of an all-seeing king now moved rapidly as one to protect their minister’s daughter who was in danger. Old and experienced Manchatura became their guide. His strategy was to put a powerful display of strength and force on the borders of three states. He wanted to frighten the enemy without the use of arms. He was conscious that his men should not use arms in the territory of another state lest they are made answerable in the court of law of that state. The enemy was certain to be discouraged faced with a large force, while the protectors were conscious that force should be used with discrimination. The troop leaders understood the intent of Manchatura’s plan. They moved swiftly not requiring further instructions. Manchatura’s instructions were executed as effortlessly as music that is produced by pressing the keys of an instrument. Abdullah, Mukhi Patel and Fatehsinh were eager to show off their prowess, but the opportunity to do so had not hitherto presented itself. Harbhamji had sought out the opportunity for himself. He had heard the plans the outlaws had hatched early that night. He was given the task of shadowing Sursinh. Harbhamji enjoyed the combination of valour, the test of his wits and intelligence-gathering that his work entailed. Manchatura and others headed towards Suvarnapur, while Harbhamji with his chosen men moved in the opposite direction. He moved towards the villages under British territory on the eastern side of the mango orchards. He entered some villages himself; in others he sent his men to spread messages; he met brave men who ventured out at night; he spoke to thieves, robbers and beggars as well. He sent messages, received information and dropped hints. He not only sought information about Sursinh and his band but he also spread the rumours that Sursinh’s activities were known to the armies of both Ratnanagari and Suvarnapur. He spread word in the villages and hamlets that armies of the two native states along with British forces were lying in wait for Sursinh and that they would capture him early that morning before he could do what he intended to do. It was difficult to locate Sursinh in the forest at night. But news of Harbhamji’s activities reached Sursinh. Sursinh and his men lost some of their determination and courage. The mukhis and guards of all the surrounding villages became alert to the imminent danger and prepared themselves to meet any eventuality. Harbhamji, devoted to Vidya Chatura, was fearless enough to move among the wild animals of the forest at night. He was also cautious and farsighted and could strategise and plan like an expert chess player. He spent most of the night moving from place to place. Finally he selected a perfect spot near the river which allowed him to receive messages under cover and, when necessary, join the other parties. Harbhamji knew that Sursinh would also locate himself at a place from where he could coordinate the movements of Pratapsinh, Vaghji and Bhimji. Shrewdly anticipating Sursinh’s movements, Harbhamji selected a cluster of ruins from where he could shadow Sursinh. It was already four in the morning when Harbhamji and his men came to halt in the ruins. They lit a small fire and rested their mounts. They put fodder for the horses and massaged their tired bodies. The men lit their bidis to refresh themselves and sat talking softly among themselves. Harbhamji sat on a boulder at the entrance of the ruins. As he sat massaging his horse and occasionally joining in the conversation of his men, his eyes scanned the horizon. Everyone waited anxiously for the day to break. As if also impatient to meet them, as they spoke, the first rays of the sun prised open the doors of night and the first light of day coloured the eastern sky.
chapters.summary: Harbhamji cleverly positions his men near the river, strategically anticipating Sursinh's movements and spreading disinformation as both sides anxiously await the coming dawn.

chapters.title: An Encounter with the Outlaws
paragraphs: An Encounter with the Outlaws The carriage moved on at a steady pace with the mounted soldiers riding alongside, encircling it in a protective cordon. They had covered a distance of about four miles when the reign of night came to an end. Except for the creaking and lurching of the carriage on the uneven dust roads, the sounds of the bullocks’ hooves and the trotting of horses, the rustling and snapping of dry branches against the moving carriage and the crowing of roosters in distant villages, the forest was silent. Kumud Sundari was in pleasant and deep sleep. The carriage driver held on to the reins and the prod firmly, but he, too, seemed to be dozing. The soldiers were alert and talked in low voices among themselves. A soft light spread upon the earth. In this first light, the colours of leaves and flowers could not yet be discerned, but their silhouettes were taking shape. As light slowly began to spread across the sky from the east, the stars could no longer be seen. At that hour, the soldiers accompanying Kumud Sundari were surprised to see Manchatura approach with some other riders. Abdullah apprised them of the situation. Both parties merged and moved forward with the carriage. Old Manchatura gently raised the curtains of the carriage and peered inside—Kumud Sundari was still fast asleep. He lowered the curtains and joined the group of riders. The soldiers grew more alert now; their hands rested impatiently upon their weapons, ready to draw them. As night lifted its veil of darkness to usher in the day, the dramatic reality of the forest burst forth. Shrubs laden with red, yellow and white flowers swayed in the dawn breeze. Fields on either side of their path were harvested.

Fields which had exhausted their fecundity seemed to be in repose, regenerating themselves like women exhausted after childbirth. As the gossamer light of dawn spread through the forest freeing it from the slumber of night, the tops of the tallest trees caught the first rays of the sun. The dreaded nocturnal predators disappeared and beautiful, delicate birds of bright plumage took their place. They flew from tree to tree, chirping and singing melodiously. The male and the female of the species played their own games of love and desire. Mother birds fed their young ones; their doting love was an example for other animals. It was a new day. The sky was clear and the forest no longer appeared impregnable. The soft breeze and morning light entered through the drawn curtains of the carriage and played on Kumud’s closed eyelids. She opened her still sleep-laden eyes. Raising herself up a little on her elbows, she rubbed delicate fingers on her eyelids. She was fully awake now. Kumud took out Vanleela’s note from the folds of her blouse. She read it hurriedly at first—the letter was a true reflection of ever affectionate and playful Vanleela. Kumud read the letter again, this time pondering over each word. She re-read important parts for the third time. The note described in detail the plan hatched by Pramaddhan and Krishna Kalika. She was pained by her husband’s deception. Kumud realised that Pramaddhan, incapable of any reflection, not only suspected her of infidelity but that in his desire to take revenge and punish her, he was ready to commit even greater crimes. And that he was still under Krishna Kalika’s evil influence—this whole plan was a part of their illicit alliance. This knowledge pierced her like a thorn. She was so far from him, but the searing pain was immediate. Oh, he indulges himself unrestrained, and yet he suspects me and wants his revenge! Is this justice? Has he decided to discredit me once I am gone? What will Devi and Alak behn think of me? What will my father-in-law make of all this? This news will also travel to Gunial. Should I turn back and return to Suvarnapur? Will not truth emerge triumphant? In her distress, Kumud remembered these lines from Nalakhyan:

O’ Lord, You are the herald of truth But I am not part of that truth Lord, what are the deeds that caused this birth? What could be worse than being a thief? I will be accused of a crime much worse than what Damayanti had to face, thought Kumud. How will I face anyone after this? God, You are my last resort. She wiped her tears and parted the curtains of the carriage. She saw new soldiers and then to her surprise, she saw Manchatura leading them. Alert to any movement inside the carriage, Manchatura immediately drew up his horse beside the carriage. ‘Behn, are you well?’ ‘Yes, Dadaji, but why are you here?’ Kumud held up the curtain and craned her neck out to converse with him. ‘Gunasundari and Sundar are at Manoharpuri. There was some danger in your path, and so I came with some men to protect you.’ Kumud was surprised. ‘Danger! What kind of danger?’ ‘Don’t be afraid, behn. We have so many men protecting you that they would not dare come near you.’ Manchatura changed the topic and asked, ‘Are your in-laws well?’ ‘Yes, father-in-law has been made the Karbhari. Yesterday he was presented with the robes.’ ‘Oh, that is very good! You must also be feeling proud and acting haughty?’ the old man laughed. ‘Dadaji, do your children understand what it is to be haughty? My parents-in-law send their pranam to you.’ Suddenly, a loud shout was heard from the banks of the Subhadra. The soldiers drew their weapons at once and stood like a fortress around the carriage which had come to a halt. Their faces were flushed with rushing blood. Manchatura sat up straight on his horse, his old frame trembling with rising valour as he drew his sword and raised it in the air. ‘Be alert, men. We shall send them to hell. Do not be scared, Kumud behn, I will be close by you. Abdullah, look around for a place, we shall halt here.’ They took out their guns and loaded them. Kumud Sundari was now visibly frightened, yet mustering all her equanimity she asked,

‘What is it, Dadaji, what has happened?’ even as her eyes searched in all directions for signs of danger. ‘Nothing. Do not be scared. Withdraw your head inside the carriage and don’t look out. It’s just some people shouting in the distance.’ The shouts grew louder, the noises came closer, gunshots were heard, their smoke rising above the tree tops; animals ran helter- skelter and birds took flight, squawking shrilly. Kumud shivered and broke out in cold sweat, her heart beat faster and she felt her limbs going numb. Abdullah rode ahead and looked closely in the direction from which the sounds of skirmishes were coming. He could see a rider approaching them at a gallop. Abdullah recognised him; he was from Fatehsinh’s group. The soldier rode up to Abdullah and breathlessly gave him the news. Abdullah took him to Manchatura. The rider greeted Manchatura with a salute of his right hand. ‘Victory to Maharaja Maniraj! His authority is stamped all over this forest. The outlaws recognised the extent of our readiness in the morning. Every village, including those in British territory, is on the alert. Those rascals have not been able to come together. Mukhi Patel is patrolling the path between the banyan tree and the river. Chandandas saw him and ran away; the bania realised he was outmatched. Vaghji has not ventured anywhere near the banyan tree and is still hiding among the mango trees, waiting for his chance. Fatehsinh encountered Bhimji and his men, but they did not confront Fatehsinh and disappeared into the taad forest. We, too, decided not to confront them. There was a man with a drum stationed near the bridge. We captured him. The man began to beat his drum. Bhimji and Pratapsinh responded to his call and rushed out. The drummer was in the territory of Suvarnapur. We came face to face with Pratapsinh and his men.’ ‘Was there a fight?’ Manchatura asked impatiently. ‘Pratapsinh demanded to know why we had captured the drummer. Fatehsinh retorted, “Go away! Who are you to ask us questions?” Fatehsinh said that Sursinh and his two sons had turned outlaws and that we had warrants for their arrest from the British and from Bhupsinh. He said, “We are authorised to move freely within the territories of all three states. This drummer is a companion of the outlaws and therefore we have taken him into our custody”.’ ‘What happened next?’ Abdullah asked in Hindustani. ‘Fatehsinh told Pratapsinh, “You fellows also appear to be outlaws. Tell me who you are, or else I will have to arrest you as well”.’ ‘Very good, Fatehsinh!’ Abdullah said, twirling his moustache. ‘Phir kya hua?’ ‘Pratapsinh turned mellow and said, “We are on our way to Bhadreshwar. We do not know any outlaws. This drummer is with us and we are going to make an offering of the drum to Mahadev”.’ Manchatura laughed, ‘Hah! Just hear that scoundrel!’ ‘Fatehsinh said, “Whatever it is, we are not going to release this man or return his drum”. Then he shouted out his command to us: “All of them are from the gang of outlaws—capture them alive or kill all the scoundrels!”’ ‘Very good, Fatehsinh. Your deeds truly justify your name,’ said Abdullah. ‘Phir kya hua?’ ‘Our men rushed in and fired a few gunshots. Pratapsinh’s men ran away. ‘The cowards!’ exclaimed Manchatura. ‘Pratapsinh was enraged. He was left alone, but he drew his sword to face Fatehsinh. The duel was about to begin when a few of his men who had run away came back and dragged him away. We allowed them to escape and I rushed to give you the news.’ ‘All the women have fled. Coachman, let us move on,’ said Abdullah. Manchatura said, ‘Patience, Abdullah. They will collect their forces. It is not good to move the carriage until they disperse’. He turned to the messenger and said, ‘You may go now. Send me a message if you have any news about Harbham and Sursinh. Also let me know when Vaghji retreats. Be careful, Pratapsinh is certain to strike back. There is no danger on this side of the river now. We will move on slowly but remain on this side of the river. Our men will be ready to assist you.

But you must ensure that when the scoundrels resurface they must be pushed inside Suvarnapur’s territory, so that in event of a battle, we are safe. Do not allow anyone to cross the river. We shall cross the bridge once the other side is secured and safe’. The messenger rushed back. The carriage moved on cautiously towards the bridge. Manchatura muttered to himself: If we were to fight them in the British territories, their courts will hold us guilty; the thieves will sit in judgement on the police! Whatever happens must happen inside the taad forest. He lifted the curtain and found Kumud shivering with fright. ‘Behn, half our worries are over. The scoundrels have run away. We are just being cautious.’ Manchatura was old but his vision was sharp. Towards the west, he saw a cloud of dust rising. He would need Fatehsinh and Mukhi to face the new danger. At his command the group moved swiftly and reached the bridge. Fatehsinh had secured the bridge from the opposite side and called out, ‘Don’t worry—all the flies are gone’. Manchatura signalled towards the west. They saw a lone rider approaching them. Buddhidhan’s soldiers accompanying Kumud Sundari immediately recognised the man. One of them asked, ‘Maharaj, what are you doing here?’ Shankar Maharaj replied, ‘Do not worry. Some men from my village will come following me. We are going to meet Sursinh. Understood?’ ‘Proceed. May victory be yours! Return soon.’ Manchatura, who understood nothing of what was said, quietly asked Buddhidhan’s soldier and was satisfied. Shankar Maharaj and his men crossed the river. Sursinh had nothing but bad news. Chandandas was the first to abandon. Bhimji was separated from the rest, and the other groups retreated without Vaghji and Pratap. Every village knew that forces of Buddhidhan and Vidya Chatura had come together to pursue the outlaws. If Sursinh were to stick to the plan, his destruction was certain. Just then Shankar Maharaj came and joined him. Sursinh felt somewhat reassured to see him. Sursinh, Vaghji, Pratapsinh and Shankar Maharaj accompanied by their brave men moved swiftly. Their force was awe-inspiring. Shankar murmured to himself: As he breathes, the mountains crumble Clouds roll into the abyss As he walks, the earth quivers We have seen such a man fall Praise the Lord! Look at these men! Despite such hardship, the earth trembles when they move. They have had nothing to eat for four days, their clothes are in tatters, and yet they move with such pride! They are my friends. If I serve the King, I shall be a traitor to my friend. But do I have a choice? Will I be able to feed myself otherwise? No. But then I have also eaten the salt of my King. Sursinh abruptly came to a halt, stood still and asked, ‘Shankar, do you hear horses in the distance?’ Everyone stopped. They strained their ears and peered closely in the direction Sursinh pointed. Shankar Maharaj said, ‘We are hallucinating. What are you scared of? Come on, let’s move.’ ‘No, no, Shankar ...’ ‘Forget your nays. There is no one. The carriage is on the other side of the bridge. All we need to do is capture Kumud Sundari. I have seen everything myself.’ Pratap was happy to hear this. ‘It is true. Let’s not delay.’ Everyone moved ahead, but Sursinh kept glancing at his back; he was not convinced. Shankar Maharaj drew his horse close to Sursinh and said, ‘Bha, your apprehension is not unfounded. These young boys don’t know anything. Fatehsinh and Mukhi Patel are waiting for us. We should take a detour towards the south, cross the road and attack the carriage from behind. Oh, yes, and we might also meet Bhimji’, Shankar added. Sursinh was drawn to the idea as iron is drawn to a magnet. ‘Yes, let’s move on, it’s broad daylight now.’

Sursinh galloped ahead, followed by his family and associates. They took a detour towards the south, crossed the road and entered the territory of Suvarnapur. None of them realised that they were now in territories administered by Buddhidhan. Shankar Maharaj had led them away from the British territories and was pleased with himself. Manchatura saw them approaching from a distance and immediately alerted all the groups. Fatehsinh guarded the northern and the eastern sides. A cloud of dust followed Sursinh at some distance—it was Harbhamji and his group. They came galloping to catch up with Sursinh and his band as Sursinh entered the territories of Suvarnapur. In no time at all, Harbhamji stood with his men between Kumud Sundari’s carriage and Sursinh’s band. Sursinh realised that his plans were botched. Any attempt to capture Kumud Sundari now was certain to result in death. He whispered to Shankar Maharaj, ‘Let us turn back. We have lost the game. We could have engaged them in battle after capturing Kumud Sundari. It is futile to imagine that we can engage them in battle, overpower them and also capture Kumud’. The logic of the experienced outlaw was accurate. But Shankar’s intention was to thwart him from acting upon it. Only if Sursinh were to attack the carriage with his men would the defenders respond; only then could Shankar reveal his true loyalties and help realise Buddhidhan’s strategy. Vidya Chatura’s men were unlikely to make the first move if Sursinh refrained from attacking the carriage; without their help, Shankar was powerless to capture the outlaws. He pretended not to have heard Sursinh, and raising his sword, he called out to Sursinh’s men, ‘What are you waiting for? Never again will we get such an opportunity. There are only a few of them guarding the carriage—just drag her out. Come, let’s charge!’ and Shankar suddenly charged towards the carriage. Seeing him, Sursinh’s companions also charged forward. It was too late for Sursinh to rein them in, so he followed them. Shankar fired blanks from his gun; the other outlaws followed his example and fired bullets. Astride their galloping horses, they felt the blood rushing through their veins and could no longer be restrained. Sursinh’s eyes searched desperately for Bhimji, but saw no one coming to his aid. As Abhimanyu caught in the Chakravyuh had called out to his uncle, Bhīma: ‘Kaka Bhimsen, where are you? Come!’ Sursinh searched for Bhimji and Chandandas, his heart pleaded with them, but no one came to his rescue. Before he knew it, he was surrounded by enemies. Fatehsinh and his men faced him, while Harbhamji with his men blocked his path from the rear. The carriage was beyond reach of even a bullet. Some soldiers of Suvarnapur flanked his right side. In a climactic moment, even cowards turn brave and the brave are filled with valour. The Rajput saw that victory was but a distant dream—at this moment, nothing but his own valour would come to his aid. As he braced himself, Sursinh’s eyes bulged fearfully, his brows creased, blood rushed through his throbbing veins; he was ready to jump down from his horse and charge on foot. He raised his sword high and gave the clarion call: ‘What are you waiting for, brothers! Charge! It is victory or death! Charge!’ Sursinh’s valour caught on like a forest fire. His companions shouted in response, ready to attack. With his sons Vaghji and Pratap flanking him on either side, Sursinh attacked Fatehsinh. The blow of his sword was so powerful that if Fatehsinh had failed to protect himself with his shield, he would have been cut into two. There was a deep cut in the shield. As soon as Sursinh had made the first strike, Shankar Maharaj called out, ‘Victory to Maharana Bhupsinh!’ and he and his men separated from the outlaws. His loyalty was revealed like a flash of lightning. ‘Sursinh, you and I are friends. But I must be true to my salt. I befriended you to serve the King of Suvarnapur. You are surrounded. You are like a mighty elephant that has fallen into a ditch and is waiting to be chained. Either you court death, or you surrender. There is no third option. Your valour is undisputed. No one can deny you the glory that is rightly yours. Bhupsinh did not take over your garas, you have no animosity towards him; he, too, recognises your worth. Even Shathrai, now fallen, knows of Rana Bhupsinh’s generosity. You are a citizen of Bhupsinh’s kingdom. Even if you shed a drop of blood in his territory you would be committing a crime; you would forfeit the right to obtain pardon from our compassionate Rana. I am not a traitor. But

I must serve my Rana. If you surrender, I will fall at his feet, sing your praises and prove that my friendship was not deceit. If you choose not to surrender, I am free to act. By not surrendering, you will also commit a crime towards your associates. Your actions will also deny them the chance of a pardon. You will be responsible for their futile death. The curses of their wives and children will haunt you for births to come like the sin of killing a brahmin. These two are your sons— they are in the prime of youth, they too will meet a pointless death; you will have no one left to carry forward your name, and your blood line will be destroyed. Hence, I tell you and your men, there are only two choices: surrender or death. Choose what seems more desirable. It is a moment of choice. Victory to Maharana Bhupsinh!’ Everyone was stunned by this unexpected turn of events. As soon as Shankar Maharaj finished his speech, his men and Maniraj’s soldiers encircled the outlaws, their rifles ready to fire. Ratnanagari’s forces were emboldened by Shankar Maharaj’s revelation of his loyalties. The outlaws lost their nerve. They were starving, weary and in tatters. Sursinh and Bhimji had egged them on with a promise that Kumud Sundari was about to fall into their hands. When they discovered that morning that their enemies had out-manoeuvred them, they turned despondent. The disappearance of Bhimji and Chandandas further depressed their morale. Vaghji and Pratap brought them the news that all the surrounding villages had been alerted to their presence. They had briefly found new vigour and hope when Shankar Maharaj joined them with his forces. Sursinh’s ultimate call to their valour had prepared them for a fight to death. But Shankar’s treachery completely devastated their morale. His long speech further dampened their spirits. They saw that by remaining with Sursinh, they would serve neither his nor their own interest. To challenge a well-fed, well-armed force with their blunt and broken weapons was like jumping blindly into raging fire. One man came forward, folded his hands in respect and addressed Sursinh: ‘Bapu! There is nothing now left of this battle. The Karbhari’s daughter has escaped from your hands like Devaki’s infant girl who flew out of Kansa’s hands. Only the living can obtain riches. Shankar is right. Our thirst will not be quenched by jumping into a dry well; we will only jump to our deaths. Each one of us has a wife and children back home. Hitherto, we pledged our lives to you because we believed we could be of some use to you. But now, surrender is the only option. We will gain nothing in death. Bapu, hitherto, we have always obeyed you. Today, we plead that you follow us. Shankar Maharaj, our life and death is now in your hands. I surrender my sword to you.’ Some outlaws immediately followed him. Others stood in a quandary, debating their choice. To Pratapsinh it was clear that he would not be able to lay even a finger on Kumud Sundari; seeing his opportunity, he quietly slunk away. All eyes were on the small heap of arms at the feet of Shankar’s horse. Hesitant, full of fear and misgiving, gradually the other outlaws came forward one by one and added their arms to the growing heap. Those who had surrendered stood aside, trying to avoid Sursinh’s wrathful gaze, shrinking in their skins with shame and mortification. Two of Shankar’s men picked up the surrendered arms. All eyes were on Sursinh. Sursinh felt bleak, despondent and full of helpless rage. His fate had turned against him. His men had deserted him; he looked at them with disdain. His legs restlessly grazed the sides of his horse. He looked for Pratap, and finding him gone, silently addressed his son: If you live my son, take revenge. There was only one man left by his side—his son Vaghji. This gave him some solace; he felt proud of Vaghji. Sursinh saw death in the face. He was merciful that even at this moment of death, his Rajput valour had not deserted him. As he sat up erect, squaring his shoulders and arching his back, his horse, too, reared up on its hind legs, neighing loudly as if to encourage his master. Sursinh touched Vaghji lightly on the shoulder, gave Shankar a scathing look and turned his horse around. He found Harbhamji blocking his way. Harbhamji’s strike of the previous day was still fresh in his mind. He turned his horse away from Harbhamji, and quite suddenly, without warning, Sursinh charged full speed into the circle formed by Shankar’s men with his sword raised high. His visage was fearful, his eyes burned like the very fires of hell. His adversaries looked on petrified, breaking ranks to let him pass. Sursinh’s men felt ashamed and sorely repented their surrender. Vaghji became his father’s bard and cried: ‘Bapa, you are fearless! Bapa, there is none as brave as you! Your enemies tremble! The earth trembles! Victory be yours, Bapa! May your Rajput blood prevail!’ Sursinh felt a rush of blood in his head and heart. He saw Shankar Maharaj before him. ‘Traitor!’ he roared, kicking his horse’s flanks—the horse jumped over Shankar and his mount like lightning as Sursinh’s sword pointed straight at Shankar’s chest. Everyone watching was stunned by the Rajput’s valour and dazzled by his swordsmanship. Sursinh astride his leaping horse looked like a lion that had caught an elephant by its neck. His long, double-edged sword seemed to have pierced Shankar’s body. Everyone took Shankar for dead. But when Sursinh charged upon him like death itself, the brahmin, familiar with Sursinh’s techniques, moved his body ever so slightly and raised his left hand, allowing the sword to pass through harmlessly without touching him. He swiftly caught Sursinh’s sword-wielding arm and, in a flash, cut it off with a powerful blow of his sword. Sursinh’s right hand fell to the ground like a cut branch, drenching him and his horse with warm blood. At that very moment, Vaghji brought down his sword to cut Shankar into pieces. But Harbhamji, ever alert, rushed in to thwart Vaghji’s blow in mid-air and there was a loud clanking noise as the two swords struck each other and sparks flew. Vaghji’s sword slipped from his hand and flew up in the air. Everyone moved away to save their head. The sword fell harmlessly to the ground and was picked up by someone. Vaghji was without his sword, but true to his name, like a leaping tiger he jumped his horse over everyone’s heads. Mount and rider flew like Hanuman crossing the sea. The horse regained its balance as it landed and galloped away to safety with its rider. The others could only watch in awe. Weakened by the sudden loss of blood, Sursinh had fallen from his horse; he was alive but unconscious. Shankar Maharaj’s men quickly bandaged his arm to contain the bleeding, made a stretcher with the long cloth of their turbans and carried him off towards Suvarnapur. Calls of ‘Victory to Maharaja Bhupsinh!’ rang through the surrounding villages. Vidya Chatura’s soldiers were all praise for Shankar Maharaj, Sursinh and Vaghji. Together they moved towards Kumud Sundari’s carriage, proclaiming victory.
chapters.summary: Kumud Sundari's carriage journey becomes fraught with danger as outlaws emerge, leading to intense skirmishes and a dramatic confrontation in the forest.

chapters.title: Smouldering Embers
paragraphs: Smouldering Embers Abdullah, Fatehsinh and their men went ahead to stop the charge of Sursinh and his men while Manchatura stayed back with a chosen few to protect Kumud Sundari. He was alert to the slightest danger, his eyes were focused on the battle and yet he observed all four directions. His body felt reinvigorated, his mind sharp, his forehead was furrowed as his eyes scanned the scene like a telescope, his white moustache twitched in anticipation—he looked like a lion ready to leap upon his prey. He held the reins of his horse in one hand and fidgeted with his sword with the other. As brave old Manchatura prepared himself for battle, his legs impatiently awaited the signal to nudge his horse into action. Kumud Sundari raised the curtain of her carriage time and again. She closely watched her grandfather’s changing expressions and from them tried to gauge the fate of the battle. Manchatura was so engrossed that he did not relate any news of the battle to Kumud. The soldiers guarding her tensely also did not talk among themselves. The driver of the carriage sat alert, holding the reins firmly, ready to move at a word. His bullocks, which could run as fast as horses, sensed the tension and were ready to gallop. But right now it was futile to move the carriage forward or backward, so they watched and waited. The men, whose energies were completely focussed on the outlaws, could think of nothing else. At that moment, weary, alone, aggrieved by Pramaddhan, Kumud’s heart, too, turned an outlaw—it wandered restlessly in search of solace; it accompanied Chandrakant in search of Sarasvatichandra through this dangerous terrain; it trembled at the thought of the ignominy that evil Kalika would have heaped on her at her in-laws’ house. It was as if Kumud were in a double bind: caught by the outlaws and defeated by the machinations of Pramaddhan and Krishna Kalika, her heart sought a way out. Time and again, she would impatiently lift the curtains to look outside and lower them again to withdraw inside and weep. She stared blankly at the canopy of her carriage, read Vanleela’s note again and again, gazed at the trees, listened to the waters of the Subhadra rushing past. She imagined the cool depths of the river, looked vacantly at the pillars of the stone bridge and sighed, and yet, she regained her composure from time to time. Sarasvatichandra! Where are you in this perilous terrain? Why must you suffer so? Have you, like Dhruv, felt slighted? What faith moves you to this penance? Are you enthused by the aspirations of a Robinson Crusoe? Or are you like Emperor Babar who sang poems in the forest when he lost his empire? You once wrote: My path is as unbridled as kites that fly Like them, I too shall soar A kite is attached to a string, and thus grounded, but you do not want even that. Neither above nor below Is there succour to be found Destitute and forlorn am I For whose sake do you suffer so? It is I, the wretched, I am the cause of your suffering. I shall be like the forest breeze, invisible, but Carrying aloft the fragrance called Kumud My forehead is inscribed with the wealth of the world And its renunciation I am the people, and I the king But in my heart, only you reside. That wretched Kumud! Why wasn’t she born a stone! Oh jewel among men, what did you see in this lustreless Kumud? Why do you offer penance for her ill fortunes?

O’ Jehangir, your Noorjahan is lustreless Why do you long for her? Even Pramaddhan does not care for her Why do you love her so? Jehangir becomes an ascetic He walks with animals in the wild He longs for worthless Kumud even as He forsakes the palace for the forest As Kumud wept, she fell into an uneasy sleep. She woke up, startled by a sound. She thought of Pramaddhan: Oh my husband and master, I would have been fortunate if you had put your sword to my neck. I cannot be with the one who pines for me. I crush my desires and cling to you, but even you are not mine. I deserve this punishment. If you had killed me, my punishment would have been complete. But why should one as wretched as I receive such good fortune? Dear Vanleela, why do you feel sorry for me? Outlaws, why have you become so heartless? Why do you let me live? Have you lost your art so completely that your bullets cannot find their mark and bring this futile existence to an end? Kumud raised the curtain and, gazing at the distant trees, murmured: Oh Lord, who will change my destiny? Who will right the wrong? But it is true—my fate is sealed on either side; even God cannot change it. She looked at the trees again and thought: Is it not possible that Chandra is hiding amid those dense trees? Who knows what all he has suffered in this forest infested with wild animals and outlaws? Whatever he endures is for my sake. He has suffered such agonies for me. And I? What have I done for him? I am ungrateful. I am cruel. I am heartless. Kumud beat her breasts in anguish, self- loathing and helpless rage. She sat up erect. Anger was unfamiliar to her heart and tongue. Her delicate features turned harsh and she wept with rage, speaking aloud: Who can be as cruel as me? I do not die to make the one who lives happy. Nor do I die for the one who longs and yearns for me. I abhor myself. Yet I don’t know how to end this miserable life! I still lust for life! Dear Chandra, you preach:

Bear with what cannot be forsaken Play the hand dealt to you ... Forget that which cannot be forgotten and Bear with reality. You may be right. But what my husband desires outweighs your wise counsel. I am a thorn in his side. He desires to be freed of me, a worthless wife. He wishes I were dead. His heart silently commands me: Die, woman! Leave me be! I, too, desire death for I know the gains it would bring. Chandra pines for me I wonder how he is today All he endures is for me Why must I then live? My death would free me from the charge of being ungrateful. The dark clouds of suspicion that hang over me will be dispelled; my parents will be freed from my abasement and ignominy. At this thought, Kumud was suddenly filled with a tranquil joy. She smiled weakly and said aloud: This life is a sea of sorrows, but death is where the sea meets land. Once I cross that path, I shall attain freedom from this wretched life. I must seek that freedom. But as this idea took root in her mind and gained strength, she heard Sarasvatichandra’s voice speaking to her: ‘Beloved Kumud, you are deceiving your soul. Only a good death gives us moksha, freedom from the cycle of births and deaths—suicide cannot grant you that freedom. To seek death is suicide. A wick that is snuffed out leaves behind odour, smoke and soot; it meets with an undesirable death. But a wick that burns itself out fully and naturally attains peace, it becomes one with the elements and attains freedom— that is moksha. Dear Kumud, to be weary of pain and to seek death is to undo the obligations and actions enjoined upon us—it is a rebellion against God’. Lost to the world, Kumud had grown completely oblivious to the danger surrounding her. She was jolted out of her reverie by loud screams and shouts. Kumud thought that the outlaws were surely upon her. Face to face with imminent and real danger, all melancholy and suicidal thoughts vanished. She instantly got up, tucked her petticoat tightly between her legs and took out the dagger that was tied at her waist. She sat up tense and alert and waited. Just then Manchatura raised the curtain and said, ‘Behn, there is no danger now. Our troops have returned triumphant’. The soldiers were celebrating Sursinh’s capture. The triumphant party now flew towards the carriage. Abdullah came forward and caught the reins of Shankar Maharaj’s horse. He addressed Manchatura in his Hindustani: ‘Bhai Sahib, this Shankar Maharaj is Buddhidhan’s man. He has bravely captured the outlaws and sent them off to Suvarnapur!’ Abdullah laughed uproariously. Manchatura and Shankar Maharaj were introduced to each other. Men from both sides introduced themselves, greeted each other and embraced joyously. Finally, Shankar Maharaj gave a graphic description of the morning’s events. He told them how he had followed Buddhidhan’s instructions and policies while dealing with the outlaws. He had been trained by Buddhidhan and he was pleased and proud that he had passed the ultimate test—Maharana Bhupsinh’s last enemy had been subjugated. All the men were in a celebratory mood. Manchatura addressed them: ‘My brave soldiers! Step down from your horses and give them some rest; give them fresh water from the Subhadra. But Mukhi, I will have to exclude you from this rest. Gunasundari must be waiting anxiously; rush to Manoharpuri with the good news. Tell her that in the next three to four hours we will be there with Kumud’. But before he had completed the sentence, Mukhi Patel had already disappeared down the road to Manoharpuri. All the others got down from their horses. They patted them, gave them water, drank some themselves, lit their bidis, chewed on betel nut and chatted. But Shankar Maharaj remained astride his horse and moved about, looking into the distance. Manchatura walked up to the carriage and said to Kumud, ‘The soldiers are taking rest. You too come out and take some fresh air, take a walk near the river. Fatehsinh, have this carpet spread on the river bank; Kumud will sit there and refresh herself ’. As Manchatura took Kumud’s hand and helped her out of the carriage, he felt a sense of accomplishment. This handsome, proud old man led his delicately beautiful granddaughter towards the carpet and made her sit on it with affection. He sat down beside her. Harbhamji also sat with them. Few others sat at some distance. Different parts of the surrounding landscape were pointed out to Kumud. Water was brought for her in a silver pitcher. Manchatura was aware of Shankar Maharaj’s uneasy movements. He got up and went to him, patted his horse and asked, ‘Shankar, why don’t you also relax?’ Shankar got off his horse and said, ‘Bhai Sahib, there is nothing to worry about. But both sons of Sursinh are alive. I am not concerned about Vaghji; he is brave and will never commit a cowardly act. But Pratap is tricky; he is evil and debased. He has no companions but, like Ravana, he can act stealthily and commit lowly acts. Where can he be? I wonder if he is not lurking somewhere nearby. While we relax he should not come and attack suddenly. I was just being cautious.’ Manchatura smiled with disdain and asked, ‘Is he so stupid as to do something so brazen?’ ‘We should not treat him with such contempt. Pratap has vowed to capture Kumud Sundari. His intelligence works treacherously. I know him well.’ ‘All right, all of us will keep an eye.’ Manchatura and Shankar Maharaj walked towards the carpet where Kumud sat. He posted a man each to guard the four directions. It was only about seven in the morning, but in the forest it looked as if it was already nine. The sun rose through the tall broad-leafed trees. Its light hurt the eye. The sky looked like an immense ground filled with sparkling sand. Sunlight spread upon the earth, the trees and the riverbank. The river flowed under the bridge, swirling playfully around its pillars. Kumud Sundari stood up and walked closer to the bank. She looked into the gurgling waters; the bottom of the river was not visible.
