She asked Manchatura, ‘Dadaji, how deep is the river?’ Harbhamji went up to her and said, ‘Behn, near the bridge the water is deep, at least as high as three-four fully grown men’.

As Kumud walked along the river, she silently contemplated the deep waters and thought: Sarasvatichandra, have you been adventurous? Have you jumped into the river? She looked at the river intently, as if searching for him. Her eyes came to focus on a point on its eddies and she murmured: My Jehangir has become a mendicant He floats with the fishes Pining for worthless Kumud He abandoned his palace Only to be washed away A jewel has fallen into your lap, O’ Subhadra, care for it well O’ Subhadra, you are clever and generous. Don’t let your waters drown him. Keep him safe. Hold him to your bosom. Why do you seem so full of joy? He is a prince among men: Hold him close to your bosom You would be a fool not to rejoice Holding this jewel against your heart You owe your glow to this union You need not be jealous of me, Subhadra. I have a husband who has no love for me. My beloved loves me deeply but I have no right to love him. I belong neither to my husband nor to my beloved. Forsaking me, my husband turns to another Having abandoned me, my beloved seeks me anew What the lover seeks is futile: I am his. Having given my body to my husband How do I reclaim it now? The husband who forsakes me Is still the master of my body While the lover cannot give up The ties that bind us If I give up this useless body If I burn this love to ashes

O’ river, help me forget The love of my beloved Do what you must to keep him alive If he cries upon your shores O’ river, wipe away his warm tears If he stands upon your shores Chanting my name and weeping Lonely when he remembers me, And falls asleep upon your sands, If he enters your waters to bathe, And lost in thought, is swept by your currents, O’ river, remember to be kind: Save his lonely heart. Standing in your waters, his tears merging with them, He will write upon your currents The letters of my name This is how he loves me. Such is his state because of me. Once wealthy, learned and wise He has lost his body and mind over me. Deep in the forest, he made a poem of me But I cannot hear it, and so He tosses his precious self away He pours his heart out to the creatures of the wild Writing poems of love on leaves and bark O’ river, I know this, I see this— Yet I let his tears flow unabated. I make myself love this ingrate body Why does it not singe and turn to ash? I do not seek my beloved I do not douse that divine body’s fire Take me into your arms, O’ river Give my dead body to the fish. Kumud’s heart wept without restraint. She accepted her husband’s mastery over her body. But her heart had set out like an outlaw to seek the one who ruled it. She stood perfectly calm and still as a statue on the riverbank under the bright blue skies, as her passions raged within.

She stood there delicate and fragile as a creeper. Like the moon sees its reflection in the river, she saw her bright face made lustreless by the pallor of sorrow in its waters. To Kumud it seemed as if the river’s responses were coded in that reflection. The clear, petal-like nails of her feet whispered something secretly to her soft lips and her arms, as if they were the wings about to carry her body away. By now the victory celebrations had subsided. Manchatura stood leaning upon his sword. Shankar Maharaj stood by his side, his eyes on the ravines where Kumud stood gazing into the river below. The soldiers were solemn and quiet as they awaited instructions for the onward journey. All at once, Shankar broke the spell—he suddenly dove into the gurgling waters like an eagle. ‘What happened? What happened?’ everyone cried out. They saw three figures in the river: Kumud, almost drowning, followed closely by Pratapsinh, and Shankar Maharaj swimming forcefully against the current behind them. A few others immediately jumped in, but the sheer force of the river flung them back. Manchatura was also about to dive into the river, but he realised it was futile—he was certain he would not be able to reach Kumud and he would lose her forever. Instead, he leapt onto his horse and rushed in the direction in which Kumud was being carried by the flow. Manchatura planned to jump into the water and bring her out as she neared the riverbank. Others acted on their own counsel. A few furlongs further downstream the river took a sudden turn. Some rushed towards that spot. A few ran towards Manoharpuri. The carriage remained where it was parked. The coachman was from Suvarnapur; he knew of Pramaddhan’s secret life. He went to the spot where Kumud Sundari had stood just moments ago and examined it carefully. He looked down at the fiercely flowing river. Neither Kumud Sundari nor any of the others who had followed her could now be seen. He examined the spot carefully once again and wondered if she had fallen into the river because the edge broke, because she was dragged in by the outlaw, or because, weary of Pramaddhan’s ways, she had attempted suicide? The coachman could not decide. He rolled up the carpet which had been laid out for her to sit on and put it back into the carriage. He picked up Kumud Sundari’s belongings and a bundle of papers and gave it to a soldier from Ratnanagari, saying, ‘Give these to Gunasundariba; it is useless to carry them back to Suvarnapur. I have no hope of their return given the force of the river. If God wills it, she will be saved. We will go on to Manoharpuri then. If something untoward happens, I will return to Suvarnapur. In that case, take her belongings to Manoharpuri. We will wait at the bridge for news’. The soldier was already in tears. He took the bundle and climbed up on his horse. The coachman yoked the bullocks. They stood waiting despondently on the bridge. The soldiers spoke of Kumud Sundari’s kindness. One of them said, ‘Today is a black day. We had vanquished the outlaws, and now this had to happen! She was so young and yet so wise. Kumud Sundari was a divine being. How could she live on this earth? Wherever she went, riches followed in her wake. Whenever she spoke, pearls fell from her mouth. She was a goddess reincarnate. Buddhidhanbhai could vanquish Shathrai because of her grace!’ The coachman replied, ‘What you say is true. She certainly had traces of the divine. Even one as haughty as Alak behn walked in her steps. It was as if she cast a spell around her—anyone who saw her and spoke to her felt affectionate and respectful towards her. Buddhidhanbhai holds her in such high esteem. She was so pure one could have bathed her feet in milk and drunk it as nectar. She was so virtuous one would wish to be born of her. Oh God, You are all merciful, let no harm come to her! Do what You will but return Kumud Sundari to us unharmed! How will we ever show our face to anyone again if we don’t find her?’ The ascetics carried away Sarasvatichandra. The river carried Kumud away. Their paths were different, but their destination was one. Many eyes followed after them. Many searched for them. But they could only imagine what God willed.
chapters.summary: After a fierce battle, Kumud Sundari, protected by Manchatura, struggles with profound despair and contemplates her fate amidst the lingering dangers.
